While curing efficiency plays a role, the intrinsic mechanical properties of the aromatic matrix and the nanofiller reinforcement qualitatively drive the modulus upward relative to standard aliphatic epoxy systems.

title: Carbon fiber/epoxy composites: effect of zinc sulphide coated carbon nanotube on thermal and mechanical properties

additives.name: ZnS coated functionalized multi-walled carbon nanotubes

processing_history: MWCNT functionalized with HNO3/H2SO4, coated with ZnS via microwave hydrothermal synthesis (150 °C, 25 min). Fillers dispersed in ethyl alcohol via ultrasonication (10 min), added to resin, stirred at 70 °C until alcohol evaporation. Hand lay-up with 3 layers carbon fiber, vacuum bagged for 24 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test using EMIC DL-1000 machine, crosshead speed 10 mm/min, gauge length 78 mm, room temperature.
hierarchical_structure: Carbon fiber laminated composite with epoxy matrix modified with 0.2 wt% MWCNTf-ZnS.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The material system comprises a carbon fiber laminated composite featuring an Epoxy resin MC 1152 matrix cured with a hardener. The epoxy matrix is modified with 0.2 wt% zinc sulfide (ZnS) coated functionalized multi-walled carbon nanotubes, where the nanotubes underwent functionalization with HNO3/H2SO4 followed by ZnS coating via microwave hydrothermal synthesis at 150 °C for 25 minutes. These fillers were dispersed in ethyl alcohol using ultrasonication for 10 minutes, added to the resin, and stirred at 70 °C to facilitate solvent evaporation. The composite was fabricated using a hand lay-up technique incorporating three layers of carbon fiber reinforcement, followed by vacuum bagging for 24 hours to consolidate the laminate. The Young's modulus was characterized by uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature using a crosshead speed of 10 mm/min and a gauge length of 78 mm.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The inclusion of three layers of continuous carbon fiber provides substantial reinforcement due to the high intrinsic stiffness of the fibers, which primarily governs the composite load-bearing capacity. The crosslinked epoxy network formed by the resin and hardener offers a rigid matrix support, while the incorporation of multi-walled carbon nanotubes adds nanoscale reinforcement. Furthermore, the functionalization of the nanotubes with HNO3/H2SO4 and the ZnS coating likely enhance interfacial adhesion between the fillers and the matrix, improving stress transfer efficiency. The vacuum bagging process for 24 hours reduces void content and ensures better consolidation, thereby increasing the effective load-bearing cross-section. Decreasing Factors: The hand lay-up processing method may introduce variability in fiber alignment and potentially higher void content compared to automated manufacturing techniques, which can reduce the effective modulus. Additionally, the aggressive acid functionalization of the carbon nanotubes may introduce structural defects into the graphitic lattice, slightly diminishing their intrinsic stiffness relative to pristine nanotubes. There is also a risk that residual ethyl alcohol from the dispersion process, if not completely evaporated during stirring at 70 °C, could act as a plasticizer within the epoxy matrix, lowering its rigidity. Dominant Factor: The continuous carbon fiber reinforcement is the dominant factor determining the overall Young's modulus, as the rule of mixtures dictates that the high volume fraction and superior stiffness of the continuous fibers outweigh the contributions from the nanofillers or matrix modifications. While the matrix modification and processing history critically influence interfacial properties and matrix-dominated regions, the macroscopic stiffness is primarily defined by the architecture and properties of the carbon fiber laminate.

title: Effect of adsorption, hardener, and temperature on mechanical properties of epoxy nanocomposites with functionalized graphene: A molecular dynamics study
processing_history: Molecular dynamics simulation using LAMMPS. NPT/NVT ensembles. Strain rate 0.7 ps^-1. Tensile test in Y direction at 300 K. Epoxy:Hardener ratio 70:30 wt%.
hierarchical_structure: Nanocomposite with functionalized graphene oxide (1 wt% oxide groups).

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting nanocomposite formed by a cycloaliphatic epoxy matrix cured with diethyltoluenediamine at a 70:30 weight ratio, incorporating 1 wt% functionalized graphene oxide as a reinforcing filler. Structural characterization indicates a nanocomposite architecture where the graphene oxide contains 1 wt% oxide groups, facilitating interaction within the network. Mechanical evaluation was conducted via molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS, where the system was equilibrated under NPT and NVT ensembles before subjecting it to a tensile test in the Y direction at 300 K with a strain rate of 0.7 ps^-1.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The rigid cycloaliphatic rings in the epoxy backbone restrict segmental rotation, enhancing intrinsic matrix stiffness, while the incorporation of graphene oxide introduces a high-modulus filler phase that significantly reinforces the composite. The functionalization of the graphene oxide with oxide groups improves interfacial adhesion, facilitating efficient stress transfer between the matrix and the filler. Additionally, the high strain rate (0.7 ps^-1) inherent to the molecular dynamics simulation limits viscoelastic relaxation times, typically resulting in an artificially elevated apparent modulus compared to quasi-static experimental conditions. Decreasing Factors: The presence of ethyl groups on the diethyltoluenediamine hardener introduces aliphatic flexibility compared to fully aromatic curing agents, which may slightly reduce the crosslink density and network rigidity. Furthermore, if the simulation temperature of 300 K approaches the glass transition temperature of the cured network, increased thermal chain mobility would act to lower the measured stiffness. Dominant Factor: The reinforcement effect of the functionalized graphene oxide within the rigid cycloaliphatic network is the dominant factor governing the mechanical response. The high aspect ratio and intrinsic modulus of the graphene sheets, coupled with improved interfacial bonding from functionalization, outweigh the flexibility introduced by the hardener's aliphatic groups, leading to a net increase in modulus relative to the neat resin, while the simulation strain rate further accentuates the stiffness measurement.

The mechanical properties were evaluated through molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS, employing NPT and NVT ensembles to conduct a tensile test in the Y direction at 300 K with a strain rate of 0.7 ps^-1.

The simulation temperature of 300 K likely places the material in the glassy state, further maximizing the modulus. Furthermore, the low filler loading of 1 wt% limits the reinforcement efficiency compared to higher concentration composites where percolation networks might form. Dominant Factor: The high crosslink density established by the 70:30 cure ratio creates a rigid three-dimensional network that qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, ensuring a high modulus characteristic of cured thermosets despite the flexible linkages in the hardener.

title: A Study of Some Mechanical Properties of Composite Materials with a Dammar-Based Hybrid Matrix and Reinforced by Waste Paper
processing_history: Composite cast with 80% Dammar hybrid resin matrix and shredded waste paper (10-20 mm length). Mixed with variable speed mixer. Uniform pressure of 27,000 N/m^2 applied. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test according to ASTM D3039 using Lrx Plus testing machine (2.5 kN force range).
hierarchical_structure: Random distribution of shredded reinforcement.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a hybrid composite material featuring a matrix blend of 80 vol% Dammar resin and 20 vol% Epoxy resin (Resoltech 1050/1055), reinforced with shredded waste paper fibers at a mass ratio of 0.41. Fabricated via a casting process, the mixture was homogenized using a variable speed mixer and consolidated under a uniform pressure of 27,000 N/m^2. The resulting hierarchical structure displays a random distribution of the 10-20 mm length shredded reinforcement within the polymer matrix, with mechanical characterization performed through uniaxial tensile testing in accordance with ASTM D3039.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of shredded waste paper introduces rigid cellulosic fibers which possess a significantly higher intrinsic stiffness compared to the resin matrix, thereby reinforcing the composite according to rule-of-mixtures principles. Additionally, the application of uniform pressure during casting likely minimizes void content and improves packing density, while the inclusion of Epoxy resin contributes to increased crosslinking density within the matrix phase. Decreasing Factors: The random distribution of the shredded reinforcement results in inefficient load transfer compared to aligned fiber architectures, reducing the effective modulus in the loading direction. Furthermore, the matrix is predominantly composed of Dammar resin (80 vol%), a natural resin typically exhibiting lower stiffness than synthetic epoxies, and the interface between the hydrophilic paper fibers and hydrophobic resin may lack optimal adhesion without coupling agents. Dominant Factor: The high mass ratio of the rigid cellulosic reinforcement serves as the primary driver for enhancing the Young's Modulus relative to the neat resin blend; however, the random orientation of the fibers and the compliance of the Dammar-rich matrix qualitatively limit the magnitude of this stiffening effect, defining the final mechanical performance.

title: Role of functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotubes on mechanical properties of epoxy-based composites at cryogenic temperature
processing_history: Oxidized MWNTs (O-MWNTs) prepared by acid mixture treatment (H2SO4:HNO3 3:1) at 110 °C. O-MWNTs added to epoxy resin, vacuum mixed for 5 min. Reacted for 4 h at 80 °C with catalyst. Curing agent D-230 added (weight ratio 100:30 to epoxy), stirred, cast into mold, cured at 80 °C for 4 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test according to ASTM D638-99 using MTS Landmark Servohydraulic test system at room temperature (RT).
hierarchical_structure: O-MWNTs reinforced epoxy composites. Some MWNTs impregnated in epoxy resin, some partially pulled out. Slightly rough fracture surface indicating slightly interfacial bonding.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises an epoxy nanocomposite formed from Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol-A resin and Polyoxypropylenediamine curing agent, reinforced with 0.5 wt% oxidized multiwalled carbon nanotubes. The nanotubes were functionalized via acid treatment at 110 °C before vacuum mixing with the resin, followed by the addition of the curing agent at a 100:30 weight ratio. The mixture was cast and cured at 80 °C for 4 hours to form a crosslinked network. Microstructural analysis indicates that the oxidized nanotubes are partially impregnated within the matrix with evidence of pull-out and a slightly rough fracture surface, suggesting moderate interfacial bonding, while mechanical properties were assessed via uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The inclusion of oxidized multiwalled carbon nanotubes provides high-stiffness reinforcement due to the intrinsic mechanical properties of the carbon nanostructures, while the acid treatment processing aims to enhance dispersion and potential chemical bonding within the matrix. The formation of a crosslinked thermoset network during the 80 °C curing cycle also contributes to structural rigidity compared to linear polymers. Decreasing Factors: The selection of Polyoxypropylenediamine as the curing agent introduces flexible aliphatic ether segments into the network backbone, significantly lowering the matrix stiffness compared to rigid aromatic curing agents. Furthermore, the observed nanotube pull-out and slightly rough fracture surface indicate imperfect interfacial adhesion, which limits stress transfer efficiency, and the low filler loading of 0.5 wt% restricts the formation of a percolating rigid network. Dominant Factor: The flexibility imparted by the polyoxypropylene curing agent combined with the limited stress transfer efficiency due to weak interfacial bonding qualitatively dominates the mechanical behavior. While the nanotubes offer reinforcement, the compliant nature of the matrix and the inability to fully utilize the filler's stiffness due to interfacial slippage determine the final modulus, keeping it lower than what would be achieved with a rigid curing agent or stronger interface.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises an epoxy network synthesized from Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol-A and Polyoxypropylenediamine, reinforced with 0.5 wt% oxidized multiwalled carbon nanotubes. title: Multiscale molecular modeling of SWCNTs/epoxy resin composites mechanical behaviour

Modulus defined as slope of stress-strain curve between strain 0.25% and 0.5%.

title: A Comparative Study on Structural, Morphological, and Tensile Properties of Binary and Ternary Epoxy Resin-Based Polymer Nanocomposites

title: Ultrasonic Velocity and Attenuation in Epoxy Resin/Granite (Marble) Powder Composite

title: The effects of CNT alignment on electrical conductivity and mechanical properties of SWNT/epoxy nanocomposites

hierarchical_structure: SWNTs aligned along stretching direction. SWNT diameter 1.2-1.5 nm, length > 2 um.

Prepared via solution casting, the SWNTs were dispersed in ethanol through sonication for 30 minutes prior to mixing with the epoxy resin and undergoing further sonication for 2 hours. The curing sequence involved adding half the BDMA hardener, semidrying the mixture, and subjecting it to repeated manual stretching at 0.5 m/s with a draw ratio of 50 applied 100 times, followed by the addition of the remaining BDMA, compression at 10 MPa for 5 minutes, and vacuum curing at room temperature for 7 days. Structural analysis indicates that the SWNTs, possessing diameters of 1.2-1.5 nm and lengths exceeding 2 μm, are aligned along the stretching direction, and the Young's modulus was characterized by tensile testing along this alignment axis at ambient temperature with a gauge length of 50 mm and speed of 15 mm/min.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The inclusion of 3.0 wt% Single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWNT) introduces a filler with exceptionally high intrinsic axial stiffness, which significantly reinforces the composite. The specific processing history involving repeated manual stretching of the semidried mixture aligns these high-aspect-ratio nanotubes parallel to the stretching direction, which corresponds to the tensile testing direction, thereby maximizing the efficiency of load transfer from the matrix to the filler. Additionally, the chemical crosslinking introduced by the BDMA hardener restricts segmental motion within the epoxy network, increasing matrix rigidity, while the compression step during processing helps minimize voids that would otherwise compromise structural integrity. Decreasing Factors: The curing process conducted at room temperature over 7 days may yield a lower degree of crosslinking conversion compared to thermal curing protocols, potentially limiting the intrinsic modulus of the epoxy matrix. Dominant Factor: The alignment of the SWNTs along the loading axis is the dominant factor determining the Young's modulus for this sample. While matrix crosslink density and potential plasticization influence the baseline properties, the extreme mechanical anisotropy of carbon nanotubes ensures that their orientation parallel to the stress direction provides a disproportionate enhancement to the composite stiffness compared to the variations induced by the matrix curing conditions.

title: Processing and Characterization of Composites Based on Hybrid Thermosets Systems
processing_history: DLP printed (365 nm, 100 μm layer thickness). UV post-treatment only (365 nm, 10 s exposure, 23 °C). Young's modulus (Flexural modulus) measured by 3-point flexural test (Shimadzu AG-X, 5-kN loading cell, 2 mm/min, 23 °C, NF EN ISO 14125).

title: Bio-Based Alternative to the Diglycidyl Ether of Bisphenol A with Controlled Materials Properties

The mixture was degassed and consolidation was achieved through compression molding under 2 tons of pressure, utilizing a stepped thermal cure cycle of 4 hours at 80 °C followed by 4 hours at 160 °C to ensure the degree of cure closely approached the theoretical maximum. title: Mechanical and low-velocity impact properties of epoxy-composite beams reinforced by MWCNTs

Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test using Standard tensile machine of Amirkabir University of Technology.

title: Hydroxyl-Terminated Triazine Derivatives Grafted Graphene Oxide for Epoxy Composites: Enhancement of Interfacial and Mechanical Properties
processing_history: GO-TCT-Tris dispersed in acetone by sonication for 1 h. Epoxy resin added and sonicated 1 h. Mixture vacuum dried 12 h. Curing agent added, stirred 15 min. Vacuum distillation. Cast into mold. Cured: 2 h at 90 °C, 2 h at 120 °C, and 4 h at 150 °C. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test on universal testing machine (Al-7000) with crosshead speed 2 mm/min, gauge length 60 mm, specimen dimensions 80x10x4 mm.
hierarchical_structure: Epoxy matrix with well-dispersed and exfoliated GO-TCT-Tris sheets (observed by SEM/TEM).

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a crosslinked epoxy network synthesized from Epoxy Resin E-51 (DGEBA) and Hardener H-256 (3,3'-diethyl-4,4'-diaminodiphenylmethane), reinforced with 0.1 wt% GO-TCT-Tris filler. The fabrication process involved dispersing the filler in acetone via sonication for 1 hour, followed by the addition of the epoxy resin and further sonication to ensure homogeneity. After vacuum drying for 12 hours, the curing agent was introduced, stirred, and subjected to vacuum distillation before casting into a mold. The system was cured using a stepped thermal protocol consisting of 2 hours at 90 °C, 2 hours at 120 °C, and 4 hours at 150 °C. Structural analysis confirmed an epoxy matrix containing well-dispersed and exfoliated GO-TCT-Tris sheets, and the mechanical properties were evaluated via uniaxial tensile testing with a crosshead speed of 2 mm/min.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The presence of rigid aromatic rings in both the DGEBA resin and the diamine hardener backbone intrinsically restricts chain segment mobility, driving the Young's modulus (E) higher. The stepped curing history promotes a high degree of crosslinking, which further constrains network deformation and enhances stiffness. Additionally, the incorporation of GO-TCT-Tris, known for its high intrinsic modulus, combined with the sonication-induced exfoliation and dispersion, facilitates efficient stress transfer between the matrix and the high-aspect-ratio nanosheets, contributing to an increase in E. Decreasing Factors: The ethyl substituents on the hardener introduce aliphatic character and steric bulk compared to unsubstituted aromatic diamines, which may increase free volume and slightly reduce packing efficiency, thereby lowering E relative to a fully rigid aromatic network. Furthermore, the low filler loading (0.1 wt%) limits the volume fraction of the stiff reinforcement phase, meaning the composite modulus is heavily weighted toward the lower modulus of the polymer matrix rather than the theoretical maximum of the filler. Dominant Factor: The high crosslink density of the aromatic epoxy matrix achieved through the multi-step thermal curing protocol is the dominant factor determining the final E, as the matrix constitutes the vast majority of the volume; while the exfoliated filler provides reinforcement, the baseline stiffness is primarily governed by the rigid, highly crosslinked network structure of the resin system.

The Young's modulus was characterized by uniaxial tensile testing on an Al-7000 universal testing machine with a crosshead speed of 2 mm/min and a gauge length of 60 mm.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The chemical composition features rigid aromatic structures in both the DGEBA resin and the diamine hardener, which intrinsically enhance chain stiffness and resistance to deformation. title: Manufacturing process improvement and mechanical modelling of multiwalled carbon nanotube/epoxy composites
processing_history: MWNT (0.5 wt-%) dispersed in Epon 862/EpiCure W (100:26.4 wt ratio) via tip sonication (ice bath). Sonication: 90 W intensity, 2 h time, 20 s pulse on, 2 s pulse off. Degassed 24 min. Cured at 177 °C for 3 h in hot press. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test (ASTM D638/D882) at 1 mm/min crosshead speed.
hierarchical_structure: MWNT/epoxy nanocomposite. Manufactured with optimised process parameters.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of a Multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWNT) reinforced epoxy nanocomposite fabricated using Epon 862 epoxy resin and EpiCure W curing agent at a weight ratio of 100:26.4. The MWNTs were incorporated at a loading of 0.5 wt% and dispersed within the resin matrix via tip sonication in an ice bath at 90 W intensity for 2 hours using a pulsed cycle, followed by a 24-minute degassing step. The composite was subsequently cured in a hot press at 177 °C for 3 hours to establish a crosslinked network structure. The Young's modulus was characterized via uniaxial tensile testing according to ASTM D638/D882 standards at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of Multiwalled carbon nanotubes introduces a filler phase with exceptionally high intrinsic stiffness, which enhances the composite modulus through load transfer mechanisms. The high-temperature curing cycle at 177 °C promotes a high degree of crosslinking within the epoxy matrix, significantly increasing the rigidity of the continuous phase. Furthermore, the intensive tip sonication processing aims to optimize nanotube dispersion, maximizing the surface area available for stress transfer between the filler and the matrix. Decreasing Factors: The relatively low filler loading of 0.5 wt% limits the volumetric contribution of the stiff nanotubes to the overall composite properties. Additionally, without explicit surface functionalization mentioned in the composition, interfacial adhesion between the nanotubes and the epoxy matrix may be suboptimal, potentially leading to interfacial slippage under load. The introduction of nanofillers also carries a risk of inducing micro-voids during processing, which can act as stress concentrators and reduce the effective load-bearing cross-section. Dominant Factor: The high crosslink density achieved through the elevated temperature curing process establishes a rigid baseline modulus for the epoxy matrix, which serves as the primary load-bearing component. However, the optimized dispersion of the high-aspect-ratio nanotubes via sonication is the dominant modifying factor that qualitatively elevates the Young's modulus above that of the neat resin, provided the interfacial stress transfer is effective.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of a thermoset epoxy network formed from Epon 862 epoxy resin and EpiCure W curing agent mixed at a weight ratio of 100 to 26.4 parts, respectively. Following dispersion, the mixture was degassed for 24 minutes and subsequently cured in a hot press at 177 °C for 3 hours. The Young's modulus was determined via uniaxial tensile testing according to ASTM D638/D882 standards at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a highly crosslinked thermoset network through the reaction of Epon 862 and EpiCure W at elevated temperatures provides a rigid matrix backbone. Although processing risks such as nanotube damage or void formation exist, the structural integrity provided by the hot-press cured thermoset matrix and the load-bearing capacity of the dispersed nanophase are the primary determinants of the Young's modulus, driving the material toward a high-stiffness regime characteristic of reinforced thermoset composites.

title: Investigating the use of natural hollow fibers from common milkweed to improve the mechanical and thermal properties of epoxy resin
processing_history: Epoxy resin and curing agent mixed in 1.6:1 ratio, homogenized at 70 °C. Blended with 15% w/w native milkweed fibers. Fibers aligned in same direction. Cast into mold, degassed under vacuum at 70 °C for 10 min. Compressed at 214 kPa at 120 °C for 120 min. Post-cured at 200 °C for 4 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test at 1 mm/min extension rate, room temperature, according to ASTM D638, using Zwick/Roell Z100 universal testing machine.
hierarchical_structure: Fiber reinforced epoxy composite. Fibers aligned in one direction. Some fibers filled with epoxy resin. Total porosity 18.4%. Cavities of about 2 nm in diameter observed in matrix.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample is a fiber-reinforced epoxy composite composed of Lindoxy 190 epoxy resin and LS-252 V curing agent mixed in a 1.6:1 mass ratio, incorporated with 15 w/w% native milkweed floss fibers. The processing protocol involved homogenizing the resin and curing agent at 70 °C, followed by blending with the fibers which were aligned in a single direction, casting into a mold, and degassing under vacuum at 70 °C for 10 minutes. The composite was subsequently compression molded at 214 kPa and 120 °C for 120 minutes and post-cured at 200 °C for 4 hours. Structural characterization reveals a morphology with unidirectionally aligned fibers, some of which are filled with epoxy resin, exhibiting a total porosity of 18.4% and nanoscale cavities approximately 2 nm in diameter within the matrix, with Young's modulus evaluated via uniaxial tensile testing at an extension rate of 1 mm/min at room temperature according to ASTM D638.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a highly crosslinked epoxy network during the 200 °C post-curing process increases the intrinsic stiffness of the matrix. Additionally, the incorporation of native milkweed fibers, which possess a higher modulus than the epoxy matrix, acts as a reinforcing phase, while their unidirectional alignment along the loading axis maximizes load transfer efficiency according to composite theory. Decreasing Factors: The exceptionally high total porosity of 18.4% significantly reduces the effective load-bearing cross-sectional area and acts as a stress concentrator, drastically lowering the composite stiffness. Furthermore, the presence of 2 nm cavities within the matrix indicates nanoscale free volume or incomplete packing, and the low compression pressure (214 kPa) during processing likely contributed to insufficient void removal and potentially incomplete wetting of the hollow fiber lumens. Dominant Factor: While the aligned fiber reinforcement provides the primary mechanism for stiffness enhancement relative to the neat resin, the exceptionally high porosity content qualitatively dominates the final Young's modulus behavior by severely compromising the structural integrity and efficiency of the fiber-matrix load transfer, preventing the composite from achieving the theoretical stiffness expected from the fiber volume fraction and alignment.

title: Mechanical and Anticorrosive Properties of Graphene/Epoxy Resin Composites Coating Prepared by in-Situ Method
processing_history: Water-borne epoxy latex (34.6 wt %) mixed with PVP-rGO aqueous solution (2.5 mg/mL) at 0.7 wt % loading, magnetic stirring for 1 h at room temperature, degassed, drop cast onto Zn plate, cured at 80 °C for 2 h. Young's modulus measured by nanoindentation using Triboscope system, Berkovich diamond indenter, 800 mN normal load, ISO 14577 standard, Oliver and Pharr analysis, Poisson's ratio 0.40.
hierarchical_structure: Graphene nanosheets (avg. size ~2 μm) dispersed in epoxy resin matrix. Smooth surface, no aggregates.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a water-borne epoxy resin matrix reinforced with 0.7 wt% polyvinylpyrrolidone-functionalized reduced graphene oxide (PVP-rGO) nanosheets. Preparation involved mixing the epoxy latex with an aqueous PVP-rGO solution under magnetic stirring at room temperature for one hour, followed by degassing and drop-casting onto a zinc plate. The composite was subsequently cured at 80 °C for two hours to form a solid film. Structural characterization reveals that graphene nanosheets with an average size of approximately 2 μm are uniformly dispersed within the epoxy matrix, resulting in a smooth surface morphology without observable aggregates. Mechanical properties were evaluated via nanoindentation using a Berkovich diamond indenter under an 800 mN normal load following ISO 14577 standards with an assumed Poisson's ratio of 0.40.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The inclusion of reduced graphene oxide nanosheets introduces a phase with exceptionally high intrinsic stiffness, which reinforces the epoxy matrix. The PVP functionalization improves interfacial adhesion between the filler and the polymer, facilitating efficient stress transfer, while the absence of aggregates ensures uniform load distribution and prevents stress concentration sites. Decreasing Factors: The low filler loading of 0.7 wt% limits the volumetric contribution of the rigid reinforcement phase. Additionally, the water-borne processing history may leave residual moisture acting as a plasticizer, and the moderate curing temperature of 80 °C might not achieve the maximum crosslink density possible for the epoxy system, potentially reducing the matrix rigidity. Dominant Factor: The high aspect ratio and intrinsic modulus of the well-dispersed graphene nanosheets, combined with the enhanced interfacial strength from PVP functionalization, qualitatively dominate the mechanical response by providing effective reinforcement that outweighs the limitations imposed by the low loading and water-borne processing constraints.

title: A Study of Some Mechanical Properties of Composite Materials with a Dammar-Based Hybrid Matrix and Reinforced by Waste Paper
processing_history: Composite cast with Epoxy resin matrix and 18 layers of waste paper sheets (pre-impregnated). Uniform pressure of 27,000 N/m^2 applied. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test according to ASTM D3039 using Lrx Plus testing machine (2.5 kN force range).

The hierarchical structure is characterized by a layered distribution of 18 layers of pre-impregnated waste paper sheets embedded within the matrix. Additionally, the application of uniform pressure during processing reduces void content and improves interfacial contact between the paper layers and the resin, enhancing stress transfer efficiency. The thermosetting nature of the Epoxy resin provides a rigid crosslinked network that supports the reinforcement. The layered structure may introduce anisotropy, and if the tensile test orientation does not align perfectly with the primary fiber orientation within the paper sheets, effective stiffness may be reduced. Dominant Factor: The substantial reinforcement loading combined with the consolidation pressure is the dominant factor. While the waste paper is less stiff than engineered fibers, the high fraction of rigid cellulose fibers within the crosslinked epoxy matrix qualitatively drives the Young's modulus significantly higher than that of the neat resin, with the processing pressure ensuring that the theoretical reinforcement potential is realized by minimizing void defects.

title: Mechanical properties of multi-walled carbon nanotube/epoxy composites
processing_history: Acid-treated MWNT (2 wt%) mixed with epoxy, sonicated (Bandelin HD3200, 20 kHz) for 2 h at 60% amplitude. Hardener added, stirred 10 min at 150 rpm. Vacuum degassed. Cured at 60 °C for 1 h followed by 2 h at 110 °C. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test at 1.5 mm/min crosshead speed, 25 °C, ASTM D638-IV, using Hounsfield H100KS machine.
hierarchical_structure: Acid-treated MWNT are dispersed much more uniformly in the polymer matrix.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting epoxy nanocomposite formed from Diglycidyl ether bisphenol-A (DGEBA) resin and a polyamine hardener, reinforced with 2 wt% acid-treated multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWNT). Fabrication involved mixing the acid-treated MWNT with the epoxy resin followed by sonication at 20 kHz for 2 hours at 60% amplitude, after which the hardener was added and stirred at 150 rpm for 10 minutes. The mixture was vacuum degassed and subjected to a two-step curing cycle of 1 hour at 60 °C followed by 2 hours at 110 °C. Hierarchical characterization indicates that the acid-treated MWNT are dispersed much more uniformly in the polymer matrix, and the Young's modulus was evaluated via uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 1.5 mm/min at 25 °C according to ASTM D638-IV.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of multi-walled carbon nanotubes, which possess an intrinsically high axial stiffness, serves as a primary reinforcement mechanism that drives the Young's modulus (E) upward relative to the neat epoxy matrix. The acid treatment of the MWNT enhances interfacial adhesion between the filler and the epoxy network, improving stress transfer efficiency, while the reported uniform dispersion minimizes stress concentration points and maximizes the effective surface area for load bearing. Additionally, the thermal curing history promotes the formation of a rigid crosslinked epoxy-amine network, establishing a stiff baseline matrix modulus. Decreasing Factors: The prolonged sonication process (2 hours) required to achieve uniform dispersion may inadvertently reduce the aspect ratio of the nanotubes through mechanical fracture, potentially diminishing their reinforcement efficiency compared to pristine long tubes. Furthermore, despite vacuum degassing, the presence of microvoids introduced during mixing or sonication could act as compliance centers, locally reducing stiffness, and the random orientation of the nanotubes within the isotropic matrix prevents the realization of the maximum theoretical axial modulus achievable with aligned fibers. Dominant Factor: The significant intrinsic stiffness of the MWNT fillers combined with the improved interfacial bonding from acid treatment and the confirmed uniform dispersion qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, leading to a net increase in Young's modulus compared to the unfilled cured epoxy system, despite potential aspect ratio reduction from processing.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises an epoxy thermoset network synthesized from Diglycidyl ether bisphenol-A resin and a polyamine hardener, reinforced with 2 wt% acid-treated multi-walled carbon nanotubes. Preparation involved mixing the nanotubes with the epoxy resin followed by sonication at 20 kHz for 2 hours at 60% amplitude to facilitate dispersion. After the addition of the hardener and stirring at 150 rpm for 10 minutes, the mixture was vacuum degassed and cured using a step-wise protocol of 1 hour at 60 °C followed by 2 hours at 110 °C. The Young's modulus was characterized via uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 1.5 mm/min at 25 °C in accordance with ASTM D638-IV standards using a Hounsfield H100KS machine.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of acid-treated multi-walled carbon nanotubes introduces a high-modulus filler phase that significantly enhances stiffness through effective load transfer, while the acid treatment improves interfacial adhesion between the nanotubes and the epoxy matrix. Additionally, the step-wise curing history promotes a high crosslink density within the epoxy-amine network, inherently rigidifying the polymer matrix. Decreasing Factors: Prolonged sonication during processing carries the risk of mechanically damaging the nanotubes, reducing their aspect ratio and reinforcement efficiency, while any potential nanotube agglomeration or residual micro-voids despite vacuum degassing could act as stress concentrators that compromise the effective load-bearing capacity. Dominant Factor: The reinforcement contribution from the rigid multi-walled carbon nanotubes qualitatively dominates the mechanical behavior; despite potential processing-induced defects, the high intrinsic stiffness of the well-dispersed nanofillers combined with strong interfacial bonding drives the Young's modulus significantly higher than that of the neat cured epoxy network.

title: Effect of adsorption, hardener, and temperature on mechanical properties of epoxy nanocomposites with functionalized graphene: A molecular dynamics study
processing_history: Molecular dynamics simulation using LAMMPS. NPT/NVT ensembles. Strain rate 0.7 ps^-1. Tensile test in Y direction at 300 K. Epoxy:Hardener ratio 70:30 wt%.
hierarchical_structure: Nanocomposite with functionalized graphene oxide (1 wt% oxide groups).

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The material system comprises an epoxy novolac resin cured with diethyltoluenediamine at a 70:30 wt% ratio, forming a crosslinked thermoset network reinforced with 1 wt% functionalized graphene oxide containing oxide groups. Characterized as a nanocomposite, the sample was evaluated using molecular dynamics simulations in LAMMPS with NPT and NVT ensembles, undergoing a uniaxial tensile test in the Y direction at 300 K with a strain rate of 0.7 ps^-1.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a densely crosslinked thermoset network via the reaction between epoxy novolac and diethyltoluenediamine provides significant structural rigidity, particularly due to the aromatic rings within the novolac backbone which restrict chain segment rotation. The incorporation of graphene oxide introduces a high-modulus filler phase that enhances stiffness through load transfer, especially given the functionalization which promotes interfacial adhesion. Furthermore, the molecular dynamics processing history involves an extremely high strain rate (0.7 ps^-1), which typically yields a higher apparent elastic modulus in viscoelastic polymer systems due to insufficient time for chain relaxation during deformation. Decreasing Factors: The use of diethyltoluenediamine introduces aliphatic and cycloaliphatic segments into the network, which possess greater conformational freedom compared to fully aromatic hardeners, potentially reducing the overall network stiffness. Additionally, the low filler content (1 wt%) limits the reinforcement efficiency compared to higher loading percolation thresholds, and the amorphous nature of the cured epoxy matrix inherently possesses lower stiffness than crystalline counterparts. Dominant Factor: The dominant factor governing the elastic modulus (E) is the rigid, crosslinked aromatic network of the epoxy novolac matrix, which establishes the baseline mechanical integrity. However, the specific processing condition of the high strain rate tensile test in the simulation environment qualitatively acts to significantly elevate the measured modulus relative to quasi-static experimental conditions, making the simulation parameters a critical determinant of the observed E behavior.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The investigated material is a nanocomposite system comprising an Epoxy Novolac matrix crosslinked with Diethyltoluenediamine hardener at a 70:30 weight ratio, incorporated with 1 wt% Graphene Oxide filler. The mechanical properties were evaluated via molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS, employing NPT and NVT ensembles to equilibrate the system. Subsequent mechanical characterization was performed through a tensile test oriented in the Y direction at 300 K, applying a strain rate of 0.7 ps^-1.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a highly crosslinked thermoset network between the aromatic Epoxy Novolac and the diamine hardener significantly restricts polymer chain segmental mobility, intrinsically increasing stiffness. The inclusion of 1 wt% Graphene Oxide introduces rigid nanoscale reinforcement that bears load and further constrains matrix deformation. Additionally, the processing history involves a molecular dynamics tensile test at an extremely high strain rate of 0.7 ps^-1, which prevents viscoelastic relaxation processes and artificially elevates the apparent modulus compared to experimental timescales, while the testing temperature of 300 K likely places the material in a glassy state. Decreasing Factors: The presence of aliphatic ethyl groups on the Diethyltoluenediamine hardener introduces localized flexibility into the network compared to a fully aromatic system, potentially reducing the maximum theoretical stiffness. Furthermore, the amorphous nature of the cured epoxy network inherently contains free volume that limits chain packing density relative to crystalline materials. Dominant Factor: The structural rigidity provided by the high crosslink density of the aromatic Epoxy Novolac matrix, synergistically enhanced by the rigid Graphene Oxide filler, qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, establishing a high modulus baseline that outweighs the flexibility introduced by the hardener aliphatic segments, although the simulation strain rate significantly amplifies the measured magnitude.

title: Investigation of mechanical, thermal and electrical properties of hybrid composites reinforced with multi‑walled carbon nanotubes and fused silica particles
processing_history: Air entrapped in epoxy resin released using vacuum desiccator with BYK-A 500 for 2 h. Hardener added at 3:1 weight ratio, mixed, degassed 10 min. Cured at room temperature for 48 h at 3 atm, then 80 °C for 6 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test (Unitech-T RB301) at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed, ASTM D638-10, 5 specimens.
hierarchical_structure: Neat epoxy matrix. No fillers.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a neat epoxy matrix synthesized from a Bisphenol-F type epoxy resin (YDF-161) and an amine hardener (Jeffamine D-230) at a 75:25 weight ratio. Processing involved vacuum desiccation with BYK-A 500 to release entrapped air, followed by mixing, degassing, and curing under 3 atm pressure at room temperature for 48 hours, concluding with a thermal post-cure at 80 °C for 6 hours. The resulting material contains no fillers, and its mechanical response was evaluated using uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 0.5 mm/min in accordance with ASTM D638-10.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The presence of aromatic rings within the Bisphenol-F epoxy backbone provides inherent chain stiffness and restricts segmental rotation, which fundamentally drives the Young's modulus (E) higher. Furthermore, the formation of a covalently crosslinked thermoset network restricts long-range chain mobility compared to linear thermoplastics. The specific processing history, particularly curing under 3 atm pressure, significantly minimizes void content and micro-defects, ensuring efficient stress transfer across the matrix, while the 80 °C post-cure likely increases the final crosslink density and conversion degree, further stiffening the network. Dominant Factor: The high crosslink density achieved through the specific two-stage curing schedule dominates the final Young's modulus behavior, as the epoxy matrix constitutes the continuous phase comprising the vast majority of the volume, thereby dictating the baseline mechanical response upon which the low-loading filler provides secondary reinforcement.

title: Manufacturing process improvement and mechanical modelling of multiwalled carbon nanotube/epoxy composites
processing_history: MWNT (0.5 wt-%) dispersed in Epon 862/EpiCure W (100:26.4 wt ratio) via tip sonication (ice bath). Sonication: 60 W intensity, 1 h time, 20 s pulse on, 2 s pulse off. Degassed 30 min. Cured at 177 °C for 3 h in hot press. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test (ASTM D638/D882) at 1 mm/min crosshead speed, average of 5 specimens.
hierarchical_structure: MWNT/epoxy nanocomposite.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of a multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWNT) reinforced epoxy nanocomposite fabricated using Epon 862 epoxy resin and EpiCure W curing agent at a weight ratio of 100 to 26.4. The MWNTs, incorporated at 0.5 wt%, were dispersed within the resin matrix via tip sonication in an ice bath at 60 W intensity for one hour using a pulsed sequence, followed by a 30-minute degassing period. The composite was subsequently cured in a hot press at 177 °C for three hours to form a crosslinked network. The mechanical properties were evaluated via uniaxial tensile testing according to ASTM D638/D882 standards at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min, with reported values representing the average of five specimens.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The high-temperature curing cycle at 177 °C promotes a high degree of crosslinking within the Epon 862/EpiCure W network, significantly restricting chain segment mobility and establishing a rigid matrix backbone. Additionally, the incorporation of multiwalled carbon nanotubes introduces a high-modulus filler phase; if effectively dispersed via the tip sonication process, these nanotubes act as rigid reinforcements that bear load through shear lag mechanisms, theoretically increasing the composite stiffness. Decreasing Factors: Despite the sonication protocol, the low loading of 0.5 wt% MWNTs carries a risk of nanotube agglomeration, which can act as stress concentrators and reduce effective load transfer. Furthermore, without explicit surface functionalization mentioned in the processing history, the interfacial adhesion between the hydrophobic nanotubes and the epoxy matrix may be suboptimal, leading to interfacial slippage that diminishes the reinforcement efficiency. Any residual voids remaining after the 30-minute degassing process could also locally reduce the effective load-bearing cross-sectional area. Dominant Factor: The dominant factor governing the Young's modulus is the high crosslink density of the cured epoxy matrix established during the hot press curing stage, which provides the primary structural rigidity. While the MWNTs contribute to stiffening, the low filler content means the matrix properties remain paramount; however, the specific sonication energy and thermal cure profile are designed to maximize the filler-matrix interaction, qualitatively pushing the modulus higher than that of the neat resin.

title: Desirable electrical and mechanical properties of continuous hybrid nano-scale carbon fibers containing highly aligned multi-walled carbon nanotubes
processing_history: PAN terpolymer dissolved in DMF with MWCNTs (10 wt%) to prepare a 14 wt% solution, electrospun at 18 kV, 180 mm distance, 6.7 m/s drum speed. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test at 20 mm/min crosshead speed, room temperature, using Instron 1121.
hierarchical_structure: Aligned electrospun nanofibers. Average diameter 170 nm.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a poly(acrylonitrile-co-methyl acrylate-co-itaconic acid) terpolymer matrix reinforced with 10.0 wt% Multi-walled Carbon Nanotubes (MWCNTs). The copolymer consists of 93.0 wt% acrylonitrile, 5.3 wt% methyl acrylate, and 1.7 wt% itaconic acid. Processing involved dissolving the terpolymer and MWCNTs in DMF to create a 14 wt% solution, followed by electrospinning at 18 kV with a 180 mm collector distance and a drum speed of 6.7 m/s to yield aligned electrospun nanofibers with an average diameter of 170 nm. Mechanical characterization was performed via uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 20 mm/min at room temperature using an Instron 1121.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of 10.0 wt% Multi-walled Carbon Nanotubes introduces a rigid, high-aspect-ratio filler phase that significantly enhances stiffness through effective stress transfer, provided interfacial adhesion is sufficient. Additionally, the electrospinning process at a high drum speed of 6.7 m/s induces substantial molecular chain orientation and fiber alignment along the loading axis, while the strong dipole-dipole interactions between nitrile groups in the acrylonitrile segments further restrict segmental mobility. Decreasing Factors: The inclusion of methyl acrylate and itaconic acid comonomers disrupts the regularity of the polyacrylonitrile backbone, potentially reducing crystallinity and intermolecular packing density compared to a pure PAN homopolymer. Furthermore, the nanofibrous morphology inherently contains inter-fiber voids which may reduce the effective load-bearing cross-sectional area, and any residual DMF solvent could act as a plasticizer. Dominant Factor: The synergistic effect of the high loading of rigid MWCNTs and the profound molecular orientation induced by the high-speed electrospinning process qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, likely resulting in a significantly enhanced Young's modulus along the fiber alignment direction despite the crystallinity disruption caused by the comonomers.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of a polyacrylonitrile-based terpolymer composed of 93.0 wt% acrylonitrile, 5.3 wt% methyl acrylate, and 1.7 wt% itaconic acid. This matrix was reinforced with 10.0 wt% multi-walled carbon nanotubes as a filler. The composite was prepared by dissolving the terpolymer and nanotubes in dimethylformamide to form a 14 wt% solution, which was subsequently processed via electrospinning at an applied voltage of 18 kV, a tip-to-collector distance of 180 mm, and a drum collection speed of 6.7 m/s. title: Multi-Scale Analysis and Testing of Tensile Behavior in Polymers with Randomly Oriented and Agglomerated Cellulose Nanofibers
processing_history: Nanocomposite consisting of epoxy matrix filled with dry CNFs (diameter 25-50 nm, length 5-50 µm). CNF concentration 3.7 vol %. Tensile tests conducted on specimens following JIS K 7164 standard. Young's modulus determined from stress-strain curves. At least five tests performed.
hierarchical_structure: Randomly oriented CNF. Agglomerated CNF clusters dispersed in epoxy matrix. Apparent aspect ratio 7.5.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of an epoxy resin matrix reinforced with cellulose nanofibers (CNFs) to form a nanocomposite material. The dry CNFs, possessing diameters between 25 and 50 nm and lengths ranging from 5 to 50 µm, were incorporated at a concentration of 3.7 vol %. Hierarchical characterization reveals a structure featuring randomly oriented CNFs with an apparent aspect ratio of 7.5, wherein agglomerated CNF clusters are dispersed throughout the epoxy matrix. Mechanical characterization was performed via tensile tests conducted on specimens following the JIS K 7164 standard, with the Young's modulus derived from the resulting stress-strain curves based on an average of at least five measurements.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of cellulose nanofibers, which possess a significantly higher intrinsic stiffness than the epoxy resin matrix, acts as the primary reinforcement mechanism driving the Young's modulus upward according to composite micromechanics. Additionally, the crosslinked nature of the epoxy matrix provides a rigid baseline modulus. Decreasing Factors: The processing history involving dry CNFs likely contributed to the observed hierarchical structure of agglomerated CNF clusters, which act as stress concentrators and reduce effective load transfer compared to exfoliated fibers. Furthermore, the random orientation of the fibers reduces the reinforcement efficiency in the tensile direction compared to aligned systems, and the low apparent aspect ratio of 7.5 limits stress transfer via shear lag mechanisms. Dominant Factor: While the high modulus of the cellulose filler dictates a net increase in stiffness relative to the neat matrix, the dominant factor governing the final magnitude of the Young's modulus is the microstructural dispersion quality; specifically, the agglomeration of CNF clusters and random orientation significantly mitigate the potential reinforcement efficiency, preventing the composite from achieving theoretical maximums.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample is a nanocomposite material consisting of an epoxy resin matrix reinforced with cellulose nanofibers (CNFs). The reinforcement phase comprises dry CNFs with diameters between 25 and 50 nm and lengths ranging from 5 to 50 µm, incorporated at a concentration of 3.7 vol %. Mechanical characterization was performed through tensile tests on specimens prepared according to the JIS K 7164 standard, with the Young's modulus calculated from stress-strain curves averaged over at least five independent tests.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The crosslinked network structure of the epoxy matrix provides a rigid baseline modulus, while the incorporation of cellulose nanofibers introduces a phase with significantly higher intrinsic stiffness and crystallinity. The high aspect ratio of the nanofibers facilitates stress transfer from the matrix to the filler, theoretically enhancing the composite stiffness according to micromechanical models. Decreasing Factors: The nanoscale dimensions of the CNFs create a high surface area that promotes agglomeration if dispersion is incomplete, which can act as stress concentrators and reduce effective reinforcement. Additionally, the absence of specified surface coupling agents in the processing history suggests potential weak interfacial adhesion, which may limit load transfer efficiency and allow for interfacial slip under tension. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic high modulus of the cellulose nanofibers relative to the epoxy matrix is the dominant factor governing the composite behavior; despite potential interfacial limitations, the presence of the rigid filler phase at 3.7 vol % qualitatively drives the Young's modulus higher than that of the neat resin, as the reinforcement effect typically outweighs the matrix compliance in such nanocomposite systems.

title: Impact of shear mixing time of epoxy-silica nanocomposites on its electrical and mechanical properties
processing_history: Silica nanoparticles heated at 110 °C for 24 h, dispersed in ethanol, sonicated 45 min. Mixed with epoxy resin, sonicated 20 kHz for 1 h. Shear mixed at 2000 rpm for 10 h. Sonicated 20 kHz for 1 h. Ethanol evaporated in oven. TETA hardener mixed. Degassed and poured in moulds. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test using Universal Testing Machine at 2 mm/min displacement rate, room temperature, according to ASTM D-638 (Type IV) standard.
hierarchical_structure: Epoxy matrix with 1 wt.% silica nanoparticles (15 nm APS). SEM shows agglomeration count increases in 10 h sample compared to 7 h sample.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a Bisphenol-A epoxy resin (CY205) crosslinked with a Tri-ethylene tetra-amine (TETA) hardener, reinforced with 1.0 wt% silica nanoparticles possessing an average particle size of 15 nm. The nanocomposite fabrication involved dispersing pre-heated silica nanoparticles in ethanol via sonication, followed by incorporation into the epoxy resin through alternating cycles of high-frequency sonication and prolonged shear mixing at 2000 rpm for 10 hours. Subsequent processing included solvent evaporation, hardener addition, degassing, and casting into moulds for curing. Structural analysis via SEM reveals the presence of nanoparticle agglomerates, noting that the agglomeration count is elevated in this 10-hour shear-mixed sample compared to those subjected to shorter mixing durations. The Young's modulus was characterized using uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature with a displacement rate of 2 mm/min, adhering to ASTM D-638 (Type IV) standards.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of rigid silica nanoparticles into the polymer matrix introduces a high-modulus phase that typically enhances the composite stiffness through load transfer mechanisms, assuming adequate interfacial bonding. Additionally, the formation of a densely crosslinked thermoset network via the reaction between the Bisphenol-A epoxy resin and TETA hardener intrinsically restricts chain mobility, providing a high baseline stiffness compared to thermoplastic counterparts. The use of sonication during processing aims to deagglomerate particles, potentially increasing the effective surface area for stress transfer. Decreasing Factors: The SEM observation of increased agglomeration counts resulting from the extended 10-hour shear mixing history suggests that excessive mechanical energy input may have induced particle re-agglomeration or cluster formation. These agglomerates act as stress concentrators and reduce the effective interfacial area between the filler and the matrix, thereby diminishing the reinforcement efficiency and potentially lowering the modulus relative to a well-dispersed system. Furthermore, if the ethanol evaporation step was incomplete, residual solvent could plasticize the matrix, though this is secondary to structural defects. Dominant Factor: While the rigid silica filler and crosslinked network architecture fundamentally drive the Young's modulus to values higher than neat epoxy, the processing-induced agglomeration observed in the hierarchical structure is the dominant factor governing the final mechanical performance. This microstructural defect limits the theoretical reinforcement potential of the nanoparticles, meaning the final modulus is determined more by the efficiency of the filler dispersion achieved during the specific 10-hour shear mixing protocol than by the filler content alone.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a Bisphenol-A epoxy resin (CY205) cured with a Tri-ethylene tetra-amine (TETA) hardener and reinforced with 1.0 wt% Silica nanoparticles. The nanoparticles were preconditioned by heating at 110 °C for 24 hours, dispersed in ethanol via sonication, and subsequently mixed with the epoxy resin through a rigorous protocol involving high-shear mixing at 2000 rpm for 10 hours and intermittent sonication. Following solvent evaporation in an oven, the TETA hardener was incorporated, and the mixture was degassed and cast into moulds. The Young's modulus was characterized via uniaxial tensile testing at a displacement rate of 2 mm/min at room temperature in compliance with ASTM D-638 (Type IV) standards.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a highly crosslinked thermoset network through the reaction of the epoxy resin with the tetra-functional TETA hardener significantly restricts chain mobility, providing a rigid structural baseline. Decreasing Factors: The low filler loading of 1.0 wt% limits the magnitude of reinforcement relative to the bulk matrix volume. Additionally, the solvent-assisted processing route involving ethanol evaporation poses a risk of residual voids or micro-defects if degassing was incomplete, which could act as stress concentrators and slightly reduce the effective modulus. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic stiffness of the crosslinked aromatic epoxy network is the dominant factor governing the final Young's modulus, as the matrix constitutes the overwhelming majority of the composite volume at this low filler concentration, meaning the bulk mechanical response is primarily defined by the cured resin architecture rather than the minor particulate addition.

title: Effect of fatigue testing on the properties of Glass-Epoxy composites using the acoustic tool
processing_history: Vacuum bag molding technique under 0.3 bar vacuum for 6 hours. Cured in oven at 80 °C for 8 hours. Specimens cut to 200x20x1 mm. Fatigue loading: 10,000 cycles, 10 Hz, sinusoidal waveform, 50% displacement at break, 10% amplitude. 1000 hours tap water immersion aging. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test at 1 mm/min crosshead speed, room temperature (15-25 °C), according to ASTM C365-57.
hierarchical_structure: Glass-Epoxy composite with 4 layers of Glass E twill weave (300 g/m2). Matrix cracking and delamination observed after fatigue and aging.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: This material is a glass-epoxy composite system comprising SR 1500 epoxy resin and SD 2505 amine hardener reinforced with 65 mass % Glass E fiber arranged in four layers of twill weave (300 g/m²). The specimens were fabricated using vacuum bag molding under 0.3 bar vacuum for 6 hours followed by oven curing at 80 °C for 8 hours, resulting in 200x20x1 mm dimensions. Prior to mechanical characterization, the composite underwent fatigue loading for 10,000 cycles at 10 Hz with 50% displacement at break and 1000 hours of tap water immersion aging, which induced observed matrix cracking and delamination. The Young's modulus was subsequently evaluated via uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min at room temperature according to ASTM C365-57.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of 65 mass % Glass E fibers provides a high-stiffness reinforcement phase that significantly elevates the composite modulus relative to the neat epoxy matrix through rule-of-mixtures contributions. Additionally, the amine curing of the epoxy resin creates a crosslinked thermoset network that provides inherent rigidity to the matrix phase, while the twill weave architecture offers bidirectional load-bearing capability. Decreasing Factors: The 1000 hours of tap water immersion likely induces hygrothermal aging, leading to plasticization of the epoxy matrix and potential hydrolytic degradation of the fiber-matrix interface, which reduces stiffness. Furthermore, the fatigue loading history generated matrix cracking and delamination, as noted in the hierarchical structure, which compromises stress transfer efficiency between the fibers and the matrix and effectively reduces the load-bearing cross-sectional area. The vacuum bag molding process may also introduce higher void content compared to autoclave processing, further diminishing effective stiffness. Dominant Factor: While the high volume fraction of rigid glass fibers establishes the fundamental baseline for a high modulus, the cumulative impact of hygrothermal aging and fatigue-induced microstructural damage (cracking and delamination) is the dominant factor governing the specific effective modulus of this sample, qualitatively reducing the stiffness significantly below that of a pristine, undamaged composite.

Fabrication involved a vacuum bag molding technique under 0.3 bar vacuum for 6 hours, followed by oven curing at 80 °C for 8 hours. Decreasing Factors: The severe fatigue loading history, specifically at 50% displacement at break over 10,000 cycles, likely induced substantial microstructural damage including matrix microcracking and fiber-matrix interfacial debonding, which reduces the effective load-bearing cross-section. title: Thermal, mechanical, and conductivity properties of cyanate ester composites
processing_history: Resin heated to 80 °C, filler added periodically over 30 min at 200 rpm, mixed another 30 min at 200 rpm (pulsing to 1000 rpm). Catalyst and co-catalyst added and mixed by hand. Poured into moulds, degassed at 80 °C for 1 h in vacuum. Cured: 2 h at 140 °C (air), 1 h at 220 °C (air), 1 h at 220 °C (N2), 2 h at 285 °C (N2). Cooled to RT over 8 h (N2). Young's modulus measured by three point bend rig (Instron 4045) at 23 ± 2 °C with cross-head speed of 1 mm/min, ASTM D790.
hierarchical_structure: Cross-linked cyanate ester matrix with dispersed spherical silica filler (70 wt%). >95% cure. No signs of filler settling.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a cross-linked AroCy B cyanate ester homopolymer matrix reinforced with 70 wt% Excelica SE 5 spherical silica filler. The formulation incorporates 360 ppm Copper (II) acetylacetonate as a catalyst and 3 wt% Nonylphenol as a co-catalyst. Processing involved heating the resin to 80 °C followed by periodic filler addition and mixing at 200 rpm with pulses to 1000 rpm, after which the catalysts were hand-mixed into the compound. The mixture was poured into moulds, degassed at 80 °C under vacuum for 1 h, and subjected to a multi-stage curing cycle consisting of 2 h at 140 °C and 1 h at 220 °C in air, followed by 1 h at 220 °C and 2 h at 285 °C under nitrogen, before cooling to room temperature over 8 h. The resulting hierarchical structure features a highly cured (>95%) matrix with dispersed spherical silica filler showing no signs of settling, and the Young's modulus was characterized via three-point bending according to ASTM D790 at 23 ± 2 °C.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of 70 wt% Excelica SE 5 spherical silica filler drastically increases stiffness due to the high intrinsic modulus of silica relative to the polymer matrix, effectively creating a percolated rigid network. The high-temperature curing cycle up to 285 °C promotes a high degree of conversion (>95%) into a rigid triazine network, maximizing the crosslink density of the cyanate ester matrix. Additionally, the slow cooling rate over 8 h minimizes residual thermal stresses that could otherwise lead to microcracking, thereby preserving structural integrity and modulus. Decreasing Factors: The inclusion of 3 wt% Nonylphenol as a co-catalyst introduces low molecular weight species that, if not fully reacted into the network, may act as plasticizers within the matrix, potentially reducing the intrinsic stiffness of the polymer phase. Furthermore, the organic-inorganic interface represents a region of potential compliance compared to the bulk silica, which can slightly dampen the theoretical maximum modulus predicted by rule of mixtures. Dominant Factor: The dominant factor is the extremely high loading of the rigid silica filler (70 wt%). At this concentration, the mechanical behavior transitions towards being filler-controlled rather than matrix-controlled, meaning the high modulus of the silica phase overwhelmingly dictates the composite's Young's modulus, overshadowing the modulating effects of the catalyst system or specific matrix crosslink density.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises an AroCy B cyanate ester homopolymer matrix loaded with 70 wt% Excelica SE 5 filler, 3 wt% Nonylphenol co-catalyst, and 360 ppm Copper (II) acetylacetonate catalyst. Preparation involved heating the resin to 80 °C followed by periodic filler addition over 30 minutes with mixing at 200 rpm, succeeded by further mixing with pulses up to 1000 rpm. After hand-mixing the catalysts, the mixture was moulded and degassed under vacuum at 80 °C for 1 hour. The curing protocol consisted of heating for 2 hours at 140 °C and 1 hour at 220 °C in air, followed by 1 hour at 220 °C and 2 hours at 285 °C under nitrogen, before cooling to room temperature over 8 hours under nitrogen. Young's modulus was subsequently measured via three-point bending at 23 ± 2 °C according to ASTM D790.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The exceptionally high filler loading of 70 wt% Excelica SE 5 introduces a rigid particulate phase that significantly restricts matrix deformation, inherently driving the Young's modulus upward through composite reinforcement mechanisms. Additionally, the AroCy B cyanate ester forms a highly crosslinked aromatic triazine network, and the high-temperature cure cycle reaching 285 °C ensures maximum conversion and crosslink density, further stiffening the polymer matrix. Decreasing Factors: The inclusion of Nonylphenol, while functioning as a co-catalyst, introduces flexible alkyl chains that may slightly reduce the overall network rigidity or act as a minor plasticizer if not fully reacted into the network. Furthermore, any residual microvoids remaining despite vacuum degassing would act as stress concentrators, reducing the effective load-bearing cross-sectional area. Dominant Factor: The volumetric dominance of the rigid filler phase is the decisive factor governing the mechanical response. At 70 wt%, the composite behavior transitions from polymer-dominated to filler-dominated mechanics, meaning the high intrinsic modulus of the Excelica SE 5 particles overwhelmingly dictates the final Young's modulus, superseding the contributions of the matrix chemistry or minor additives.

title: Toughening of Epoxy/ Polycaprolactone Composites via Reaction Induced Phase Separation
processing_history: Epoxy oligomer degassed at 90°C for 1 h, blended with 30 wt% Tonediol-1270 at 150°C. 28 phr DDS added. Cast into mold. Precured at 120°C for 2 h, postcured at 200°C for 2 h. Elastic modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test at 5.08 mm/min crosshead speed, room temperature (25°C), according to ASTM D638.
hierarchical_structure: Reaction induced phase separation via spinodal decomposition. Co-continuous morphology of interconnected epoxy spheres (3.5-7 μm) wrapped with thermoplastic layers.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The material system is a thermoset network formed from Bisphenol-A diglycidyl ether epoxy oligomers cured with 28 phr of Diaminodiphenyl sulfone (DDS) and modified with 30 wt% Tonediol-1270 toughener. Processing involved degassing the epoxy at 90°C, blending with the toughener at 150°C, adding the hardener, and casting into a mold followed by a two-stage thermal cure consisting of precuring at 120°C for 2 hours and postcuring at 200°C for 2 hours. This thermal history induced reaction-induced phase separation via spinodal decomposition, resulting in a hierarchical co-continuous morphology characterized by interconnected epoxy spheres ranging from 3.5 to 7 μm wrapped with thermoplastic layers. The elastic modulus was subsequently characterized using a uniaxial tensile test at a crosshead speed of 5.08 mm/min at room temperature in accordance with ASTM D638.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The presence of rigid aromatic rings within both the Bisphenol-A diglycidyl ether backbone and the Diaminodiphenyl sulfone hardener significantly restricts segmental chain mobility, intrinsically enhancing the stiffness of the network. Furthermore, the processing history includes a high-temperature postcure at 200°C, which maximizes the conversion of epoxy groups and achieves a high crosslink density, thereby substantially increasing the elastic modulus. Decreasing Factors: The incorporation of 30 wt% Tonediol-1270 toughener introduces a secondary phase that typically possesses a lower modulus than the highly crosslinked epoxy matrix, acting to reduce the overall composite stiffness. Additionally, the reaction-induced phase separation creates interfacial regions between the epoxy spheres and thermoplastic layers which may act as sites of reduced load transfer efficiency compared to a homogeneous network. Dominant Factor: Despite the compliance introduced by the toughener and phase morphology, the high crosslink density and intrinsic rigidity of the aromatic epoxy network established by the rigorous thermal curing cycle qualitatively dominate the mechanical response, maintaining a high elastic modulus characteristic of structural thermosets.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of a Bisphenol-A diglycidyl ether (DGEBA) epoxy resin system cured with Diaminodiphenyl sulfone (DDS) hardener at 28 phr. To enhance toughness, 30 wt% Tonediol-1270 was blended into the epoxy oligomer at 150°C following degassing at 90°C for 1 hour. The mixture was cast into a mold and subjected to a thermal curing cycle comprising a precure at 120°C for 2 hours followed by a postcure at 200°C for 2 hours. The elastic modulus was subsequently characterized via uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 5.08 mm/min at room temperature (25°C) in accordance with ASTM D638.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The chemical composition features rigid aromatic structures in both the DGEBA resin and the DDS hardener, along with the polar sulfone group, which inherently restrict chain segment mobility and increase stiffness. Furthermore, the processing history includes a high-temperature postcure at 200°C, which maximizes the crosslink density of the thermoset network, and degassing at 90°C, which minimizes void content that would otherwise act as stress concentrators and reduce effective load-bearing area. Decreasing Factors: The addition of 30 wt% Tonediol-1270 toughener introduces a compliant, flexible phase into the matrix. Tougheners typically possess a significantly lower modulus than the cured epoxy network, and their inclusion, likely resulting in phase-separated domains, disrupts the continuity of the rigid matrix and lowers the overall composite stiffness to accommodate energy dissipation mechanisms. Dominant Factor: The continuous, highly crosslinked aromatic epoxy network established by the DDS curing agent and high-temperature postcure serves as the primary load-bearing phase. While the substantial loading of the flexible toughener qualitatively reduces the modulus relative to a neat resin, the intrinsic rigidity and structural integrity of the cured thermoset matrix remain the dominant factors determining the final magnitude of the elastic modulus.

title: Characterization of mechanical properties of epoxy resin reinforced with submicron-sized ZnO prepared via in situ synthesis method
processing_history: Neat epoxy resin mixed with curing agent (Me-THPA) and accelerant (BDMA) (1:1:0.015 wt), cured 1h at 80 °C + 2h at 120 °C. Tensile modulus measured by universal testing machine WDW-5, ISO 527/2, 2.0 mm/min, 23 ± 1 °C.

title: Characterization of tensile property of high-performance fiber bundles combined with epoxy resin using advanced video extensometer

title: High porosity cellulose nanopapers as reinforcement in multi-layer epoxy laminates

title: Ultrahigh Performance of Nanoengineered Graphene-Based Natural Jute Fiber Composites

hierarchical_structure: Unidirectional jute fiber reinforced epoxy composite. Fiber volume fraction (Vf) ~54%. Alkali treated fiber surface with removed hemicellulose and lignin.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of a unidirectional jute fiber reinforced epoxy composite fabricated using EL2 epoxy laminating resin and AT30 epoxy hardener as the matrix system. Reinforcement is provided by jute fibers with a volume fraction of approximately 54%, which were individualized by hand combing and subjected to alkali treatment using a 0.5 wt% sodium hydroxide solution to remove surface hemicellulose and lignin. The composite manufacturing involved compacting the treated fibers via hot pressing at 120 °C under 1 Ton/inch² pressure for 30 minutes, followed by vacuum resin infusion and curing at room temperature for 24 hours. Mechanical characterization was performed via longitudinal tensile testing according to ASTM D3039 standards using an Instron 5985 machine at a cross-head speed of 2 mm/min.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The high fiber volume fraction of approximately 54% significantly enhances the modulus according to the rule of mixtures, as the stiff cellulose structure of the jute fibers bears the majority of the longitudinal load. The unidirectional alignment of the fibers ensures optimal load transfer along the testing axis, while the alkali treatment with sodium hydroxide removes weak boundary layers such as lignin and hemicellulose, improving interfacial adhesion and stress transfer efficiency between the fiber and the epoxy matrix. Additionally, the hot pressing compaction step likely reduces void content, further densifying the structure. Decreasing Factors: The intrinsic Young's modulus of natural jute fibers is generally lower than that of synthetic reinforcements like glass or carbon fibers, limiting the upper bound of the composite stiffness. Furthermore, curing the epoxy matrix at room temperature rather than elevated temperatures may result in a lower crosslink density, reducing the matrix modulus and potentially compromising the interphase rigidity. Minor fiber misalignment arising from the hand combing process could also deviate from ideal unidirectional behavior, slightly diminishing the longitudinal modulus. Dominant Factor: The high fiber volume fraction combined with the unidirectional architecture qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, as the composite stiffness is primarily governed by the reinforcing phase rather than the matrix; however, the realization of this theoretical maximum is critically dependent on the interfacial quality improved by the alkali treatment.
