title: Physical, Mechanical and Thermal Properties of an Epoxy Composite Reinforced With Nauclea diderrichii (Bilinga) Wood Particles
processing_history: Cold pressure moulding. Wood particles dried at 105 °C for 3 h. Particles, epoxy resin, and hardener homogenized manually for 5 min. Moulded in metal mould (180x150x10 mm) under 4 MPa pressure for 2 h. Demoulded and cured for 24 h. Particle size range: 2.5 ≤ t < 4 mm. Young's modulus measured by three-point bending test according to ASTM D790, load 5 kN, speed 5 mm/min, samples measuring 150 × 15 × 7 mm.
hierarchical_structure: Composite with dispersed Bilinga wood particles in epoxy matrix. Porosity observed. Particle size 2.5 ≤ t < 4 mm.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting epoxy matrix synthesized from Bisphenol A diglycidyl ether and an aromatic diamine hardener, reinforced with 85 vol% Nauclea diderrichii (Bilinga) wood particles. The composite was fabricated via cold pressure moulding, wherein wood particles dried at 105 °C for 3 hours were manually homogenized with the resin system before being pressed in a metal mould at 4 MPa for 2 hours, followed by demoulding and a 24-hour cure period. The resulting hierarchical structure is characterized as a particle-reinforced composite with wood particle sizes ranging between 2.5 and 4 mm, though microstructural analysis indicated the presence of porosity. Mechanical characterization was performed using a three-point bending test according to ASTM D790 to determine the Young's modulus.

Additionally, the crosslinked network formed by the Bisphenol A diglycidyl ether and aromatic diamine provides a rigid thermoset baseline that supports load transfer between the filler particles. Furthermore, the cold pressure moulding and manual homogenization processing history may result in suboptimal wetting of the hydrophilic wood particles by the hydrophobic epoxy, leading to poor interfacial adhesion which limits stress transfer efficiency. The relatively large particle size (2.5 to 4 mm) may also contribute to stress concentrations compared to finer reinforcements. Dominant Factor: The extremely high volume fraction of the stiff wood filler qualitatively dominates the final modulus behavior, establishing a stiffness significantly higher than the neat epoxy matrix; however, the magnitude of this increase is substantially attenuated by the processing-induced porosity and likely interfacial defects, preventing the composite from achieving its theoretical maximum stiffness.

title: Ultrasonic Velocity and Attenuation in Epoxy Resin/Granite (Marble) Powder Composite
processing_history: Epoxy resin and hardener mixed at 50:50 ratio. Granite powder grafted with styrene (gamma irradiation 30 kGy) added at 100 wt%, mixed for 3 minutes. Cured at room temperature for 24 h in mold. Young's modulus calculated from ultrasonic compression and shear wave velocities measured by pulse-echo technique at 4 MHz, room temperature.
hierarchical_structure: Epoxy matrix with styrene grafted granite powder filler.

title: The Effect of Shear Mixing Speed and Time on the Mechanical Properties of GNP/Epoxy Composites
processing_history: Acetone shear mixed in epoxy at 5000 rpm for 1 h. Acetone evaporated by heating to constant mass. Curing agent added. Cured for 2 h at 80 °C followed by 8 h at 140 °C. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test according to ASTM D634. (Reported value 2.68 MPa corrected to GPa based on context).
hierarchical_structure: Neat epoxy matrix processed with acetone.

The system was subsequently cured using a two-stage thermal protocol comprising 2 hours at 80 °C followed by 8 hours at 140 °C to form a neat epoxy matrix. The mechanical properties were characterized via uniaxial tensile testing according to ASTM D634 standards.

title: Tetraglycidyl ether 1.1.2.2-tetraphenyl ethane epoxy resin modified by carbon nanotubes

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting epoxy network synthesized from a blend of tetraglycidyl ether 1.1.2.2-tetraphenyl ethane (80 parts by weight) and bisphenol A diglycidyl ether (20 parts by weight), cured with methyl tetrahydrophthalic anhydride (80 parts by weight) using 2-(4-aminophenyl)-5-aminobenzimidazole as an accelerator (1 part by weight). Structural analysis confirms even dispersion of the carbon nanotubes, while fracture surface examination reveals an increased number of cracks propagating in different directions compared to the neat resin. The high-temperature post-cure at 220°C ensures maximum conversion of functional groups, further densifying the network and increasing stiffness. Dominant Factor: The high crosslink density derived from the tetrafunctional majority monomer and the rigorous thermal curing schedule, augmented by the stiff carbon nanotube filler, qualitatively dominates the flexibility introduced by the minority bisphenol A component, resulting in a net directional increase in the Young's modulus for this composite system.

title: Physico-Mechanical, Thermal, and Coating Properties of Composite Materials Prepared With Epoxy Resin/Steel Slag

title: Hybrid POSS-Hyperbranched polymer additives for simultaneous reinforcement and toughness improvements in epoxy networks

Subsequent hot press curing was conducted at 50 MPa with a thermal profile of 100 °C for 2 hours and 175 °C for 4 hours. The resulting hierarchical structure features laterally aligned SWCNTs within the epoxy matrix with a Herman's orientation factor of 0.59 and an intertube distance of less than 30 nm. Mechanical characterization was performed via uniaxial tensile testing using a Micro Autograph MST-I with a 100 N load cell at an extension rate of 1.0 mm/min, with the load applied perpendicular to the direction of SWCNT alignment.

Decreasing Factors: The mechanical testing condition specifies that the load was applied perpendicular to the SWCNT alignment, meaning the reinforcement relies on the transverse modulus of the nanotubes and shear deformation of the matrix rather than the superior axial stiffness of the CNTs, significantly reducing reinforcement efficiency. Furthermore, an intertube distance of less than 30 nm suggests potential nanotube bundling, which may decrease the effective surface area for stress transfer compared to individually dispersed tubes. Dominant Factor: The high volume fraction (33 wt%) of the ultra-stiff SWCNTs is the dominant factor qualitatively driving the Young's modulus higher than the neat epoxy baseline; however, the perpendicular loading direction relative to the nanotube alignment acts as a critical limiting factor that prevents the composite from achieving the theoretical maximum modulus associated with longitudinally aligned nanotube composites.

title: Effect of Terminal Groups on Thermomechanical and Dielectric Properties of Silica–Epoxy Composite Modified by Hyperbranched Polyester
processing_history: Molecular dynamics simulation using Material Studio (COMPASS force field). Amorphous cell (50x50x50 A^3) constructed with DGEBA and 44DDS (2:1 molar ratio). Following energy optimization and thermal annealing between 300 and 900 K, equilibration was performed under NVT conditions for 500 ps at 300 K and NPT conditions for 1000 ps at 1 atm. Crosslinking was implemented via a PERL script to achieve a target conversion degree of 80%, and the Young's modulus was subsequently calculated using the static constant strain method involving uniaxial tensile, compressive, and shear deformations at 300 K.

The thermal annealing during the simulation processing history also promotes denser packing, reducing free volume and contributing to a higher modulus. Decreasing Factors: The ether linkages within the DGEBA backbone introduce a degree of flexibility that lowers the modulus relative to purely carbonaceous aromatic networks. Dominant Factor: The dominant factor is the formation of the rigid, crosslinked aromatic network structure. title: Physico-Mechanical, Thermal, and Coating Properties of Composite Materials Prepared With Epoxy Resin/Steel Slag

title: Bio-marine shell powder-filled jute fabric/epoxy composites: Chemical, combustion, and mechanical properties

title: Effect of alkali treatment on interfacial bonding in abaca fiber-reinforced composites

The reported 50% crystallinity index provides a significant volume fraction of rigid crystalline domains that resist deformation. Decreasing Factors: The hierarchical structure reveals bundle fibrillation and twisting, which misaligns the cellulose microfibrils relative to the loading axis, reducing the efficiency of stress transfer and lowering the effective modulus. The relatively large fiber diameter may also correlate with a higher probability of internal defects compared to finer microfibrils. Decreasing Factors: The relatively low concentration of multi-walled carbon nanotubes at 0.1539 wt% limits the extent of reinforcement compared to higher loading fractions, potentially staying below the percolation threshold for maximum mechanical benefit. Furthermore, the curing cycle temperatures of 35 °C and 70 °C are moderate for epoxy systems; if these temperatures are insufficient to achieve full conversion of the curing agent, the resulting crosslink density may be lower than optimal, thereby reducing the matrix stiffness. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic rigidity of the covalently crosslinked epoxy network establishes the primary contribution to the Young's modulus, as the matrix constitutes the bulk volume of the material; however, the high-shear dispersion processing is the critical factor that ensures the multi-walled carbon nanotubes effectively reinforce this matrix rather than acting as defects, qualitatively defining the composite's enhanced stiffness relative to the neat resin.

title: Bio-based tri-functional epoxy resin (TEIA) blend cured with anhydride (MHHPA) based crosslinker: Thermal, mechanical and morphological characterization

processing_history: Blended using digital mechanical stirrer and ultrasonication for 30 minutes. Degassed in vacuum oven at 70°C for 20 minutes. MHHPA and 2-MI added, stirred, degassed at 60°C for 15 minutes. Poured into preheated stainless steel mould sprayed with silicon spray. Cured at 160°C for 2 hours. Young's modulus measured by Universal testing machine (Instron 3382), crosshead speed 1 mm/min, 24°C, 50% RH, according to ASTM-D 3039.
hierarchical_structure: Fracture surface rough with massive ridges. TEIA well dispersed throughout epoxy matrix. Bright regions are nodules, dark regions are interstitial domains. Completely miscible confirmed by single Tg.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting epoxy network synthesized from a blend of Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol-A (70 wt%) and a tri-functional epoxy resin derived from itaconic acid (30 wt%). This resin system was cured using Methylhexahydrophthalic anhydride at a 0.85 molar ratio to epoxy groups, catalyzed by 0.9 wt% 2-methylimidazole. Processing involved blending via mechanical stirring and ultrasonication, followed by vacuum degassing and curing in a preheated stainless steel mould at 160°C for 2 hours. Morphological analysis indicates the tri-functional epoxy is well dispersed throughout the matrix with a fracture surface exhibiting massive ridges, bright nodular regions, and dark interstitial domains, yet the system remains completely miscible as confirmed by a single glass transition temperature. Young's modulus was characterized using a universal testing machine at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min under ambient conditions according to ASTM-D 3039.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol-A provides a rigid aromatic backbone that inherently resists deformation, while the addition of the tri-functional epoxy resin from itaconic acid significantly increases the crosslink density of the network compared to standard difunctional systems. The use of Methylhexahydrophthalic anhydride as a crosslinker combined with a high-temperature cure at 160°C ensures a high degree of conversion and network rigidity. Furthermore, testing at 24°C places the material well below its glass transition temperature, ensuring it behaves as a stiff glassy solid. Decreasing Factors: The presence of aliphatic segments within the itaconic acid-derived resin may introduce slight flexibility compared to a purely aromatic network. Additionally, testing under 50% relative humidity allows for potential moisture absorption, which can act as a plasticizer within the epoxy network, reducing intermolecular forces and lowering stiffness. The residual catalyst (2-methylimidazole) remaining in the matrix could also theoretically disrupt packing efficiency. Dominant Factor: The high crosslink density achieved through the tri-functional epoxy component and anhydride curing agent, coupled with the intrinsic rigidity of the bisphenol-A aromatic structures, qualitatively dominates the mechanical response. These structural features establish a highly constrained network in the glassy state, outweighing the minor softening effects of moisture or aliphatic content.

title: Multiscale bridging method to characterize elasto-plastic properties of polymer nanocomposites
processing_history: Interphase properties characterized via Multiscale Bridging Method (MBM) combining MD (Materials Studio 5.5, PCFF) and Finite Element Homogenization (FEH, Digimat 2021, Abaqus 2021). Interphase thickness 7.72 Å. Young's modulus derived from inverse characterization.
hierarchical_structure: Interphase region near SiC nanoparticle (Radius 8.25 Å). Crosslink ratio 85.0%. Volume fraction 5.4%.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a crosslinked epoxy-amine network synthesized from Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol F (EPON862) and Triethylenetetramine (TETA) in a 3:1 ratio, reinforced with 5.4 vol% Silicon Carbide (SiC) nanoparticles. The hierarchical structure focuses on the interphase region surrounding SiC nanoparticles with a radius of 8.25 Å, exhibiting an interphase thickness of 7.72 Å and a crosslink ratio of 85.0%. Interphase properties were characterized via a Multiscale Bridging Method combining Molecular Dynamics simulations using the PCFF force field and Finite Element Homogenization, from which the Young's modulus was derived through inverse characterization.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of rigid Silicon Carbide nanoparticles acts as a high-modulus reinforcement phase, significantly driving the overall stiffness of the composite upward through load transfer mechanisms. Additionally, the aromatic bisphenol F backbone provides intrinsic chain rigidity, while the 85.0% crosslink ratio restricts segmental mobility within the epoxy network, further enhancing the modulus. The confinement of polymer chains within the thin interphase region near the nanoparticle surface also limits conformational freedom, contributing to a localized increase in stiffness. Decreasing Factors: The crosslink ratio of 85.0% implies that 15.0% of potential crosslinking sites remain unreacted, introducing network defects and dangling chains that reduce the effective network density and lower the modulus compared to a fully cured system. Furthermore, nanoscale interfacial regions can sometimes exhibit increased free volume or packing frustration if polymer-filler adhesion is imperfect, which would qualitatively reduce the local modulus. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic high stiffness of the ceramic SiC filler combined with the rigid aromatic epoxy network and substantial crosslink density qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, leading to a reinforced Young's modulus that exceeds that of the neat polymer matrix despite the presence of minor network defects.

The Young's modulus was not determined through direct mechanical testing but was derived via inverse characterization utilizing a Multiscale Bridging Method that integrated Molecular Dynamics simulations using the PCFF force field with Finite Element Homogenization. This computational workflow facilitated the modeling of interphase properties, specifically identifying an interphase thickness of 7.72 Å within the composite structure.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a covalently crosslinked thermoset network between EPON862 and TETA restricts polymer chain segment mobility, establishing a rigid baseline modulus compared to linear thermoplastics. title: Preparation, dielectric and thermomechanical properties of a novel epoxy resin system cured at room temperature
processing_history: Mixed by magnetic stirrer at 92 °C until diamine melted, cooled to room temperature, acrylic acid added (fixed –NH/–COOH ratio of 0.5), poured into Teflon molds, cured at room temperature for 4 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test using Instron 3359 at 1 mm/min crosshead speed.
hierarchical_structure: Crosslinked epoxy network. Fracture surface displays river-like structure indicating brittle failure characteristics.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a crosslinked epoxy network synthesized from Bisphenol A-type epoxy resin (E51) and 4,4'-Diaminodiphenyl methane (DDM) hardener, modified with Acrylic acid (HAA) at a fixed –NH/–COOH ratio of 0.5. The preparation involved mixing the epoxy and diamine components via magnetic stirring at 92 °C until the diamine melted, followed by cooling to room temperature prior to the addition of acrylic acid. The mixture was cast into Teflon molds and cured at room temperature for 4 hours. Mechanical properties were evaluated using a uniaxial tensile test on an Instron 3359 at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min. Hierarchical characterization of the fracture surface revealed a river-like morphology, consistent with brittle failure mechanisms typical of rigid thermoset networks.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The presence of rigid aromatic rings within both the Bisphenol A epoxy backbone and the DDM hardener significantly restricts segmental chain mobility, intrinsically enhancing the stiffness of the material. Furthermore, the formation of a crosslinked network through the epoxy-amine reaction prevents viscous flow and chain slippage under load, which is a primary driver for a high Young's Modulus. The observed river-like fracture structure further supports the presence of a rigid network structure that fails via brittle mechanisms rather than plastic deformation. Decreasing Factors: The curing process conducted at room temperature for only 4 hours may result in incomplete conversion of functional groups compared to elevated temperature curing protocols, potentially leading to a lower crosslink density and reduced modulus. Additionally, the incorporation of Acrylic acid (HAA) modifies the network topology; depending on the reaction efficiency, this modification can introduce free volume or flexible segments that disrupt the dense packing of the pure epoxy-amine network, potentially lowering the overall stiffness. Dominant Factor: The inherent rigidity of the aromatic constituents and the establishment of a crosslinked thermoset network qualitatively dominate the mechanical response. Despite the potential limitations imposed by room temperature curing and chemical modification, the structural integrity provided by the covalently bonded aromatic network ensures a high baseline stiffness, as evidenced by the brittle failure mode observed in the hierarchical structure.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a Bisphenol A-type epoxy resin (E51) cured with 4,4'-Diaminodiphenyl methane (DDM) and modified with acrylic acid (HAA). Preparation involved mixing the resin and diamine via magnetic stirrer at 92 °C until melting, followed by cooling to room temperature. Acrylic acid was then added to maintain a fixed –NH/–COOH ratio of 0.5, after which the mixture was poured into Teflon molds and cured at room temperature for 4 hours. The Young's modulus was characterized using a uniaxial tensile test on an Instron 3359 at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The chemical composition features rigid aromatic structures within both the Bisphenol A epoxy backbone and the DDM hardener, which inherently restrict segmental mobility and enhance stiffness. Decreasing Factors: The processing history specifies curing at room temperature for only 4 hours, which likely results in incomplete conversion and a lower crosslink density compared to elevated temperature curing cycles, thereby reducing the overall stiffness. Additionally, the incorporation of acrylic acid may introduce free volume or disrupt the optimal network topology if it consumes amine hardener without contributing proportionally to network rigidity, potentially acting as a softening agent. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic structural rigidity provided by the aromatic epoxy-amine network formation is the dominant factor, ensuring the material behaves as a rigid solid; however, the final modulus is qualitatively constrained by the mild curing conditions which limit the maximum achievable crosslink density.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting epoxy network formed from Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A (DGEBA) resin cured with Polyoxypropylenediamine (Jeffamine D-230). To enhance toughness, 1.0 wt-% Core-Shell Rubber (EM500A) particles were incorporated as a filler phase. The fabrication process involved ultrasonication of the CSR particles and epoxy resin for 4 hours, followed by the addition of the stoichiometric curing agent and stirring. The mixture was cast into a metallic mould and subjected to a thermal curing cycle of 80°C for 4 hours, followed by post-curing at 125°C for 2 hours. Morphological analysis reveals a heterogeneous structure where some CSR particles are well dispersed within the epoxy matrix while others exist as aggregates. Mechanical characterization was performed at Room Temperature using an MTS Landmark Servohydraulic test system with a 10 kN load cell at a crosshead speed of 2 mm/min, following ASTM D638-96 standards.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A (DGEBA) monomer features rigid aromatic rings that restrict segmental motion, inherently contributing to a high stiffness. Additionally, the processing history includes a post-curing step at 125°C, which likely maximizes the crosslink density of the thermoset network, thereby increasing the Young's Modulus. The use of ultrasonication during mixing promotes the dispersion of filler particles, which can enhance load transfer for the well-dispersed fraction. Decreasing Factors: The use of Polyoxypropylenediamine (Jeffamine D-230) as the curing agent introduces flexible polyether segments between crosslinks, which increases chain mobility and reduces the network stiffness compared to rigid aromatic amines. Additionally, the Core-Shell Rubber (EM500A) filler has a significantly lower modulus than the epoxy matrix; adding a compliant phase generally lowers the overall Young's Modulus. The observed aggregation of some CSR particles creates stress concentrations and reduces the effective interfacial area for load transfer, further diminishing the modulus. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic rigidity of the DGEBA backbone combined with the high crosslink density achieved through the elevated post-curing temperature qualitatively dominates the final modulus behavior, establishing a stiff thermoset baseline. However, the presence of the flexible curing agent and the compliant rubber filler, exacerbated by particle aggregation, acts as a modifying factor that qualitatively reduces the modulus relative to a fully rigid, neat epoxy system.

title: Composition as a Means To Control Morphology and Properties of Epoxy Based Dual-Phase Structural Electrolytes
processing_history: MTM57 resin mixed with EMIM-TFSI + LiTFSI (50:50 wt% ratio). LiTFSI concentration 2.3 mol/L in electrolyte. Components preheated at 75 °C for 5 min and mixed using a speedmixer at 3000 rpm for 4 min. Transferred into a preheated mold and cured using cycle: ramp to 120 °C at 0.5 °C/min, dwell at 120 °C for 60 min, ramp to room temperature at 3 °C/min. Young's modulus measured by three-point bending tests at room temperature using a Zwick testing frame equipped with a 1 kN load cell and an optical Heidenhain displacement transducer on rectangular samples (length 30-35 mm, width 4 mm, thickness 2-3 mm).
hierarchical_structure: Bicontinuous morphology containing continuous (coarse) epoxy networks (cross-section ~100 μm) surrounded by connected spherical epoxy nodules.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a MTM57 epoxy/amine system blended with EMIM-TFSI ionic liquid electrolyte and LiTFSI salt, formulated with a 50:50 weight ratio between the resin system and the electrolyte phase containing a LiTFSI concentration of 2.3 mol/L. Processing involved preheating components at 75 °C followed by high-shear mixing at 3000 rpm for 4 minutes using a speedmixer, after which the mixture was transferred to a preheated mold and cured via a thermal cycle ramping to 120 °C at 0.5 °C/min, dwelling for 60 minutes, and cooling to room temperature at 3 °C/min. The resulting material exhibits a bicontinuous morphology characterized by continuous coarse epoxy networks with a cross-section of approximately 100 μm surrounded by connected spherical epoxy nodules, and its Young's modulus was evaluated at room temperature using three-point bending tests on rectangular specimens via a Zwick testing frame equipped with a 1 kN load cell and optical displacement transducer.

The bicontinuous morphology featuring continuous coarse epoxy networks acts as a structural scaffold that supports mechanical load, while the high-shear mixing process promotes homogeneous dispersion which may minimize stress concentration points that could otherwise lower effective stiffness. Decreasing Factors: The incorporation of EMIM-TFSI ionic liquid at 50 wt% acts as a potent plasticizer, significantly increasing free volume and chain segment mobility within the matrix, thereby drastically reducing stiffness relative to a neat epoxy. Additionally, the presence of LiTFSI salt dissolved in the electrolyte phase further fluidizes the system, and the bicontinuous structure implies a substantial volume fraction of this soft electrolyte phase interspersed within the epoxy, compromising the continuity of the rigid load-bearing phase. Dominant Factor: The massive dilution effect caused by the 50 wt% ionic liquid content is the dominant factor. Although the cured epoxy network provides a rigid framework, the percolation of the soft liquid electrolyte phase throughout the bicontinuous morphology fundamentally shifts the material behavior from a rigid thermoset toward a soft polymer electrolyte gel, qualitatively resulting in a Young's modulus significantly lower than that of the pristine cured epoxy resin.

The formulation comprises a 50:50 wt% ratio of resin to electrolyte, with a LiTFSI concentration of 2.3 mol/L within the electrolyte phase. analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a covalently crosslinked network via the MTM57 epoxy/amine curing cycle provides a structural scaffold that inherently resists deformation. The thermal cure at 120 °C ensures sufficient crosslink density, while the presence of LiTFSI salt may introduce ionic coordination interactions that slightly reinforce the electrolyte phase. The resulting morphology resembles an ionogel rather than a rigid thermoset, leading to a substantial reduction in stiffness. Dominant Factor: The plasticization effect induced by the high mass fraction of the ionic liquid dominates the mechanical response. Despite the rigid epoxy backbone, the continuity and volume fraction of the soft electrolyte phase dictate the macroscopic stiffness, resulting in a Young's modulus significantly lower than that of the neat cured epoxy resin.

title: A Study of Some Mechanical Properties of Composite Materials with a Dammar-Based Hybrid Matrix and Reinforced by Waste Paper
processing_history: Composite cast with 80% Dammar hybrid resin matrix and 18 layers of waste paper sheets (pre-impregnated). Uniform pressure of 27,000 N/m^2 applied. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test according to ASTM D3039 using Lrx Plus testing machine (2.5 kN force range).
hierarchical_structure: Layered distribution of reinforcement (18 layers).

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample constitutes a hybrid composite material featuring a matrix blend of 80 vol% Dammar resin and 20 vol% Epoxy resin (Resoltech 1050/1055). This matrix reinforces 18 layers of waste paper sheets, incorporated at a mass ratio of 0.51, resulting in a layered distribution of reinforcement throughout the bulk. The composite was fabricated via a casting method where the waste paper sheets were pre-impregnated, followed by the application of a uniform pressure of 27,000 N/m^2 to ensure consolidation. Mechanical characterization was performed via uniaxial tensile testing in accordance with ASTM D3039 standards using an Lrx Plus testing machine.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of waste paper sheets acts as a rigid cellulosic reinforcement, significantly enhancing stiffness compared to the neat resin matrix due to the high intrinsic modulus of cellulose fibers. The high mass ratio of 0.51 suggests a substantial volume fraction of fibers, which typically drives the composite modulus upward according to rule-of-mixtures behavior. Additionally, the application of uniform pressure during processing promotes better consolidation, reducing void content and improving fiber packing density, which positively correlates with stiffness. The epoxy component in the hybrid matrix provides a rigid thermoset network that supports load transfer to the reinforcement. Decreasing Factors: The inclusion of Dammar resin, a natural terpene resin, may introduce a phase with lower intrinsic stiffness compared to synthetic high-performance epoxies, potentially lowering the overall matrix modulus. The layered structure introduces interfaces between paper sheets which could act as stress concentrators or sites for delamination if interlaminar shear strength is insufficient, potentially reducing the effective modulus measured in tension. Furthermore, natural fiber variability in the waste paper can lead to inconsistencies that limit the maximum achievable stiffness compared to synthetic continuous fibers. Dominant Factor: The high loading fraction of cellulosic reinforcement combined with the consolidation pressure is likely the dominant factor. While the Dammar resin might soften the matrix slightly compared to pure epoxy, the sheer volume and stiffness of the paper layers, effectively bonded due to pre-impregnation and pressure, will dictate the composite behavior, resulting in a modulus significantly higher than the unreinforced hybrid resin.

The composite was processed via casting with the pre-impregnated layers subjected to a uniform consolidation pressure of 27,000 N/m^2. Mechanical characterization involved measuring the Young's modulus by uniaxial tensile test according to ASTM D3039 using an Lrx Plus testing machine with a 2.5 kN force range.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The addition of waste paper sheets introduces cellulose-based reinforcement which typically possesses a higher intrinsic stiffness than the polymer matrix, driving the modulus up through the rule of mixtures. Decreasing Factors: The Dammar resin component may have a lower intrinsic modulus compared to fully synthetic thermosets, potentially reducing the baseline stiffness of the matrix phase. Furthermore, potential hydrophilic-hydrophobic mismatches between the waste paper fibers and the resin matrix could result in weak interfacial bonding, limiting the effective reinforcement efficiency. Dominant Factor: The substantial reinforcement loading, evidenced by the 18 layers and 0.51 mass ratio, qualitatively dominates the mechanical response. The high volume fraction of stiff cellulose fibers generally overrides the matrix properties and interfacial defects, resulting in a net increase in Young's modulus relative to the unreinforced hybrid resin.

title: Improvement Mechanical and Antibacterial Properties of Epoxy by Polyethylene Glycol and Ag/CuO Nanoparticles
processing_history: Epoxy resin blended with PEG, poured into silicone mold, cured in oven at 91.9 °C for 3.59 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test according to ASTM D638-10 using universal TB1 machine. (Run 16)
hierarchical_structure: Amorphous epoxy matrix with PEG plasticizer.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises an amorphous epoxy matrix synthesized from KER 828 epoxy resin and an epoxy hardener, incorporated with 15.95 wt% polyethylene glycol (PEG-200) serving as a plasticizer. Preparation involved blending the resin with the PEG additive, casting the mixture into a silicone mold, and thermally curing at 91.9 °C for 3.59 hours. The resulting crosslinked network was subjected to uniaxial tensile testing following ASTM D638-10 standards using a universal TB1 machine to evaluate its mechanical properties.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a covalently crosslinked network between the KER 828 epoxy resin and the hardener inherently restricts chain mobility, establishing a baseline stiffness. The thermal curing history at 91.9 °C facilitates crosslink density development, which typically correlates with increased resistance to elastic deformation. Decreasing Factors: The incorporation of 15.95 wt% PEG-200 acts as a significant plasticizing agent; the flexible ether linkages and low glass transition temperature of PEG increase the free volume within the epoxy matrix and shield intermolecular interactions, thereby reducing the material's resistance to deformation. Additionally, the amorphous nature of the matrix lacks crystalline domains that could otherwise reinforce the modulus. Dominant Factor: While the crosslinked network provides structural integrity, the substantial loading of the low-modulus PEG plasticizer is the dominant factor. The plasticization effect qualitatively overrides the stiffening contribution of the crosslinks relative to a neat epoxy system, resulting in a net reduction in Young's modulus compared to the unmodified cured resin.

title: Bio-Based Alternative to the Diglycidyl Ether of Bisphenol A with Controlled Materials Properties
processing_history: Diphenolic acid esterified with 1-pentanol (heated to 90 °C, 16 h), then glycidated with epichlorohydrin and NaOH (reflux 30 min). Resulting DGEDP-n-pentyl ester mixed with nearly stoichiometric amounts of isophorone diamine, degassed, compression molded for 4 h at 80 °C and 4 h at 160 °C with 2 t of pressure. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test at 1 mm/min crosshead speed using Instron 4204 according to ASTM D638.
hierarchical_structure: Cured epoxy thermoset network. No significant glycidyl ester coproduct. Degree of cure closely approached theoretical maximum.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The material is a cured epoxy thermoset network synthesized via the esterification of diphenolic acid with a large excess of 1-pentanol at 90 °C for 16 hours, followed by glycidation with 15 equivalents of epichlorohydrin and sodium hydroxide under reflux. The resulting DGEDP-n-pentyl ester was mixed with stoichiometric isophorone diamine, degassed, and compression molded under 2 tons of pressure using a stepped cure cycle of 4 hours at 80 °C and 4 hours at 160 °C. Structural analysis confirms a highly cured network with no significant glycidyl ester coproducts, and the Young's modulus was determined by uniaxial tensile testing at 1 mm/min according to ASTM D638.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The presence of rigid aromatic rings within the diphenolic acid backbone provides intrinsic chain stiffness, while the use of isophorone diamine introduces a rigid cycloaliphatic structure into the crosslinking nodes, both of which restrict segmental motion and increase stiffness. Furthermore, the processing history involving compression molding under pressure minimizes void content, and the high-temperature cure cycle ensures the degree of cure approaches the theoretical maximum, maximizing crosslink density and network rigidity. Decreasing Factors: The esterification with 1-pentanol introduces flexible aliphatic pentyl spacers into the polymer backbone, which increases the free volume and chain flexibility between crosslinking points compared to unmodified aromatic epoxy systems. Additionally, the large excess of 1-pentanol during synthesis ensures these flexible units are fully incorporated, potentially lowering the overall network stiffness. Dominant Factor: The formation of a highly crosslinked thermoset network driven by the rigid aromatic backbone and cycloaliphatic crosslinker qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, establishing a high Young's modulus baseline, although the flexible pentyl esters prevent the modulus from reaching the upper limits typical of rigid bisphenol-based epoxies.

title: Experimental study of the CTBN effect on mechanical properties and mode I and II fracture toughness of a new epoxy resin
processing_history: Mixed using magnetic mixer on hot plate, degassed with vacuum pump. Cast into 4 mm thick silicone mold. Cured for 24 h and post-cured for 7 days at room temperature. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test according to ASTM D638-99 standard using SANTAM STM-20 machine at 5 mm/min crosshead speed, room temperature. E calculated from stress-strain curve slope between 0.05% and 0.25% strain.
hierarchical_structure: Isotropic epoxy/CTBN blend.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises an isotropic epoxy/CTBN blend formulated with Epoxy resin R510 as the matrix component at 100 phr and Carboxyl-terminated butadiene acrylonitrile (CTBN) as a toughening agent at 15 phr. Preparation involved mixing the components using a magnetic mixer on a hot plate, followed by degassing with a vacuum pump and casting into a 4 mm thick silicone mold. The system was cured for 24 hours and subsequently post-cured for 7 days at room temperature to facilitate network formation. Mechanical characterization was performed via uniaxial tensile testing according to ASTM D638-99 standards using a SANTAM STM-20 machine at a crosshead speed of 5 mm/min and room temperature, with Young's modulus (E) derived from the stress-strain curve slope between 0.05% and 0.25% strain.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a three-dimensional crosslinked network within the Epoxy resin R510 matrix intrinsically provides high rigidity and resistance to elastic deformation. Furthermore, the extended post-curing period of 7 days allows for continued crosslinking reactions at room temperature, potentially increasing the crosslink density and enhancing the stiffness of the thermoset network compared to a shorter cure cycle. The isotropic structure ensures uniform mechanical response without anisotropy-induced weaknesses. Decreasing Factors: The incorporation of 15 phr Carboxyl-terminated butadiene acrylonitrile (CTBN) introduces a rubbery phase with a significantly lower modulus than the epoxy matrix, which acts to reduce the overall composite stiffness. Additionally, the curing history relies on room temperature conditions rather than elevated thermal curing, which may result in a lower final degree of conversion and crosslink density, thereby limiting the maximum achievable rigidity of the epoxy network. The phase-separated morphology typical of toughened epoxies creates soft domains that comply more easily under stress than the continuous rigid phase. Dominant Factor: The dominant factor influencing the Young's modulus is the addition of the rubbery CTBN toughening agent. While the crosslinked epoxy backbone provides structural integrity, the substantial loading of the low-modulus elastomer qualitatively overrides the intrinsic stiffness of the neat resin, leading to a net reduction in modulus. This effect is compounded by the room temperature curing history, which likely prevents the network from reaching the maximum crosslink density achievable with thermal curing, further consolidating the trend toward a lower modulus relative to fully cured, unmodified epoxy systems.

title: Multiscale molecular modeling of SWCNTs/epoxy resin composites mechanical behaviour
processing_history: Computational modeling using Materials Studio 5.0 with COMPASS forcefield. Atomistic periodic systems built with periodic boundary conditions. Multistage equilibration: energy minimization (Steepest descent, Conjugate gradient), NVT-MD (300,000 steps, 1 fs), NPT-MD (1 GPa, 300 K, 5000 steps), annealing (750 K to 300 K). Young's modulus calculated using Discover Analysis tool via virtual uniaxial traction tests along x, y, z directions, averaged.
hierarchical_structure: Amorphous epoxy matrix with dispersed SWCNTs (8,8). Computational bulk models.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises an amorphous epoxy network synthesized from Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A (DGEBA) and ethylene tetra-amine, reinforced with 5.0 wt% (8,8) single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs). This system was modeled using Materials Studio 5.0 with the COMPASS forcefield, constructing atomistic periodic systems subject to periodic boundary conditions. The processing protocol involved multistage equilibration including energy minimization via steepest descent and conjugate gradient algorithms, followed by NVT and NPT molecular dynamics simulations at 300 K and 1 GPa, and a thermal annealing cycle from 750 K to 300 K. The resulting computational bulk models feature dispersed SWCNTs within the matrix, with the Young's modulus determined through averaged virtual uniaxial traction tests along the x, y, and z directions using the Discover Analysis tool.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of 5.0 wt% (8,8) single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) introduces a phase with exceptionally high intrinsic stiffness, serving as a primary reinforcement mechanism within the composite. The aromatic backbone of the Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A (DGEBA) monomer provides inherent rigidity to the epoxy matrix, while the computational processing history involving high-pressure NPT equilibration at 1 GPa significantly densifies the atomistic model, reducing free volume and thereby increasing the calculated stiffness. Additionally, the thermal annealing from 750 K to 300 K promotes structural relaxation into a lower energy state, further enhancing packing efficiency. Decreasing Factors: The amorphous nature of the cured epoxy network lacks the long-range order of crystalline polymers, which generally limits the maximum achievable modulus compared to semi-crystalline counterparts. Furthermore, the ethylene tetra-amine curing agent introduces flexible aliphatic segments between crosslinks, adding compliance to the network structure that counteracts the rigidity of the aromatic epoxide. In the computational context, if the interface between the SWCNTs and the matrix relies solely on van der Waals interactions without covalent functionalization, interfacial slip during virtual traction tests could reduce the effective load transfer efficiency. Dominant Factor: The exceptional intrinsic modulus of the SWCNT fillers combined with the high-density state enforced by the 1 GPa computational equilibration protocol qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, driving the Young's modulus (E) significantly higher than that of a neat, ambient-pressure cured epoxy system, despite the compliance introduced by the aliphatic curing agent.

title: Effect of adsorption, hardener, and temperature on mechanical properties of epoxy nanocomposites with functionalized graphene: A molecular dynamics study
processing_history: Molecular dynamics simulation using LAMMPS. NPT/NVT ensembles. Strain rate 0.7 ps^-1. Tensile test in Y direction at 300 K. Epoxy:Hardener ratio 70:30 wt%.
hierarchical_structure: Nanocomposite with functionalized graphene oxide (3 wt% oxide groups).

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The material system comprises a cycloaliphatic epoxy matrix cured with diethyltoluenediamine hardener at a weight ratio of 70:30, reinforced with 3 wt% graphene oxide filler to form a nanocomposite. The hierarchical structure is characterized by functionalized graphene oxide dispersed within the crosslinked network. Mechanical characterization was performed via molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS under NPT and NVT ensembles, specifically conducting a tensile test in the Y direction at 300 K with a strain rate of 0.7 ps^-1.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The cycloaliphatic structure of the epoxy monomer introduces rigid saturated rings into the backbone, restricting segmental mobility and increasing intrinsic stiffness compared to linear aliphatic chains. The formation of a crosslinked thermoset network via the amine hardener further constrains chain motion, while the incorporation of 3 wt% graphene oxide provides significant reinforcement due to the filler's exceptionally high intrinsic modulus and aspect ratio. Additionally, the molecular dynamics processing history involves an extremely high strain rate (0.7 ps^-1), which limits viscoelastic relaxation time and qualitatively results in a higher apparent modulus compared to quasi-static experimental conditions. Decreasing Factors: The functionalization of the graphene oxide, while aiding dispersion, introduces structural defects into the carbon lattice that may reduce the filler's intrinsic stiffness relative to pristine graphene. Furthermore, the simulation temperature of 300 K allows for thermal vibrations and free volume expansion within the polymer network, which generally reduces stiffness compared to simulations performed at 0 K. Dominant Factor: The combination of the rigid cycloaliphatic backbone, the dense crosslink density of the thermoset network, and the high stiffness of the graphene oxide reinforcement qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, driving the Young's Modulus significantly higher than that of a neat, linear polymer, despite the softening effects of thermal motion and filler defects.

title: Carbon fiber/epoxy composites: effect of zinc sulphide coated carbon nanotube on thermal and mechanical properties
processing_history: MWCNT functionalized with HNO3/H2SO4. Fillers dispersed in ethyl alcohol via ultrasonication (10 min), added to resin, stirred at 70 °C until alcohol evaporation. Hand lay-up with 3 layers carbon fiber, vacuum bagged for 24 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test using EMIC DL-1000 machine, crosshead speed 10 mm/min, gauge length 78 mm, room temperature.
hierarchical_structure: Carbon fiber laminated composite with epoxy matrix modified with 0.2 wt% MWCNTf.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a carbon fiber laminated composite utilizing an Epoxy resin MC 1152 matrix cured with a hardener. The epoxy matrix is modified with 0.2 wt% functionalized multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), which underwent acid treatment with HNO3/H2SO4 and were dispersed in ethyl alcohol via ultrasonication for 10 minutes prior to mixing with the resin and stirring at 70 °C to facilitate solvent evaporation. Fabrication involved a hand lay-up procedure with three layers of carbon fiber, followed by vacuum bagging for 24 hours to consolidate the structure. Mechanical characterization was performed via uniaxial tensile testing on an EMIC DL-1000 machine at a crosshead speed of 10 mm/min and a gauge length of 78 mm at room temperature.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The integration of three layers of continuous carbon fiber serves as the primary reinforcement, leveraging the high intrinsic stiffness of the fibers to drastically increase the composite Young's modulus along the loading axis. The addition of functionalized multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) provides secondary reinforcement within the matrix, where the HNO3/H2SO4 functionalization improves interfacial bonding and stress transfer efficiency between the nanotubes and the epoxy network. Furthermore, the vacuum bagging process for 24 hours likely minimizes void content and maximizes fiber packing density, contributing to enhanced structural rigidity. Decreasing Factors: The hand lay-up processing technique may introduce variability in fiber alignment and higher void content compared to automated methods, potentially limiting the maximum achievable modulus. There is also a risk that ultrasonication was insufficient to fully prevent MWCNT agglomeration, which could create stress concentration points that detract from stiffness. Additionally, incomplete evaporation of the ethyl alcohol solvent during the 70 °C stirring phase could leave residual plasticizing agents within the matrix, slightly reducing the matrix modulus. Dominant Factor: The continuous carbon fiber reinforcement is the qualitatively dominant factor determining the Young's modulus, as the rule of mixtures indicates that the high-modulus fibers bear the majority of the applied load in the longitudinal direction. While the MWCNTs and processing parameters refine the matrix performance and interfacial quality, the macroscopic stiffness is primarily governed by the volume fraction and orientation of the carbon fiber laminate.

title: Multi-Scale Analysis and Testing of Tensile Behavior in Polymers with Randomly Oriented and Agglomerated Cellulose Nanofibers
processing_history: Nanocomposite consisting of epoxy matrix filled with dry CNFs (diameter 25-50 nm, length 5-50 µm). CNF concentration 0.73 vol %. Tensile tests conducted on specimens following JIS K 7164 standard. Young's modulus determined from stress-strain curves. At least five tests performed.

Structurally, the nanofibers are randomly oriented and exist as agglomerated clusters dispersed throughout the epoxy matrix. Mechanical characterization was performed via tensile tests conducted on specimens following the JIS K 7164 standard, with the Young's modulus derived from stress-strain curves based on an average of at least five measurements.

Furthermore, the random orientation of the fibers reduces the effective modulus in the loading direction compared to aligned systems, while the observed agglomeration and low apparent aspect ratio of 7.5 indicate poor dispersion and reduced efficiency in stress transfer via shear lag mechanisms. title: Influence of carbon nanotubes grown on the fibres on damage progression in woven carbon-epoxy composites
processing_history: CNT grown on fabric (300°C heat, Ni catalyst dip, 120°C dry, 600°C reactor 90s). VARTM processing with 5 plies. Cured at 70°C for 1 h, post-cured at 160°C for 2 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test on Instron 4505 at 5 mm/min crosshead speed. Modulus calculated from stress-strain curve over strain range 0.1-0.3%.
hierarchical_structure: 2/2 Twill woven carbon fabric composite. Fiber volume fraction 50.6 ± 0.24%. CNT on fibers (2-4 wt% on fabric).

The composite laminate was manufactured via vacuum-assisted resin transfer molding (VARTM) utilizing five plies, followed by a curing cycle at 70°C for 1 hour and a post-cure at 160°C for 2 hours. Mechanical characterization involved uniaxial tensile testing on an Instron 4505 at a crosshead speed of 5 mm/min, with the Young's modulus derived from the stress-strain curve over a 0.1-0.3% strain range.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The high volume fraction (50.6%) of high-modulus 6K HTA carbon fibers serves as the primary load-bearing component, significantly elevating the composite stiffness according to rule-of-mixtures principles. The in-situ growth of multi-walled carbon nanotubes on the fiber surface creates a hierarchical structure that enhances interfacial shear strength and stress transfer efficiency between the fiber and the epoxy matrix. Additionally, the thermal post-curing at 160°C promotes a high crosslink density within the epoxy network, maximizing the intrinsic modulus of the matrix phase. Decreasing Factors: The 2/2 twill woven architecture introduces fiber crimp and undulation, which reduces the effective axial stiffness compared to unidirectional laminates due to misalignment of fibers relative to the tensile loading axis. Dominant Factor: The high volume fraction of the continuous carbon fiber reinforcement is the dominant factor determining the Young's modulus. While the hierarchical CNT modification improves interfacial properties and the cured matrix provides structural integrity, the intrinsic high stiffness of the carbon fibers aligned primarily along the load direction overwhelmingly dictates the overall composite modulus.
