title: Extraction of reinforced epoxy nanocomposite using agricultural waste biomass
processing_history: Hand lay-up fabrication. Epoxy resin and hardener mixed in 10:3 ratio with 3 wt.% organosolv lignin filler (extracted via Organosolv method). Sonication for 3 min at 0°C, vacuum degassing for 5 min. Cured at room temperature for 24 hours, then in oven at 100°C for 3 hours. Flexural Young's modulus measured by LLYOD LR 10K Plus UTM at 1.3 mm/min crosshead speed, according to ASTM D790.
hierarchical_structure: Epoxy matrix with dispersed organosolv lignin filler.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting epoxy matrix reinforced with 3 wt.% organosolv lignin filler. Fabricated via hand lay-up, the epoxy resin and hardener were combined in a 10:3 ratio with the lignin additive, followed by sonication for 3 minutes at 0°C and vacuum degassing for 5 minutes to promote dispersion and remove entrapped air. The composite was cured at room temperature for 24 hours and post-cured in an oven at 100°C for 3 hours, resulting in an epoxy matrix with dispersed organosolv lignin filler. The flexural Young's modulus was subsequently measured using an LLYOD LR 10K Plus UTM at a crosshead speed of 1.3 mm/min according to ASTM D790.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of rigid organosolv lignin particles acts as a reinforcing phase within the compliant epoxy matrix, theoretically increasing the composite stiffness according to rule-of-mixtures behavior. Furthermore, the thermal curing history, specifically the post-cure at 100°C, promotes high crosslink density within the epoxy network, significantly restricting chain segment mobility and enhancing the intrinsic modulus of the matrix. The vacuum degassing and sonication steps minimize void content and improve filler dispersion, preventing stress concentrators that would otherwise lower the effective modulus. Decreasing Factors: The relatively low filler loading of 3 wt.% limits the magnitude of reinforcement achievable compared to higher loading fractions. Additionally, the absence of explicit surface coupling agents in the processing history suggests potential weaknesses in interfacial adhesion between the hydrophilic lignin and hydrophobic epoxy, which could lead to debonding under stress and inefficient stress transfer. The hand lay-up fabrication method may also introduce slight inconsistencies in filler distribution compared to automated processing. Dominant Factor: The high crosslink density achieved through the specific thermal curing cycle is the dominant factor establishing the baseline stiffness of the material; while the rigid lignin filler contributes positively, the final modulus is primarily governed by the integrity and density of the cured epoxy network, with the filler providing a secondary reinforcement effect contingent upon interfacial quality.

title: Ultrahigh Performance of Nanoengineered Graphene-Based Natural Jute Fiber Composites
processing_history: Unidirectional S-Glass fiber preform used as reinforcement. Composite manufactured by vacuum resin infusion process with EL2 epoxy resin and AT30 hardener. Cured at room temperature for 24 h. Young's modulus measured by longitudinal tensile test according to ASTM D3039 using Instron 5985 testing machine at 2 mm/min cross-head speed.
hierarchical_structure: Unidirectional S-Glass fiber reinforced epoxy composite. Fiber volume fraction (Vf) 58%.

Manufactured via vacuum resin infusion with an unidirectional S-Glass fiber preform, the composite achieved a fiber volume fraction of 58%. The system was cured at room temperature for 24 hours to form the crosslinked matrix network. Mechanical characterization involved longitudinal tensile testing performed on an Instron 5985 machine at a cross-head speed of 2 mm/min in compliance with ASTM D3039 standards.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The high intrinsic stiffness of the S-Glass fibers relative to the epoxy matrix significantly enhances the composite modulus, particularly due to the unidirectional alignment which maximizes load transfer along the fiber axis during longitudinal testing. The high fiber volume fraction of 58% further amplifies this effect by ensuring the stiff reinforcement phase constitutes the majority of the load-bearing cross-section. Additionally, the formation of a crosslinked thermoset network during curing provides a rigid matrix capable of effective stress transfer between fibers. Decreasing Factors: The room temperature curing cycle, lacking elevated temperature post-curing, may result in a lower degree of crosslinking density within the epoxy matrix compared to heat-cured systems, potentially reducing the matrix contribution to overall stiffness. Furthermore, any residual voids inherent to the vacuum infusion process, however minimal, could decrease the effective load-bearing area and act as compliance sources. Dominant Factor: The high volume fraction and unidirectional orientation of the S-Glass fibers qualitatively dominate the Young's modulus behavior. In longitudinal loading, the rule of mixtures dictates that the composite stiffness is primarily governed by the fiber properties and volume fraction, rendering the specific cure state of the compliant epoxy matrix a secondary influence on the final modulus.

title: Physical, Mechanical and Thermal Properties of Jute and Bamboo Fiber Reinforced Unidirectional Epoxy Composites
processing_history: Vacuum technique used for preparation. Aligned fibers arranged on aluminium plate, covered, and surrounded by polypropylene sheet. Resin mixed with hardener pumped into mould. Cured in Pinette press (hot press) at 65 °C for 1 hour. Specimens dried in vacuum oven at 60 °C for 24 hours, conditioned at 30 °C and 50% RH for 72 hours. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test (ASTM D638) using Instron 3369 machine at 10 mm/min crosshead speed.
hierarchical_structure: Unidirectional void free composite. Eight layers of aligned jute fibers. Fiber distribution not uniform.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a composite system fabricated from PrimeTM 20LV epoxy resin and a hardener matrix reinforced with 52 wt% jute fibers. Preparation involved a vacuum technique where aligned fibers were arranged on an aluminum plate, enclosed by a polypropylene sheet, and impregnated by pumping the resin mixture into a mould. The material was cured in a Pinette hot press at 65 °C for one hour, followed by vacuum drying at 60 °C for 24 hours and conditioning at 30 °C and 50% relative humidity for 72 hours. Hierarchically, the structure consists of eight layers of aligned jute fibers forming a unidirectional composite described as void-free, though the fiber distribution is noted as non-uniform. Mechanical characterization was performed via uniaxial tensile testing according to ASTM D638 standards using an Instron 3369 machine at a crosshead speed of 10 mm/min.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The high loading of jute fibers at 52 wt% significantly enhances stiffness, as the natural fibers possess a higher intrinsic modulus than the epoxy matrix. The unidirectional alignment of the eight fiber layers ensures that the tensile load is applied parallel to the fiber axis, maximizing reinforcement efficiency according to the rule of mixtures. Additionally, the hot press curing process promotes crosslinking within the epoxy matrix, establishing a rigid network capable of effective load transfer, while the reported void-free structure minimizes stress concentrators that would otherwise compromise stiffness. Decreasing Factors: The non-uniform fiber distribution creates localized resin-rich regions or fiber bundling, leading to stress concentrations and inefficient load transfer that reduce the overall composite modulus. Furthermore, conditioning at 50% relative humidity may introduce moisture into the hydrophilic jute fibers and the fiber-matrix interface, potentially causing swelling or plasticization that lowers interfacial shear strength and effective stiffness. The relatively low curing temperature of 65 °C might also result in a lower crosslinking density compared to higher temperature cures, limiting the full rigidity of the matrix phase. Dominant Factor: The dominant factor governing the Young's Modulus is the high weight fraction and unidirectional alignment of the jute fibers. Despite the non-uniform distribution and potential moisture effects from conditioning, the sheer volume of stiff reinforcement oriented in the loading direction dictates the mechanical response, resulting in a modulus significantly higher than the neat epoxy matrix, governed primarily by the fiber properties and alignment rather than matrix imperfections.

title: Combining Mechanical Fortification and Ultralow Flammability in Epoxy Networks
processing_history: Epoxy resin (DGEBA) mixed with DDS (stoichiometric equivalent). Degassed and cured in N2 atmosphere at 160 °C for 6 h, followed by 220 °C for 2 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial compression testing using Instron 5800 at 2 mm/min crosshead rate on cylindrical specimens (10 mm diameter, 1:1 height-to-diameter).
hierarchical_structure: Glassy amorphous epoxy network.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: This material system comprises a crosslinked epoxy network synthesized from Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A (DGEBA) and 4,4'-Diphenyl diamino sulfone (DDS) mixed at stoichiometric equivalents. The precursor mixture was degassed and subjected to a thermal curing cycle in a nitrogen atmosphere, consisting of 6 hours at 160 °C followed by a post-cure at 220 °C for 2 hours, yielding a glassy amorphous epoxy network. Mechanical characterization was conducted via uniaxial compression testing using an Instron 5800 system at a crosshead rate of 2 mm/min on cylindrical specimens with a 10 mm diameter and a 1:1 height-to-diameter ratio.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of 4,4'-Diphenyl diamino sulfone (DDS) introduces rigid sulfone groups and aromatic rings into the network backbone, significantly increasing chain stiffness and intermolecular interactions. Furthermore, the stoichiometric mixing combined with the high-temperature post-cure at 220 °C promotes a high degree of crosslinking and conversion, minimizing free volume and restricting segmental motion, which substantially elevates the Young's modulus. Decreasing Factors: The presence of flexible ether linkages within the DGEBA prepolymer backbone provides some rotational freedom compared to purely aromatic structures, which may slightly mitigate the overall stiffness. Additionally, the inherently amorphous nature of the epoxy network lacks the reinforcing effect of crystalline domains often found in semi-crystalline polymers. Dominant Factor: The high crosslink density achieved through the elevated temperature curing cycle, combined with the intrinsic rigidity of the sulfone-containing aromatic network, qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, resulting in a high Young's modulus characteristic of fully cured glassy thermosets.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting epoxy network synthesized from Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A (DGEBA) and 4,4'-Diphenyl diamino sulfone (DDS) hardener. The components were blended at stoichiometric equivalents, degassed to eliminate entrapped volatiles, and cured under a nitrogen atmosphere utilizing a sequential thermal profile of 160 °C for 6 hours followed by a post-cure at 220 °C for 2 hours. Mechanical characterization was performed via uniaxial compression testing on cylindrical specimens with a 10 mm diameter and 1:1 height-to-diameter aspect ratio using an Instron 5800 system at a crosshead rate of 2 mm/min.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The molecular structure incorporates rigid aromatic rings from both the bisphenol A backbone and the diamino sulfone hardener, alongside a polar sulfone group, which significantly restricts segmental mobility and inherently increases stiffness. The stoichiometric mixing ratio optimizes the crosslink density of the thermoset network, while the high-temperature post-cure at 220 °C ensures a high degree of conversion, minimizing compliant unreacted monomers and maximizing network integrity. Additionally, the degassing step reduces void content, preventing stress concentrators that would otherwise lower the effective load-bearing area. Decreasing Factors: Potential reduction in modulus could arise if the high cure temperature induced slight thermal degradation or chain scission, though this is less common within standard processing windows. Furthermore, residual thermal stresses generated during cooling from the elevated cure temperature could theoretically introduce micro-defects, and any incomplete degassing would leave micro-voids that reduce the effective cross-sectional area resisting deformation. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic rigidity of the aromatic-rich chemical structure combined with the high crosslink density achieved through the stoichiometric formulation and aggressive thermal cure cycle qualitatively dominates the mechanical response. These structural and processing factors ensure a highly constrained network, driving the Young's modulus to higher values relative to less crosslinked or aliphatic epoxy systems, outweighing potential minor defects from processing.

title: Effect of adsorption, hardener, and temperature on mechanical properties of epoxy nanocomposites with functionalized graphene: A molecular dynamics study

The hierarchical structure was modeled as a nanocomposite and subjected to molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS within NPT and NVT ensembles. Mechanical characterization was performed via a tensile test oriented in the Y direction at 300 K with a strain rate of 0.7 ps^-1, simulating the behavior of a crosslinked thermoset matrix embedded with nanoscale fillers.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The presence of rigid aromatic rings within both the Bisphenol F diglycidyl ether and Diethyltoluenediamine monomers restricts segmental motion, intrinsically enhancing the stiffness of the polymer backbone. The formation of a crosslinked thermoset network further constrains chain mobility, while the incorporation of Graphene Oxide, which possesses a significantly higher intrinsic modulus than the polymer matrix, contributes to reinforcement through the rule of mixtures. Additionally, the functionalized oxide groups on the filler improve interfacial adhesion, facilitating efficient stress transfer, and the high strain rate (0.7 ps^-1) inherent to the molecular dynamics simulation limits viscoelastic relaxation, typically resulting in a higher calculated modulus compared to experimental timescales. Decreasing Factors: The introduction of nanoscale fillers can potentially disrupt the packing density of the epoxy network, introducing local free volume that may slightly reduce stiffness. title: Ultrahigh Performance of Nanoengineered Graphene-Based Natural Jute Fiber Composites

Dominant Factor: The dominant factor governing the Young's modulus is the high volume fraction of unidirectionally aligned jute fibers, which dictates the primary load-bearing capacity of the composite. title: Effect of Boron Nanoparticles on Epoxy Composites on Mechanical and Ionizing Radiation Protection Properties

Decreasing Factors: The curing process conducted at ambient room temperature for 24 hours may result in a lower final crosslink density compared to elevated temperature curing protocols, potentially leaving unreacted functional groups and increasing free volume which reduces matrix rigidity. title: Improving tensile properties of double-walled carbon nanotube strands by intercalation of epoxy resin

title: Mechanical properties of multi-walled carbon nanotube/epoxy composites

title: Synthesis of Aralkyl Novolac Epoxy Resins and Their Modification with Polysiloxane Thermoplastic Polyurethane for Semiconductor Encapsulation

Dominant Factor: The presence of the dense jute fiber reinforcement is the dominant factor determining the mechanical behavior, as the addition of the stiff fibrous phase fundamentally shifts the material response from a pure polymer to a composite, yielding a higher modulus than the neat resin despite the mitigating effects of the transverse orientation and ambient curing conditions.

title: Multiscale bridging method to characterize elasto-plastic properties of polymer nanocomposites
processing_history: Interphase properties characterized via Multiscale Bridging Method (MBM) combining MD (Materials Studio 5.5, PCFF) and Finite Element Homogenization (FEH, Digimat 2021, Abaqus 2021). Interphase thickness 7.72 Å. Young's modulus derived from inverse characterization.

title: Reinforcing the bandaged joint of double-walled carbon nanotube strands by intercalation of epoxy resin
processing_history: DWNT strands synthesized by CVD, bandaged into joints (~7 mm length). Joints intercalated by soaking in epoxy resin E-44 and polyamide hardener solution (volume ratio 1:1) in acetone at 30 vol.% concentration for 1 min. Cured for 8 h at 70 °C. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test on Instron 3365 tensile test machine.
hierarchical_structure: Bandaged joint of DWNT strands with intercalated epoxy resin. Structure consists of outer wrapping film and inner overlapped DWNT strands. Epoxy resin provides bonding between DWNT bundles.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The inclusion of double-walled carbon nanotubes provides an exceptionally high intrinsic stiffness that serves as the primary reinforcement phase, significantly elevating the composite modulus. Decreasing Factors: The use of acetone solvent during intercalation introduces the risk of residual plasticization if not fully evaporated, which could soften the matrix. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic high modulus of the DWNT strands qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, as the nanotube network bears the majority of the applied load; however, the ultimate magnitude is critically dependent on the efficiency of the epoxy matrix in transferring stress between the nanotubes, which is governed by the quality of intercalation and curing.

title: An experimental investigation of the mechanical behavior and damage of thick laminated carbon/epoxy composite
processing_history: Unidirectional Hexply M21 T700 prepreg (36 layers). Compaction using vacuum pump, vacuum bag evacuated to 0.7 bars. Loading rate 1 mm/min. Span length 150.4 mm. ASTM-D790-03. Instron model LM-U150. 10 kN load cell. Strain measured using digital image correlation (DIC). Room temperature.
hierarchical_structure: Thick laminated carbon/epoxy composite. 36 layers. Thickness 9.4 mm. Typical aeronautical stacking sequence. Fiber volume fraction 59%.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample is a thick laminated carbon/epoxy composite fabricated from unidirectional Hexply M21 T700 prepreg, consisting of an epoxy resin matrix reinforced with Toray T700GC carbon fibers at a fiber volume fraction of 59%. The laminate was constructed from 36 layers following a typical aeronautical stacking sequence to achieve a final thickness of 9.4 mm. Processing involved compaction via vacuum bagging evacuated to 0.7 bars, followed by autoclave curing at 180 °C with a heating rate of 2 °C/min for 120 minutes under 7 bar pressure. Rectangular specimens measuring 182 mm × 15.2 mm × 9.4 mm were prepared via waterjet cutting, and the Young's modulus was determined at room temperature using three-point bending tests according to ASTM-D790-03 standards with a loading rate of 1 mm/min and strain measured via digital image correlation.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of Toray T700GC carbon fibers at a high volume fraction of 59% drastically enhances stiffness due to the high intrinsic modulus of the carbon fibers compared to the epoxy matrix, adhering to the rule of mixtures. The autoclave curing cycle at 180 °C under 7 bar pressure ensures optimal crosslinking of the M21 epoxy matrix and minimizes void content, thereby maximizing interfacial load transfer efficiency and matrix contribution to overall stiffness. Decreasing Factors: The use of a typical aeronautical stacking sequence implies the presence of off-axis plies which contribute less to the longitudinal stiffness compared to a purely unidirectional 0° laminate, effectively reducing the macroscopic modulus in the loading direction. Additionally, the inherent compliance of the epoxy matrix limits the upper bound of the composite modulus, and waterjet cutting may introduce microstructural damage or edge delamination that could slightly compromise the measured stiffness. Dominant Factor: The high volume fraction of high-modulus carbon fibers is the dominant factor governing the mechanical response. Despite the multi-directional stacking and matrix compliance, the structural integrity and stiffness are overwhelmingly determined by the fiber reinforcement network consolidated by the high-pressure autoclave processing.

title: DGEBA thermosets modified with an amphiphilic star polymer. Study on the effect of the initiator on the curing process and morphology
processing_history: SP dissolved in epoxy at 80 °C. Yb(OTf)3 dissolved in acetone, added, vacuum for 1 h. Cured 5 h at 160 °C and post-cured 1 h at 180 °C. Young's modulus measured by nanoindentation using Berkovich tip, strain rate 0.05 s^-1, CSM at 45 Hz, 2 nm amplitude, Oliver and Pharr method, average of 16 indents.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A (DGEBA) epoxy system initiated by 1.0 phr Ytterbium triflate and modified with 5.0 phr Star Polymer. Preparation involved dissolving the Star Polymer in the epoxy resin at 80 °C, followed by the addition of Ytterbium triflate dissolved in acetone and a one-hour vacuum treatment to eliminate the solvent. The system was cured for 5 hours at 160 °C and post-cured for 1 hour at 180 °C to establish the final crosslinked network. Mechanical characterization was performed via nanoindentation using a Berkovich tip and the Oliver and Pharr method with continuous stiffness measurement at 45 Hz.

Furthermore, the aggressive thermal processing history, involving curing at 160 °C and post-curing at 180 °C, promotes a high degree of conversion and crosslink density, which severely restricts segmental motion and drives the Young's modulus upward. The vacuum treatment also ensures the removal of acetone, preventing solvent-induced plasticization that would otherwise lower stiffness. Additionally, modifiers are often utilized to improve toughness, which can come at the expense of bulk stiffness if the modifier phase is less rigid than the cured epoxy network. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic rigidity of the aromatic epoxy backbone combined with the high crosslink density achieved through the elevated temperature curing schedule qualitatively dominates the mechanical response. While the star polymer modifier introduces potential compliance, the dense network formation driven by the Ytterbium triflate initiation and high-temperature post-cure establishes a stiff structural baseline that likely outweighs the softening effects of the low-concentration modifier.

title: A Study of Tensile Properties and Performance of Bamboo Fiber-Epoxy Resin Composites
processing_history: Hand mixing of epoxy resin and hardener (2:1) with bamboo fiber powder. Poured into 3.2 mm stainless-steel mold. Cured 24h at room temperature. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test at 10 mm/min crosshead speed, ASTM D638, at 38°C. Particle size 0.25 μm.
hierarchical_structure: Bamboo fiber reinforced epoxy composite. Fiber-matrix interface analyzed by SEM.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The material is a bamboo fiber-reinforced epoxy composite consisting of Epoxy resin (E-182) and Hardener (H-192) mixed in a 2:1 parts ratio. Gigantochloa scortechinii bamboo fiber powder with a particle size of 0.25 μm was incorporated as a filler at a loading of 9 wt%. The composite was fabricated via hand mixing of the resin, hardener, and fiber powder, followed by casting into a 3.2 mm stainless-steel mold and curing for 24 hours at room temperature. The resulting structure was characterized as a fiber-matrix composite with interface analysis performed via SEM, and the mechanical properties were evaluated using uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 10 mm/min according to ASTM D638 at 38°C.

Additionally, the formation of a crosslinked thermoset network between the Epoxy resin (E-182) and Hardener (H-192) provides a rigid structural backbone that resists deformation. Decreasing Factors: The curing process conducted at room temperature for 24 hours may result in incomplete crosslinking conversion compared to thermal post-curing, thereby reducing the matrix stiffness. Furthermore, hand mixing can introduce micro-voids or fiber agglomerates that act as stress concentrators, while the testing temperature of 38°C is elevated above standard ambient conditions, promoting increased segmental mobility and thermal softening of the polymer matrix. The relatively low fiber loading of 9 wt% and the fine particle size (0.25 μm) may also limit the aspect ratio-dependent reinforcement efficiency. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic stiffness of the bamboo fibers and the crosslinked epoxy network establishes a baseline modulus higher than neat resin; however, the room temperature curing history and elevated testing temperature are likely the dominant factors limiting the final modulus relative to a fully cured composite tested at ambient conditions, as these factors reduce matrix rigidity and stress transfer efficiency.

title: Development of completely bio‐based epoxy networks derived from epoxidized linseed and castor oil cured with citric acid
processing_history: Citric acid dissolved in THF, DGEBA added (1:1 epoxy:acid equivalent), stirred at 70-80°C to evaporate THF, poured into steel mold at 90°C, cured for 6 hours, postcured at 120°C for 2 hours. Young's modulus measured by tensile test using Instron 3365 at 1 mm/min crosshead speed, 50 mm span length, according to ASTM D3039.
hierarchical_structure: Amorphous network (no crystallization in DSC). Plane fractured surface with nonuniformity observed by FE-SEM indicating brittleness.

Structural characterization via DSC confirmed an amorphous state with no crystallization, while FE-SEM analysis revealed a plane fractured surface with observed nonuniformity indicative of brittle behavior. Mechanical properties were evaluated via tensile testing according to ASTM D3039 using an Instron 3365 at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min.

Furthermore, the FE-SEM observation of surface nonuniformity suggests the presence of microstructural defects or voids potentially arising from solvent evaporation or network heterogeneity, which can reduce the effective load-bearing cross-sectional area and lower the measured modulus. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic rigidity of the aromatic epoxy backbone combined with the constraints imposed by the high crosslink density of the cured network qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, establishing a high modulus characteristic of brittle thermosets, despite the softening influence of the aliphatic acid spacers and morphological imperfections.

title: A comparative study on effects of natural and synthesised nano-clays on the fire and mechanical properties of epoxy composites
processing_history: Epoxy resin, hardener (weight ratio 5.36:1) and APP mixed using three roll mill (20 μm gap, 3 passes). Degassed at room temperature (21 °C). title: Epoxy Networks Modified by a New Class of Oligomeric Silsesquioxanes Bearing Multiple Intramolecular Rings Formed through Si–O–C Bonds

title: Mechanical and thermal properties of high volume-fraction carbon nanotube/epoxy composites, and property enhancement by UV ozone treatment of carbon nanotubes

Additionally, while the dispersion is noted as well-dispersed, the high filler loading increases the viscosity during infusion which could trap micro-voids or lead to incomplete wetting despite the vacuum assistance, locally compromising modulus. The intrinsic axial stiffness of the nanotubes combined with their percolated network structure within the composite overwhelmingly outweighs the matrix properties and potential interfacial deficits, driving the overall modulus significantly higher than that of the neat cured epoxy system.

title: In Situ Analysis of the Relationship between Cure Kinetics and the Mechanical Modulus of an Epoxy Resin

The resulting hierarchical structure is characterized as a cross-linked polymer network with a final degree of cure of approximately 0.75. The use of Brillouin Light Scattering to derive the modulus probes high-frequency mechanical responses, which typically yields higher modulus values compared to static mechanical testing due to the suppression of slow relaxation modes. Decreasing Factors: The final degree of cure of approximately 0.75 indicates incomplete conversion of reactive groups, resulting in a lower cross-link density than theoretically possible, which reduces the network stiffness. Additionally, curing at room temperature (22 °C) limits molecular mobility during network formation, often leading to a less dense network architecture compared to elevated temperature cures. Hand mixing may also introduce micro-voids or inhomogeneities that decrease the effective load-bearing cross-section. Dominant Factor: The formation of the covalently cross-linked network incorporating rigid aromatic bisphenol structures is the dominant factor establishing a high Young's Modulus baseline; however, the incomplete degree of cure achieved during ambient processing is the critical factor qualitatively limiting the stiffness from reaching its maximum theoretical potential for this epoxy system.

title: Synthesis of Aralkyl Novolac Epoxy Resins and Their Modification with Polysiloxane Thermoplastic Polyurethane for Semiconductor Encapsulation

Young's modulus (E') measured by DMA (Perkin-Elmer 7) in 3-point bending mode at 1 Hz, 5°C/min, at 20°C.
hierarchical_structure: Sea-island structure with dispersed polysiloxane TPU particles (1 µm or less) in epoxy matrix.

The system utilizes a phenol-formaldehyde novolac crosslinker in stoichiometric amounts and triphenylphosphine as an accelerator, processed through a condensation reaction and epoxide-isocyanate modification at 160°C before undergoing a staged thermal cure from 150°C to 210°C. Furthermore, the use of a stoichiometric phenol-formaldehyde novolac crosslinker combined with a high-temperature cure schedule up to 210°C promotes a high crosslink density, which significantly restricts segmental chain mobility and enhances stiffness. Decreasing Factors: The incorporation of 12.5 wt% polysiloxane TPU introduces a soft, flexible phase characterized by low-modulus siloxane bonds and urethane linkages. The formation of a sea-island structure with these compliant particles dispersed within the matrix creates regions of lower resistance to deformation, thereby reducing the overall bulk modulus compared to a neat epoxy system. Dominant Factor: The continuous epoxy-novolac matrix serves as the primary load-bearing phase, meaning its high aromatic content and extensive crosslinking qualitatively dominate the final stiffness behavior, although the dispersed soft phase effectively mitigates the maximum achievable modulus relative to the unmodified network.

title: Effect of silica fume and rice husk silica in bio-epoxy composites
processing_history: Solventless preparation, mechanical stirring (2500 rpm for 1 min), cured at room temperature for 7 days, post-cured at 80 °C for 2 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test (ASTM D638-14 Type IV) using Shimadzu AG-1S 10kN at 1 mm/min crosshead speed, room temperature.

Structural analysis via SEM identified the presence of the bio-silica within the matrix, noting some agglomerations and uneven dispersion resulting from silica-silica aggregated structures. Decreasing Factors: The use of Polyetheramine EDR-148 introduces flexible aliphatic and ether linkages into the network backbone, which increases segmental mobility and lowers the modulus compared to aromatic curing agents. Additionally, the observed silica agglomerations and uneven dispersion create microstructural defects that act as stress concentrators and inhibit effective stress transfer between the matrix and the filler, diminishing the reinforcing efficiency of the bio-silica. Dominant Factor: The crosslink density of the bio-epoxy matrix, governed by the curing and post-curing history, qualitatively dominates the final modulus behavior. While the rigid filler offers potential stiffening, the low loading fraction and significant agglomeration limit its contribution, making the intrinsic rigidity of the cured polyetheramine-epoxy network the primary determinant of the sample's Young's modulus.

title: Fire Retardancy of Aluminum Hydroxide Reinforced Flame Retardant Modifi ed Epoxy Resin Composite1
processing_history: Virgin DGEBA cured with TETA at room temperature. Samples prepared in cylindrical shape (14 mm x 28 mm). Young's modulus measured by compression test (ASTM D-695) using TIRA 2810 universal testing machine, 10 KN load cell, 1.3 mm/min crosshead speed.

title: Structure, morphology and properties of epoxy networks with dangling chains cured by anhydride
processing_history: DGEBF mixed with BGE, HHPA and DMP-30, stirred 15 min. Heated at 90 °C for 3 h, 120 °C for 3 h, 150 °C for 1 h. Tensile modulus measured by tensile tester (SANS UTM5205XHD) at room temperature according to GB/T 1040.2-2006.

Decreasing Factors: The inclusion of Butyl glycidyl ether acts as a mono-functional reactive diluent, which terminates growing polymer chains and reduces the overall crosslink density of the network. Dominant Factor: The structural rigidity provided by the aromatic epoxy backbone and the high crosslink density achieved through the stoichiometric anhydride curing and optimized thermal treatment qualitatively dominate the final modulus behavior. Although the reactive diluent introduces compliant elements, the percolated rigid network structure remains the primary determinant of the material's resistance to tensile deformation.

title: Influence of Commercial Biochar Fillers on Brittleness/Ductility of Epoxy Resin Composites

hierarchical_structure: Epoxy matrix with 2 wt.% Rice husk biochar filler. Biochar shows external core covered by spikes enveloping a honeycomb structure (avg size 1 µm, wall thickness 700 nm). High ash content (47.93 wt.%). Particle size distribution peak at 10 µm and higher dimension 50-100 µm.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The material is a thermoset epoxy composite comprising a BFA diglycidyl resin matrix crosslinked with a primary amine mixture consisting of 1,3-phenylenedimethanamine and N1,N3-dimethylpropane-1,3-diamine. Processing involved mechanical pulverization and dispersion of the biochar into the epoxy monomer using tip ultrasonication for 15 minutes with a pulsed cycle, followed by the addition of the curing agent and further ultrasonication for 2 minutes. The incorporation of Rice husk biochar, characterized by a high ash content, introduces rigid inorganic phases that are stiffer than the polymer matrix, thereby reinforcing the composite. Additionally, the use of tip ultrasonication during processing promotes filler dispersion and reduces agglomeration, which maximizes the effective surface area for stress transfer and supports higher modulus values. Decreasing Factors: The inclusion of N1,N3-dimethylpropane-1,3-diamine, an aliphatic diamine, introduces flexible methylene segments into the crosslinking network, which increases chain mobility and reduces the overall stiffness compared to a purely aromatic hardener system. Furthermore, the relatively large particle size distribution combined with the low filler loading may limit reinforcement efficiency and act as stress concentrators if interfacial adhesion between the biochar spikes and the epoxy matrix is imperfect. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic rigidity of the cured epoxy network reinforced by the high-ash content biochar filler qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, driving the Young's modulus behavior towards higher stiffness relative to the unfilled matrix. However, the final modulus is significantly modulated by the flexibility introduced by the aliphatic hardener components and the efficiency of stress transfer at the filler-matrix interface governed by the ultrasonication processing history.

title: Mechanical Behavior of Carbon Nanofibre-Reinforced Epoxy Composites

DETA hardener (10 phr) mixed, cured at room temperature for 24 h. analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a carbon nanofibre (CNF) reinforced epoxy nanocomposite formulated from Bisphenol A Diglycidyl Ether (DGEBA) resin and Diethylene triamine (DETA) hardener at 10 phr. The CNF filler was incorporated at 0.1 wt% using ultrasonication for 2 hours at 40°C to promote dispersion, followed by vacuum degassing overnight at 40°C to remove air bubbles prior to hardener mixing and room temperature curing for 24 hours. The resulting hierarchical structure is defined as a nanocomposite with improved CNF dispersion relative to shorter sonication times, though the processing induced some mechanical damage to the CNF length. Mechanical properties were evaluated via uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min following ASTM D638-03.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a covalently crosslinked thermoset network between the aromatic DGEBA resin and DETA hardener inherently restricts segmental motion, providing a high baseline stiffness compared to linear thermoplastics. The addition of Carbon Nanofibres, which possess an exceptionally high intrinsic axial modulus, introduces a rigid reinforcing phase that theoretically elevates the composite modulus through load transfer mechanisms. Additionally, the extended ultrasonication duration improves filler dispersion, reducing agglomeration-related stress concentrations and enhancing interfacial adhesion. Decreasing Factors: The high-energy ultrasonication required for dispersion likely caused mechanical shearing that reduced the aspect ratio of the CNFs, diminishing their reinforcement efficiency according to shear-lag theory. The relatively low filler loading of 0.1 wt% limits the volumetric contribution of the high-modulus phase to the bulk property. Furthermore, curing at room temperature may result in a lower final crosslink density compared to elevated temperature post-curing protocols, potentially reducing the intrinsic stiffness of the epoxy matrix. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic rigidity of the aromatic crosslinked epoxy matrix qualitatively dominates the absolute magnitude of the Young's Modulus due to the low filler loading. However, the net composite behavior is determined by the competition between the modulus enhancement from improved dispersion and the efficiency loss from fibre damage, resulting in a modest qualitative increase relative to the neat resin.

Decreasing Factors: The use of Diethylene triamine, an aliphatic amine, introduces flexible methylene sequences between crosslink points, which may result in a lower modulus compared to systems cured with rigid aromatic amines. Furthermore, curing at room temperature for 24 hours may not achieve full conversion or the maximum possible crosslink density compared to elevated temperature curing cycles, potentially leaving the network slightly under-cured. The very low loading of nanofibres (0.1 wt%) also limits the magnitude of the composite reinforcement effect. Dominant Factor: The fundamental stiffness is primarily governed by the crosslink density of the epoxy-amine network, as the matrix constitutes the overwhelming majority of the volume. While the carbon nanofibres provide reinforcement, their low concentration renders the matrix properties the principal determinant of the Young's modulus, though the vacuum degassing ensures these properties are not degraded by porosity.

title: Effect of adsorption, hardener, and temperature on mechanical properties of epoxy nanocomposites with functionalized graphene: A molecular dynamics study
processing_history: Molecular dynamics simulation using LAMMPS. NPT/NVT ensembles. Strain rate 0.7 ps^-1. Tensile test in Y direction at 300 K. Epoxy:Hardener ratio 70:30 wt%.
hierarchical_structure: Nanocomposite with functionalized graphene oxide (5 wt% oxide groups).

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a crosslinked epoxy nanocomposite system formed by reacting Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A with Diethyltoluenediamine at a 70:30 wt% ratio, reinforced with 5 wt% functionalized Graphene Oxide containing oxide groups. analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The rigid aromatic rings within the bisphenol A backbone and the high crosslink density established by the diamine hardener restrict segmental motion, inherently elevating E. The addition of 5 wt% Graphene Oxide introduces a high-modulus filler phase that reinforces the matrix through effective stress transfer, particularly given the functionalization which improves interfacial bonding. Additionally, the processing history involves a molecular dynamics simulation with an extremely high strain rate of 0.7 ps^-1, which suppresses time-dependent relaxation mechanisms and results in a higher apparent E compared to quasi-static conditions. Decreasing Factors: The aliphatic ethyl segments present in the Diethyltoluenediamine hardener introduce flexible links into the network structure that are less stiff than the aromatic components, potentially lowering the overall modulus. Furthermore, the introduction of oxide functional groups on the graphene filler may disrupt the perfect crystalline structure of the graphene sheets, slightly reducing the intrinsic stiffness of the filler compared to pristine graphene. Dominant Factor: The composite reinforcement effect of the functionalized Graphene Oxide within the rigid thermoset network is the primary driver for a high E, though the ultra-high strain rate defined in the simulation processing history qualitatively dominates the final calculated value by preventing viscoelastic relaxation.

Additionally, if the dispersion of Graphene Oxide within the epoxy matrix is non-uniform during the simulation initialization, agglomeration could create stress concentration points or reduce the effective interfacial area for load transfer, potentially lowering the composite modulus relative to a perfectly dispersed system. Dominant Factor: The synergistic effect of the rigid covalent crosslinks within the epoxy network and the high aspect ratio stiffness of the Graphene Oxide filler qualitatively dominates the final modulus behavior, establishing a high-stiffness composite structure. While the high simulation strain rate inflates the absolute value, the fundamental material architecture defined by the crosslinked matrix and nanoreinforcement dictates the primary mechanical resistance to deformation.

title: Improvement Mechanical and Antibacterial Properties of Epoxy by Polyethylene Glycol and Ag/CuO Nanoparticles

title: 3D-Printing of Lightweight Cellular Composites
processing_history: 3D extrusion printing of SiC-filled epoxy ink. Pre-cured at 100 °C for 15 h, cured for 2 h at 220 °C. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test at strain rate 2.0e-4 s^-1 using Instron 5566, longitudinal direction (along printing path).

Processing involved 3D extrusion printing of the SiC-filled epoxy ink, followed by a thermal curing sequence of 15 hours at 100 °C and 2 hours at 220 °C. Structural characterization indicates that the high aspect ratio silicon carbide whiskers are aligned with the printing direction resulting from shear flow within the nozzle. Mechanical characterization was performed via uniaxial tensile testing at a strain rate of 2.0e-4 s^-1 using an Instron 5566, with measurements taken along the longitudinal direction parallel to the printing path.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The inclusion of silicon carbide whiskers, which possess a significantly higher intrinsic stiffness than the polymer matrix, serves as a primary reinforcement mechanism. This effect is maximized by the processing-induced alignment of the high aspect ratio whiskers along the longitudinal testing direction, optimizing load transfer efficiency. Additionally, the high-temperature curing stage at 220 °C promotes a high crosslink density within the epoxy network, restricting chain segment mobility and increasing matrix stiffness, while the nano-clay platelets may provide secondary reinforcement. Decreasing Factors: The addition of 10 wt% dimethyl methyl phosphonate introduces free volume and reduces intermolecular forces within the matrix, acting as a plasticizer to lower the overall stiffness. Furthermore, the 5 wt% Basionics VS03 ionic liquid may disrupt polymer packing and act as a soft phase or internal lubricant, potentially reducing the modulus relative to a neat epoxy system. Dominant Factor: The reinforcement efficiency gained from the alignment of high-modulus silicon carbide whiskers along the stress axis is the dominant factor. In composite mechanics, the orientation of high-aspect-ratio rigid fillers parallel to the loading direction typically exerts a stronger influence on the macroscopic Young's modulus than the softening effects introduced by matrix modifiers, leading to a net stiffening effect relative to the unreinforced plasticized matrix.

title: Tunable reinforcement of epoxy-silica nanocomposites with ionic liquids†

hierarchical_structure: Fine nanocomposite morphology with well dispersed silica nanodomains.

The formulation includes a sol-gel precursor system comprising tetraethoxysilane (TEOS) and 3-glycidyloxypropyltrimethoxysilane (GTMS), reinforced with 11 wt% silica filler and modified with 0.6 wt% 1-triethylene glycol monomethyl ether-3-methylimidazolium methanesulfonate ionic liquid. Processing followed a two-step hybrid protocol where the silane precursors were pre-hydrolyzed with the ionic liquid at room temperature for 1 hour, followed by a sequential curing schedule of 2 hours at 60 °C, 2 days at 130 °C, and a vacuum post-cure at 150 °C for 2 hours. The resulting material displays a fine nanocomposite morphology with well-dispersed silica nanodomains, and its Young's modulus was characterized via tensile testing at 22 °C with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of 11 wt% rigid silica filler and the formation of an inorganic silica network via TEOS and GTMS sol-gel chemistry significantly enhance stiffness by introducing hard phases that restrict polymer chain deformation. Additionally, the aromatic structure of the DGEBA monomer contributes intrinsic rigidity, while the high-temperature curing profile (up to 150 °C) ensures a high degree of crosslinking density within the organic matrix. Decreasing Factors: The use of Jeffamine D2000 as the curing agent introduces long, flexible polyether segments between crosslinks, which increases chain mobility and free volume, thereby reducing the overall modulus compared to short-chain hardeners. Furthermore, the presence of the ionic liquid additive may induce a plasticization effect, further lowering intermolecular forces and stiffness. Dominant Factor: While the flexible Jeffamine backbone inherently lowers the baseline modulus of the organic phase, the formation of a percolated rigid inorganic silica network combined with the well-dispersed silica filler qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, providing substantial reinforcement that defines the final stiffness of the hybrid nanocomposite relative to a neat organic system.

title: Effective in situ material properties of micron-sized $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ particles in $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ particulate polymer composites

title: Preparation and physical characteristics of epoxy resin/ bacterial cellulose biocomposites

Processing involved dispersing the cellulose suspension and silane into the resin through mechanical stirring and ultrasonication followed by ethanol removal and a step-wise curing cycle at 80°C and 100°C. title: Development and characterization of thermoset green composites reinforced by unidirectional abaca fibers

title: Effects of moisture exposure on the crosslinked epoxy system: an atomistic study

The model was equilibrated under NPT conditions for 2 ns at 300 K and 101.3 kPa, resulting in a hierarchical structure characterized by water clustering into nano-droplets, increased free volume segregation compared to a dry system, and disrupted network-network hydrogen bonds. Furthermore, the hierarchical structure reveals water clustering into nano-droplets and increased free volume segregation, which create structural defects and reduce the effective load-bearing cross-section. The disruption of network-network hydrogen bonds also removes secondary interactions that typically reinforce stiffness, further driving E down. Dominant Factor: The covalent crosslinked network structure combined with the rigid aromatic DGEBA backbone qualitatively dominates the final E behavior by establishing the fundamental mechanical integrity and high stiffness baseline of the thermoset; however, the plasticizing effect of the 8 mass% water and the associated disruption of hydrogen bonds represent the significant modifying factors that suppress the modulus relative to a dry, densely packed network.

hierarchical_structure: Homogeneous cured epoxy network.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of a homogeneous cured epoxy network derived from the condensation of p-xylylene glycol (25 mol%) and 2-naphthol (75 mol%), followed by epoxidation using epichlorohydrin and sodium hydroxide. The resulting prepolymer was cured with a stoichiometric amount of phenol-formaldehyde novolac acting as a crosslinker and triphenylphosphine as an accelerator through a multi-step thermal treatment involving heating at 150°C for 1 hour, 180°C for 2 hours, and 210°C for 3 hours. The Young's modulus (E') was subsequently characterized using dynamic mechanical analysis in 3-point bending mode at 1 Hz with a heating rate of 5°C/min, specifically measured at 100°C.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The high molar ratio of 2-naphthol (75 mol%) introduces bulky, rigid naphthalene rings into the polymer backbone, significantly restricting chain segment mobility through steric hindrance and intrinsic chain stiffness. Furthermore, the use of phenol-formaldehyde novolac as a stoichiometric crosslinker establishes a dense three-dimensional network, while the aggressive multi-step thermal curing protocol up to 210°C maximizes crosslink density and conversion, both of which substantially increase the material's stiffness. Decreasing Factors: The incorporation of ether linkages during the epoxidation step introduces flexible points within the chain structure compared to purely carbonaceous backbones, potentially allowing for some segmental relaxation. Additionally, the measurement condition at 100°C represents an elevated temperature; if this approaches the glass transition region, increased thermal energy would enhance chain mobility and reduce the modulus relative to ambient conditions. Dominant Factor: The structural rigidity imparted by the high content of fused aromatic rings from the naphthol monomer combined with the high crosslink density achieved through the high-temperature curing cycle dominates the mechanical response. Despite the elevated measurement temperature, the highly aromatic and densely crosslinked network structure ensures the material remains in a rigid glassy state, qualitatively driving the Young's modulus to high values.

title: Mechanical properties of multi-walled carbon nanotube/epoxy composites
processing_history: MWNT (1.5 wt%) mixed with epoxy, sonicated (Bandelin HD3200, 20 kHz) for 2 h at 60% amplitude. Hardener added, stirred 10 min at 150 rpm. Vacuum degassed. Cured at 60 °C for 1 h followed by 2 h at 110 °C. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test at 1.5 mm/min crosshead speed, 25 °C, ASTM D638-IV, using Hounsfield H100KS machine.
hierarchical_structure: Untreated MWNT form agglomerates in the polymer matrix.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting epoxy matrix derived from Diglycidyl ether bisphenol-A and a polyamine hardener, reinforced with 1.5 wt% untreated multi-walled carbon nanotubes. Preparation involved dispersing the nanotubes in the epoxy resin via probe sonication at 20 kHz for 2 hours at 60% amplitude, followed by the addition of the hardener and stirring at 150 rpm for 10 minutes. The mixture was vacuum degassed and subjected to a sequential curing process of 1 hour at 60 °C and 2 hours at 110 °C. Hierarchical characterization indicates that the untreated nanotubes form agglomerates within the polymer matrix, and the Young's modulus was determined using uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 1.5 mm/min at 25 °C in compliance with ASTM D638-IV.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The development of a highly crosslinked thermoset network provides a rigid baseline stiffness, while the incorporation of multi-walled carbon nanotubes introduces a phase with exceptionally high intrinsic modulus that theoretically enhances the composite stiffness. The two-step curing cycle up to 110 °C promotes high conversion and crosslink density, further maximizing the rigidity of the epoxy matrix. Decreasing Factors: The formation of nanotube agglomerates acts as stress concentrators and reduces the effective aspect ratio available for load bearing, significantly diminishing reinforcement efficiency compared to an exfoliated state. The absence of surface functionalization on the untreated nanotubes leads to weak interfacial adhesion, causing interfacial slippage under load rather than effective stress transfer. Additionally, prolonged sonication may have shortened the nanotubes, further reducing their aspect ratio and reinforcing capability. Dominant Factor: Although the intrinsic stiffness of the fillers and the crosslinked matrix drive the modulus upward, the dominant factor governing the final mechanical response is the microstructural morphology defined by nanotube agglomeration and poor interfacial bonding. These structural defects limit load transfer efficiency, resulting in a Young's modulus that is constrained below the theoretical potential for this filler loading despite the rigid matrix foundation.

Mechanical characterization was performed using uniaxial tensile testing at 25 °C with a crosshead speed of 1.5 mm/min in compliance with ASTM D638-IV.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The aromatic structure of the DGEBA monomer and the formation of a dense crosslinked network via the polyamine hardener and high-temperature curing step (110 °C) intrinsically enhance the stiffness of the matrix. Additionally, the high intrinsic Young's modulus of the multi-walled carbon nanotubes contributes to reinforcement, while the vacuum degassing process minimizes void content that would otherwise act as compliance centers, and the prolonged sonication aims to improve filler dispersion. Decreasing Factors: The untreated nature of the multi-walled carbon nanotubes implies a lack of chemical functionalization, leading to weak interfacial adhesion between the filler and the epoxy matrix which limits stress transfer efficiency. Furthermore, the high amplitude and duration of the sonication process risk damaging the nanotube aspect ratio, potentially reducing their reinforcement capability. Dominant Factor: The high crosslink density established by the two-step thermal curing schedule provides the primary contribution to the bulk stiffness of the material; however, the overall modulus is qualitatively constrained by the weak interfacial bonding associated with the untreated fillers, which prevents the composite from fully realizing the theoretical stiffening potential of the carbon nanotubes.

title: Multifunctional naphthalene containing epoxy resins and their modification by hydrosilation for electronic application
processing_history: Synthesized from 1,1'-Bis(2,7-dihydroxy-1-naphthyl)methane novolac and epichlorohydrin. Mixed with stoichiometric DDS. Cured in aluminum tray at 150°C for 1hr, 180°C for 2hr, postcured at 200°C for 4hr. Storage modulus (E') measured by DMA (Perkin-Elmer 7 Series) in 3-point bending mode at 1 Hz, 10°C/min heating rate, at 20°C.
hierarchical_structure: Neat epoxy network, densely crosslinked.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of a neat, densely crosslinked epoxy network derived from a 1,1'-Bis(2,7-dihydroxy-1-naphthyl)methane based novolac epoxy resin and 4,4'-Diaminodiphenylmethane. The material was synthesized by reacting the novolac with epichlorohydrin, mixed with the hardener, and cured in an aluminum tray using a stepped thermal profile of 150°C for 1 hour, 180°C for 2 hours, and a post-cure at 200°C for 4 hours. The storage modulus was characterized by dynamic mechanical analysis in 3-point bending mode at 1 Hz with a heating rate of 10°C/min, measured at 20°C.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The presence of bulky naphthyl groups in the epoxy backbone provides significant steric hindrance and backbone rigidity, which restricts segmental mobility and inherently drives the modulus (E) higher. Additionally, the processing history indicates a high-temperature post-cure at 200°C, which promotes high conversion and creates a densely crosslinked network structure that further constrains chain motion and increases stiffness. Decreasing Factors: The methylene bridges (-CH2-) connecting the aromatic rings in both the novolac precursor and the diamine hardener introduce flexible linkages that allow for some rotational freedom, potentially limiting the maximum achievable modulus compared to fully fused rigid systems. Furthermore, the absence of reinforcing fillers in this neat resin system means the modulus relies solely on the polymer network without composite enhancement. Dominant Factor: The high intrinsic rigidity of the naphthyl aromatic structures combined with the dense crosslinking achieved through the rigorous thermal curing cycle qualitatively dominates the behavior, resulting in a high modulus typical of highly crosslinked aromatic epoxy networks in the glassy state.

The resin precursor was prepared from the corresponding novolac and epichlorohydrin, then mixed with a stoichiometric amount of the curing agent. Processing involved a multi-stage thermal cure in an aluminum tray, consisting of heating at 150°C for 1 hour, 180°C for 2 hours, and a post-cure at 200°C for 4 hours. Decreasing Factors: The methylene bridges connecting the naphthalene units introduce localized flexibility compared to directly fused aromatic systems, potentially allowing for some segmental motion. Furthermore, residual thermal stresses generated during cooling from the high post-cure temperature might introduce micro-defects or free volume fluctuations that could slightly reduce stiffness. Dominant Factor: The structural rigidity imparted by the naphthalene-based epoxy backbone, compounded by the high crosslink density achieved through the aggressive multi-step thermal curing profile, qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, ensuring a high storage modulus in the glassy region at the measurement temperature.

title: Improvement Mechanical and Antibacterial Properties of Epoxy by Polyethylene Glycol and Ag/CuO Nanoparticles
processing_history: Epoxy resin blended with PEG, poured into silicone mold, cured in oven at 80 °C for 3 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test according to ASTM D638-10 using universal TB1 machine. (Run 8)
hierarchical_structure: Amorphous epoxy matrix with PEG plasticizer.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The material system comprises an amorphous epoxy network synthesized from Epoxy Resin (KER 828) and an epoxy hardener, modified with 10 wt% polyethylene glycol (PEG-200) serving as a plasticizer. Preparation involved blending the resin with PEG, pouring the mixture into a silicone mold, and curing in an oven at 80 °C for 3 hours to finalize the crosslinked structure. The Young's modulus was subsequently evaluated through uniaxial tensile testing conducted in accordance with ASTM D638-10 using a universal TB1 machine.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a covalently crosslinked network between the Epoxy Resin (KER 828) and the hardener creates a rigid three-dimensional structure that restricts chain mobility, inherently driving the Young's modulus higher compared to linear thermoplastic counterparts. The curing process at 80 °C facilitates this network formation, establishing the structural integrity necessary for load bearing. Decreasing Factors: The addition of 10 wt% PEG-200 acts as a significant plasticizing agent; its low molecular weight and flexible ether linkages increase the free volume within the epoxy matrix and lubricate polymer segments, thereby reducing intermolecular friction and lowering the modulus. Additionally, the amorphous nature of the matrix lacks crystalline reinforcement, and if the 80 °C cure temperature was insufficient to reach maximum crosslink density, the resulting network defects could further decrease stiffness. Dominant Factor: While the crosslinked epoxy network provides the fundamental baseline rigidity required for a solid material, the presence of 10 wt% PEG-200 is the dominant factor influencing the final modulus behavior relative to a neat epoxy system. The plasticizer's ability to enhance segmental mobility and free volume qualitatively overrides the stiffening potential of the moderate thermal cure, resulting in a material with significantly reduced stiffness compared to the unmodified resin.

title: High mechanical properties of epoxy networks with dangling chains and tunable microphase separation structure
processing_history: DGEBF mixed with DDM/H-DDM (20/80 molar) and n-octylamine (5 mass%). Stirred 10 min. Pre-cured 60 °C/2 h. Cured 100 °C/2 h, 130 °C/2 h, 150 °C/4 h. Tensile test at room temperature, GB/T 1040.2-2006, SANS UTM5205XHD.
hierarchical_structure: Homogeneous morphology (no microphase separation observed by AFM). Amorphous (WAXS).

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting epoxy network synthesized from Bisphenol F diglycidyl ether cured with a mixed amine system consisting of 80 molar % 4,4'-diaminodiphenylmethane and 20 molar % 4,4'-diaminodicyclohexylmethane, modified with 5 mass parts of n-octylamine per 100 parts epoxy. The material was processed via initial stirring followed by a multi-step thermal curing schedule involving pre-curing at 60 °C and sequential curing stages up to 150 °C to ensure complete crosslinking. Structural analysis indicates a homogeneous morphology without microphase separation and an amorphous state, with mechanical performance evaluated through tensile testing at room temperature.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The presence of rigid aromatic rings within both the Bisphenol F diglycidyl ether backbone and the majority 4,4'-diaminodiphenylmethane curing agent significantly restricts segmental chain mobility, intrinsically driving the modulus (E) higher. Furthermore, the multi-step thermal curing history promotes a high degree of conversion and crosslink density, which stiffens the network structure. Decreasing Factors: The incorporation of n-octylamine introduces flexible aliphatic chains that act as internal plasticizers, increasing free volume and reducing the effective crosslink density, thereby lowering the modulus. Additionally, the substitution of 20 % of the aromatic curing agent with 4,4'-diaminodicyclohexylmethane introduces cycloaliphatic units that possess slightly greater conformational flexibility compared to purely aromatic links. Dominant Factor: The high stiffness imparted by the densely crosslinked aromatic network formed by the epoxy resin and the predominant aromatic amine curing agent qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, maintaining a high modulus despite the softening influence of the aliphatic modifier and cycloaliphatic co-agent.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting epoxy network synthesized from Bisphenol F diglycidyl ether cured with a mixed amine system consisting of 4,4'-diaminodiphenylmethane and 4,4'-diaminodicyclohexylmethane, incorporating n-octylamine as a modifier. The preparation involved stirring the components for 10 minutes followed by a multi-stage thermal curing cycle including pre-curing at 60 °C for 2 hours and subsequent curing steps at 100 °C, 130 °C, and 150 °C for 2, 2, and 4 hours respectively. Mechanical characterization was performed via tensile testing at room temperature in accordance with GB/T 1040.2-2006 standards using a SANS UTM5205XHD universal testing machine.

Dominant Factor: The intrinsic rigidity provided by the high concentration of aromatic rings from the primary curing agent and the high-temperature thermal treatment establishes a highly crosslinked, stiff network structure that qualitatively dominates the final Young's Modulus, although the flexible modifier serves to mitigate the brittleness and slightly lower the stiffness relative to a unmodified system.

title: Weldable, malleable and programmable epoxy vitrimers with high mechanical properties and water insensitivity
processing_history: Synthesized by curing DGEBF with TA curing agent (synthesized from Terephthalaldehyde and 3-aminobenzylamine). Mixture degassed at 60 °C for 1 h, cured at 80 °C for 3 h, 120 °C for 2 h, 150 °C for 3 h. Stoichiometric ratio of amine H to epoxy group (m) = 1.75. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test (Instron 5567) at room temperature, cross-head speed 1 mm/min. Immersed in deionized water at room temperature for 1 day.
hierarchical_structure: Crosslinked epoxy vitrimer network with dynamic imine bonds. High crosslinking density.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: This material is a crosslinked epoxy vitrimer network constructed from Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol F (DGEBF), Terephthalaldehyde, and 3-aminobenzylamine, featuring dynamic imine bonds and a high crosslinking density. The synthesis involved curing DGEBF with a curing agent derived from Terephthalaldehyde and 3-aminobenzylamine, where the mixture was degassed at 60 °C for 1 hour and subjected to a step-wise curing protocol at 80 °C for 3 hours, 120 °C for 2 hours, and 150 °C for 3 hours with an amine hydrogen to epoxy group stoichiometric ratio of 1.75. Prior to characterization, the samples were immersed in deionized water at room temperature for 24 hours, and the Young's modulus was subsequently determined via uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature with a cross-head speed of 1 mm/min.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The chemical composition incorporates rigid aromatic structures from DGEBF, Terephthalaldehyde, and 3-aminobenzylamine, which restrict segmental chain mobility through steric hindrance and intrinsically increase stiffness. Additionally, the hierarchical structure is defined by a high crosslinking density, which significantly constrains network deformation and drives the Young's modulus upward. The step-wise curing history up to 150 °C promotes high conversion of functional groups, reinforcing the network integrity. Decreasing Factors: The processing history includes immersion in deionized water for one day, where water absorption acts as a plasticizer by increasing free volume and reducing intermolecular friction, thereby lowering the modulus. Furthermore, the dynamic imine bonds may be susceptible to hydrolysis or exchange reactions in the presence of water, potentially loosening the network topology. The off-stoichiometric amine-to-epoxy ratio of 1.75 implies an excess of amine, which may result in unreacted species acting as internal plasticizers. Dominant Factor: While the water immersion and off-stoichiometric ratio introduce softening mechanisms, the high crosslinking density combined with the rigid aromatic backbone qualitatively dominates the final behavior, ensuring the material retains the high stiffness characteristic of a thermoset network despite the environmental conditioning.

Dominant Factor: While the aromatic backbone and thermal curing provide a rigid structural foundation, the combination of off-stoichiometric network topology and, most critically, the hygroscopic plasticization induced by water immersion qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, leading to a depressed Young's modulus relative to a dry, stoichiometrically balanced sample.

title: Characterization of carbon fiber reinforced resin composites by the nanoindentation technique
processing_history: Composite cured at 200 °C under 0.6 MPa pressure. Samples cut, inlaid with epoxy, lapped and polished. Young's modulus measured by nanoindentation (CSM indenter, Berkovich tip, 20 nm radius) with max load of 3 mN.
hierarchical_structure: CFRP with 48 layers [(45/0/-45/90)6]s. Carbon fiber/epoxy interface region.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample is a carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) composite consisting of an epoxy resin matrix reinforced with 60 vol% T800 carbon fibers. It features a hierarchical laminate structure composed of 48 layers with a symmetric stacking sequence of [(45/0/-45/90)6]s, specifically highlighting the carbon fiber/epoxy interface region. The material was processed by curing at 200 °C under 0.6 MPa pressure, followed by sample preparation involving cutting, epoxy inlaying, lapping, and polishing. Mechanical characterization was performed via nanoindentation using a Berkovich tip with a 20 nm radius under a maximum load of 3 mN to determine the Young's modulus.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of T800 carbon fibers, which possess an intrinsically high stiffness, serves as the primary reinforcement mechanism. The high fiber volume fraction of 60 vol% maximizes the load-bearing capacity of the stiff phase, while the curing process at 200 °C ensures a high crosslink density within the epoxy matrix, enhancing its rigidity. Additionally, the application of 0.6 MPa pressure during processing promotes consolidation and minimizes void content, which prevents compliance issues associated with porosity. Decreasing Factors: The epoxy matrix itself exhibits a significantly lower modulus compared to the carbon fibers, and the quasi-isotropic stacking sequence [(45/0/-45/90)6]s includes off-axis plies that reduce the effective stiffness in any single principal direction compared to a unidirectional laminate. Furthermore, the surface preparation involving lapping and polishing for nanoindentation may induce surface damage or smear the softer epoxy phase, potentially lowering the measured contact stiffness, while the nanoscale indentation depth might probe local heterogeneities such as the softer interface region or matrix between fibers. Dominant Factor: The high volume fraction of the high-modulus T800 carbon fibers qualitatively dominates the mechanical response, as the continuous fiber network provides a rigid scaffold that overwhelmingly dictates the composite's Young's modulus relative to the compliant epoxy matrix and processing-induced surface effects.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The material system comprises an epoxy resin matrix reinforced with T800 carbon fiber fillers at a loading of 60 vol%. The composite was fabricated by curing the mixture at 200 °C under an applied pressure of 0.6 MPa to ensure consolidation. Following fabrication, samples were cut, inlaid with epoxy, and subsequently lapped and polished to prepare the surface for mechanical characterization. The Young's modulus was determined using nanoindentation techniques employing a Berkovich tip with a 20 nm radius and a maximum load of 3 mN.

Furthermore, the curing process at 200 °C promotes a high degree of crosslinking within the epoxy network, increasing the matrix rigidity, while the applied pressure of 0.6 MPa minimizes void content, ensuring efficient load transfer between the phases. Decreasing Factors: Potential factors that could depress the measured modulus include interfacial weaknesses between the fiber and matrix which might limit stress transfer efficiency, or if the nanoindentation probe primarily contacts the softer epoxy-rich regions between fibers rather than the fibers themselves. Additionally, residual thermal stresses generated during cooling from the cure temperature could induce microcracking in the matrix, slightly compromising structural integrity. Dominant Factor: The dominant factor governing the Young's modulus is the high volume fraction of the T800 carbon fiber reinforcement. According to composite micromechanics, at 60 vol%, the fiber phase dictates the bulk mechanical response, rendering the contributions of the matrix properties and processing-induced variations secondary to the overwhelming stiffness contribution of the carbon fiber network.

title: Role of functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotubes on mechanical properties of epoxy-based composites at cryogenic temperature
processing_history: Oxidized MWNTs (O-MWNTs) prepared by acid mixture treatment (H2SO4:HNO3 3:1) at 110 °C. O-MWNTs added to epoxy resin, vacuum mixed for 5 min. Reacted for 4 h at 80 °C with catalyst. Curing agent D-230 added (weight ratio 100:30 to epoxy), stirred, cast into mold, cured at 80 °C for 4 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test according to ASTM D638-99 using MTS Landmark Servohydraulic test system at liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K).
hierarchical_structure: O-MWNTs reinforced epoxy composites. Some MWNTs impregnated in epoxy resin, some partially pulled out. Slightly rough fracture surface indicating slightly interfacial bonding.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises an epoxy composite network synthesized from Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol-A and Polyoxypropylenediamine (D-230) curing agent, reinforced with 0.5 wt% oxidized multiwalled carbon nanotubes (O-MWNTs). The nanotubes were pre-treated with an acid mixture at 110 °C prior to vacuum mixing with the resin, followed by the addition of the curing agent at a 100:30 weight ratio and curing at 80 °C for 4 hours. Hierarchical characterization indicates a composite structure where nanotubes are partially impregnated within the matrix with evidence of pull-out and a slightly rough fracture surface, suggesting moderate interfacial bonding. The Young's modulus was determined via uniaxial tensile testing according to ASTM D638-99 at liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K).
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of oxidized multiwalled carbon nanotubes introduces a high-modulus filler phase with a large aspect ratio, which intrinsically drives the composite Young's modulus upward. The acid oxidation treatment aims to improve dispersion and chemical compatibility, while the crosslinked epoxy network structure provides a rigid backbone. Furthermore, the processing history specifies testing at liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K), which significantly reduces polymer chain segmental mobility and places the matrix in a deep glassy state, drastically increasing the measured stiffness. Decreasing Factors: The use of Polyoxypropylenediamine (D-230) as the curing agent introduces flexible ether and propylene segments into the network, which increases free volume and chain mobility compared to rigid aromatic amines, thereby lowering the matrix modulus. Additionally, the hierarchical structure reveals nanotube pull-out and only a slightly rough fracture surface, indicating suboptimal interfacial bonding that limits stress transfer efficiency between the matrix and the reinforcement. Dominant Factor: While the cryogenic testing condition ensures a high baseline matrix stiffness, the composite's mechanical performance is qualitatively dominated by the interfacial characteristics; the observed interfacial weakness limits the load transfer efficiency, preventing the high-modulus nanotubes from fully realizing their reinforcement potential relative to the flexibility introduced by the curing agent.

Furthermore, the relatively short vacuum mixing time may limit the dispersion quality of the nanotubes, potentially leading to agglomeration that reduces reinforcement efficiency.
