Furthermore, curing under a constant tensile force helps maintain this alignment and minimizes nanotube waviness, further promoting an increase in Young's modulus. Decreasing Factors: Conversely, the room temperature curing process may result in a lower crosslinking density within the epoxy matrix compared to thermal curing protocols, potentially limiting the matrix contribution to the overall stiffness. Additionally, such a high filler loading increases the likelihood of nanotube agglomeration or incomplete resin impregnation within the yarn bundle, which could introduce voids or stress concentrations that detract from the theoretical modulus. Dominant Factor: The dominant factor governing the Young's modulus is the high volume fraction and strategic alignment of the Multi-walled carbon nanotubes achieved through the pultrusion and tension-assisted curing process. While matrix crosslinking density and interface quality play roles, the sheer intrinsic stiffness and orientation of the nanotube reinforcement phase overwhelmingly dictate the composite's mechanical response in the axial direction.

title: Development of epoxy resin-bamboo composites through toughening modification of epoxy resin
processing_history: EP dried at 70 °C under vacuum for 10 h. PES dried at 140 °C under vacuum for 4 h. EP and PES combined at ratio 100:8, heated with stirring at 140 °C until homogeneous. DDM added at ratio 1:3 relative to EP. Bamboo framework (BF) impregnated with EP-PES under vacuum at 40 °C for 90 min. Molded to 2.5 mm thickness. Hot pressed at 120 °C, 10 MPa for 7 h. Rested for 12 h. Elastic modulus measured by three-point bending test (CMT-5504) at loading speed of 1 mm/min, specimen dimensions 100 × 20 × 2.5 mm³.
hierarchical_structure: Co-continuous phase structure of the EP/PES blend. Dispersed PES particles and co-continuous phase structures developed during curing. Rigid PES segments maintain structural integrity.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The composite material comprises an E-51 epoxy resin matrix cured with 33.3 parts of 4,4'-diaminodiphenylmethane (DDM) and modified with 8 parts of polyether sulfone (PES-E2020P) as a toughening agent, reinforced within a Moso bamboo framework. Preparation involved vacuum drying of the epoxy and PES components at 70 °C and 140 °C, respectively, followed by blending at 140 °C to ensure homogeneity before impregnating the bamboo framework under vacuum at 40 °C. The assembly was hot pressed at 120 °C and 10 MPa for 7 hours to cure and consolidate the 2.5 mm thick specimens, which were subsequently rested for 12 hours prior to elastic modulus characterization via three-point bending at a loading speed of 1 mm/min. The resulting hierarchical structure features a co-continuous phase morphology within the EP/PES blend, where dispersed PES particles and rigid segments support the structural integrity of the bamboo-reinforced system.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a densely crosslinked epoxy network through the reaction with DDM provides a rigid matrix baseline with high inherent stiffness. The incorporation of the Moso bamboo framework introduces a high-modulus reinforcement phase that significantly enhances load-bearing capacity according to composite mechanics. Additionally, the rigid segments of the PES toughener and the co-continuous phase structure contribute to resisting deformation, while the hot pressing at 10 MPa minimizes void content, maximizing the effective load-bearing cross-sectional area. Decreasing Factors: The introduction of the PES thermoplastic phase creates interfaces within the matrix that may exhibit lower stiffness compared to the fully cured neat epoxy network, potentially limiting the maximum achievable modulus. Furthermore, the absence of explicit coupling agents for the natural bamboo fibers may lead to interfacial slip between the fiber and matrix, reducing the efficiency of stress transfer and lowering the composite modulus relative to the theoretical rule of mixtures. Dominant Factor: The presence of the Moso bamboo framework serves as the dominant factor, as the high intrinsic stiffness of the natural fiber scaffold fundamentally dictates the composite's resistance to elastic deformation, outweighing the subtle modulus variations introduced by the EP/PES matrix phase separation and toughening mechanisms.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The composite system consists of an E-51 epoxy resin matrix cured with 4,4'-diaminodiphenylmethane (DDM) and modified with Polyether sulfone (PES-E2020P) as a toughening agent. Prior to processing, the epoxy and PES were dried under vacuum at 70 °C and 140 °C respectively, then blended at a 100:8 ratio and heated to 140 °C to achieve homogeneity before DDM addition. This mixture was used to impregnate a Moso bamboo framework under vacuum at 40 °C for 90 minutes, followed by molding to a 2.5 mm thickness. The final cure was achieved via hot pressing at 120 °C under 10 MPa for 7 hours, followed by a 12-hour rest period, with the Elastic Modulus characterized by a three-point bending test at a loading speed of 1 mm/min.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a densely crosslinked thermoset network between the E-51 epoxy and DDM provides a rigid matrix backbone that inherently resists deformation. The incorporation of the Moso bamboo framework serves as a high-stiffness reinforcement, significantly driving the Elastic Modulus up through effective load transfer to the cellulose fibers. Additionally, the processing history involving vacuum impregnation and hot pressing at 10 MPa minimizes void content and enhances fiber-matrix interfacial adhesion, further maximizing structural efficiency. Decreasing Factors: The addition of PES as a toughening agent introduces a thermoplastic phase which may disrupt the continuity of the crosslinked network or create phase boundaries with lower stiffness than the cured epoxy, potentially driving the Elastic Modulus down relative to a pristine thermoset. Furthermore, inherent variability in the natural bamboo fibers or residual stresses from the thermal cycle could introduce compliance. Dominant Factor: The reinforcement effect of the Moso bamboo framework combined with the high-pressure consolidation during hot pressing is the dominant factor. The intrinsic stiffness of the fibrous reinforcement within the cured matrix overwhelmingly dictates the mechanical response, resulting in a net increase in Elastic Modulus compared to the unreinforced polymer system, despite the potential moderating influence of the toughening agent.

title: High-performance and multifunctional epoxy composites filled with epoxide-functionalized graphene
processing_history: Epofix resin mixed with G-EP dispersion in DMF, stirred 500 rpm 30 min, sonicated 40 kHz 1 hr. DMF removed. Hardener added (resin/hardener weight ratio 25/3), stirred 3 min. Cast into PTFE mold, degassed vacuum RT. Cured 60°C 12 hr + 120°C 4 hr. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test using Zwick/Roell Z030 machine at 5 mm/min crosshead speed, specimens 60x10x1 mm³.
hierarchical_structure: Epoxide-functionalized graphene filler. Uniform dispersion. Sheet thickness 1.3-3.1 nm. Covalent bonding with matrix.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: This material system comprises a thermoset epoxy composite matrix synthesized from Bisphenol-A-diglycidylether and Alkyl (C12-C14) glycidyl ether cured with a Triethylenetetramine hardener. Epoxide-functionalized graphene filler was incorporated at 5.0 wt% via dispersion in DMF followed by high-energy sonication and solvent removal prior to hardener addition. The mixture was cast into a PTFE mold, degassed under vacuum at room temperature, and subjected to a stepwise curing protocol involving 12 hours at 60°C followed by 4 hours at 120°C. Structural characterization indicates a uniform dispersion of the graphene sheets with thicknesses ranging from 1.3 to 3.1 nm, featuring covalent bonding between the filler surface and the epoxy matrix, with Young's modulus subsequently determined via uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 5 mm/min.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of 5.0 wt% epoxide-functionalized graphene serves as a primary reinforcement mechanism due to the exceptionally high intrinsic stiffness of the graphene lattice. The uniform dispersion and nanoscale sheet thickness maximize the surface area available for stress transfer, while the covalent bonding between the filler and matrix ensures efficient load transfer, significantly enhancing the composite modulus. Additionally, the stepwise curing history promotes a high degree of crosslinking within the epoxy-amine network, rigidifying the matrix. Decreasing Factors: The inclusion of Alkyl (C12-C14) glycidyl ether introduces long, flexible aliphatic chains into the network architecture, acting as internal plasticizers that increase chain mobility and reduce overall crosslinking density compared to a pristine system. Furthermore, the solvent casting process involving DMF removal introduces a risk of micro-void formation, and the aliphatic Triethylenetetramine hardener contains flexible ethylene linkages that contribute to segmental mobility relative to rigid aromatic alternatives. Dominant Factor: While the flexible alkyl glycidyl ether and aliphatic hardener segments reduce the intrinsic stiffness of the neat resin, the dominant factor governing the final Young's modulus is the presence of the covalently bonded, uniformly dispersed graphene nanosheets. The efficiency of stress transfer enabled by the covalent interface combined with the high aspect ratio of the filler typically outweighs the softening effects of the reactive diluent, leading to a net enhancement in stiffness relative to the unfilled modified epoxy matrix.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a thermosetting epoxy network synthesized from Bisphenol-A-diglycidylether and Alkyl (C12-C14) glycidyl ether cured with Triethylenetetramine. Epoxide-functionalized graphene was incorporated at 5.0 wt% by dispersing the filler in DMF with the resin via stirring at 500 rpm for 30 minutes and sonication at 40 kHz for 1 hour, followed by solvent removal. The hardener was added at a resin-to-hardener weight ratio of 25/3, and the mixture was stirred, cast into a PTFE mold, and degassed under vacuum at room temperature. Final curing was achieved through a thermal schedule of 12 hours at 60°C followed by 4 hours at 120°C, and the Young's modulus was characterized using uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 5 mm/min.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of 5.0 wt% epoxide-functionalized graphene significantly enhances stiffness due to the high intrinsic modulus of the nanofiller and improved stress transfer at the interface facilitated by chemical functionalization and sonication-assisted dispersion. Additionally, the rigid aromatic rings in the Bisphenol-A-diglycidylether backbone and the high-temperature post-cure at 120°C promote a high crosslink density, restricting segmental motion and increasing structural rigidity. Decreasing Factors: The presence of Alkyl (C12-C14) glycidyl ether introduces long, flexible aliphatic chains into the network, acting as an internal plasticizer that increases free volume and lowers the modulus relative to a pure aromatic epoxy system. Furthermore, the solvent casting process involving DMF removal poses a risk of micro-void formation if residual solvent remains, which could act as defects and reduce the effective load-bearing capacity. Dominant Factor: The reinforcement mechanism provided by the well-dispersed graphene filler combined with the high crosslink density achieved through the elevated temperature cure qualitatively dominates the final mechanical behavior. While the aliphatic diluent introduces flexibility, the high aspect ratio and stiffness of the graphene network within the rigid aromatic matrix establish the primary resistance to deformation, driving the Young's modulus toward higher values characteristic of nanocomposite reinforced thermosets.

title: Cryogenic mechanical behaviors of carbon nanotube reinforced composites based on modified epoxy by poly(ethersulfone)
processing_history: MWCNTs blended with DGEBF via three-roll mill. PES melted at 130 °C, added to blend. Degassed 30 min. Cured 80 °C for 8 h and post-cured 130 °C for 12 h. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test at 2 mm/min crosshead speed, 77 K (liquid nitrogen), according to ASTM D638–96.
hierarchical_structure: MWCNTs dispersed in epoxy matrix. CNT aggregates observed at 1.0 wt%. Cryogenic temperature condition.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: This composite system comprises a Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol-F (DGEBF) epoxy matrix cured with Diethyl toluene diamine (DETDA), modified with 15.0 phr Poly(ethersulfone) (PES) and reinforced with 1.0 wt% Multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs). The manufacturing process involved blending MWCNTs with the epoxy resin using a three-roll mill, followed by the incorporation of melted PES at 130 °C and a 30-minute degassing step. The material was subjected to a curing cycle of 80 °C for 8 hours and a post-cure at 130 °C for 12 hours to establish the crosslinked network. Structural characterization reveals MWCNTs dispersed within the epoxy matrix, although CNT aggregates were observed at the 1.0 wt% loading level. The Young's modulus was determined via uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 2 mm/min under cryogenic conditions (77 K) in compliance with ASTM D638–96.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The rigid aromatic backbones of the DGEBF and DETDA monomers, combined with the high crosslink density achieved through the specified curing and post-curing cycle, create a stiff thermoset network that inherently resists deformation. The incorporation of Multi-walled carbon nanotubes introduces a filler with an exceptionally high intrinsic modulus, which theoretically enhances the composite stiffness through load transfer mechanisms. Furthermore, the testing condition at 77 K places the polymer matrix deep within the glassy regime, freezing segmental chain motion and maximizing the material's resistance to elastic deformation. Decreasing Factors: The observed aggregation of MWCNTs at 1.0 wt% loading reduces the effective aspect ratio and interfacial surface area, limiting stress transfer efficiency and acting as potential stress concentrators that diminish the reinforcement potential. Additionally, the inclusion of 15.0 phr Poly(ethersulfone) introduces a thermoplastic phase which, while high-performance, may possess a lower modulus than the fully cured epoxy network at cryogenic temperatures, potentially diluting the overall stiffness of the composite relative to a neat epoxy system. Dominant Factor: The dominant influence on E is the combination of the highly crosslinked epoxy network and the cryogenic testing temperature, which establishes a maximized baseline stiffness by eliminating viscoelastic relaxation; while the MWCNTs contribute to reinforcement, their effect is qualitatively secondary to the matrix state and is moderated by the observed dispersion limitations.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: This composite material comprises a thermosetting epoxy network formed from Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol-F and Diethyl toluene diamine. Multi-walled carbon nanotubes were initially blended with the epoxy resin using a three-roll mill to ensure dispersion, followed by the addition of melted Poly(ethersulfone) at 130 °C. The mixture was degassed for 30 minutes prior to undergoing a curing cycle of 80 °C for 8 hours and a post-cure at 130 °C for 12 hours. The Young's modulus was subsequently determined via uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 2 mm/min at cryogenic conditions (77 K) in accordance with ASTM D638–96.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The aromatic structures within the Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol-F and Diethyl toluene diamine monomers provide a rigid backbone that restricts chain mobility, inherently raising the modulus. Furthermore, the extended curing and post-curing schedule ensures a high crosslink density, while the testing temperature of 77 K places the polymer deep within the glassy state, significantly maximizing stiffness. Decreasing Factors: The addition of Poly(ethersulfone) as a thermoplastic modifier may introduce phases with lower modulus compared to the highly crosslinked epoxy matrix or reduce the overall crosslink density, potentially lowering the bulk stiffness. Additionally, the methylene bridge in the bisphenol-F structure offers slightly less steric hindrance compared to bisphenol-A analogs, which could marginally reduce rigidity. Dominant Factor: The combined effect of the rigid aromatic thermoset network, the high-modulus nanotube reinforcement, and the cryogenic testing condition qualitatively dominates the potential softening influence of the thermoplastic modifier, resulting in a material formulation driven towards high stiffness.

title: Mechanical Behavior of Natural Fiber-Based Bi-Directional Corrugated Lattice Sandwich Structure
processing_history: Composite prepared by impregnating ultra-dense jute fiber cloth (C) with epoxy resin, placed in corrugated mold, 0.3 MPa pressure, cured at room temperature for 48 h. Cut into strips and assembled. Fiber layup angle (90/90). Thickness 2.0 mm. Young's modulus measured by axial compression test.
hierarchical_structure: Composite strut. Density 1.13 g/cm3.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of a composite strut fabricated from an epoxy resin matrix reinforced with ultra-dense jute fiber cloth. The composite was prepared by impregnating the fiber cloth with the resin and placing it into a corrugated mold under 0.3 MPa pressure, followed by curing at room temperature for 48 hours. The resulting material, having a density of 1.13 g/cm³ and a thickness of 2.0 mm, was cut into strips and assembled with a fiber layup angle of 90/90. The Young's modulus was subsequently characterized via an axial compression test.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of ultra-dense jute fiber cloth into the epoxy matrix introduces stiff cellulosic reinforcements that typically possess a higher modulus than the cured resin, thereby increasing the composite stiffness according to rule-of-mixtures principles. Additionally, the application of 0.3 MPa pressure during molding promotes fiber wetting and consolidation, which minimizes macro-voids and enhances stress transfer between the matrix and fibers. The formation of a crosslinked epoxy network during the 48-hour cure also provides intrinsic rigidity to the matrix phase. Decreasing Factors: The room temperature curing condition likely results in a lower degree of crosslinking conversion compared to thermal curing, reducing the intrinsic modulus of the epoxy matrix. Furthermore, the measured density of 1.13 g/cm³ is relatively low for a jute-epoxy composite, suggesting the presence of significant micro-voids or porosity introduced during impregnation or by the corrugated mold, which acts as stress concentrators and reduces the effective load-bearing area. The 90/90 fiber layup may also result in off-axis loading components during axial compression, lowering the effective modulus compared to a unidirectional alignment. Dominant Factor: While the jute reinforcement provides the primary mechanism for stiffness enhancement relative to neat epoxy, the processing-induced porosity evidenced by the low density and the incomplete network formation from room temperature curing are the dominant factors that qualitatively suppress the final Young's modulus relative to a fully dense, heat-cured composite system.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises an epoxy resin matrix reinforced with ultra-dense jute fiber cloth. The composite was fabricated by impregnating the fiber cloth with the resin, placing it into a corrugated mold under 0.3 MPa pressure, and curing at room temperature for 48 hours. Post-curing, the material was cut into strips and assembled with a 90/90 fiber layup angle to yield a 2.0 mm thick specimen, upon which the Young's modulus was measured using an axial compression test.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The incorporation of ultra-dense jute fiber cloth introduces cellulosic reinforcement which possesses higher intrinsic stiffness than the epoxy matrix, theoretically increasing the composite modulus via the rule of mixtures. Additionally, the crosslinked network formed during the curing of the epoxy resin provides a rigid structural baseline. Decreasing Factors: The room temperature curing process likely results in a lower degree of crosslinking density compared to elevated temperature cures, reducing the stiffness of the matrix phase. Furthermore, the specific fiber layup angle of 90/90 suggests the fibers are oriented transverse to the axial compression load, meaning the measured modulus will rely heavily on the weaker matrix and fiber transverse properties rather than the longitudinal fiber stiffness. The relatively low consolidation pressure of 0.3 MPa may also introduce voids or imperfect interfacial bonding, further diminishing effective stress transfer. Dominant Factor: The geometric alignment of the reinforcement relative to the loading axis is the dominant factor. Despite the high density of the jute cloth, the 90/90 layup orientation during an axial compression test prevents the utilization of the fibers' longitudinal stiffness, causing the mechanical response to be dominated by the softer matrix properties and the incomplete crosslinking from room temperature curing.

title: Tensile properties of Graphene Epoxy Nanocomposite (Sifat Ketegangan Nanokompisit Grafin Epoksi)
processing_history: Graphene added to epoxy, stirred at 500 rpm for 30 minutes. Hardener added (2:1 weight ratio). Mixture stirred at 200 rpm for 15 minutes. Poured into 12 cm plastic mould (1 cm diameter). Cured in fume cupboard for 24 hours at room temperature. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test using Instron Tensile Test Machine with extensometer.
hierarchical_structure: Graphene epoxy nanocomposite. Graphene dispersed in epoxy matrix. Optimum dispersion.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a graphene epoxy nanocomposite synthesized from Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol-A (DGEBA) and Hardener CP 812P at a 2:1 weight ratio. Graphene nanoplatelets were incorporated as a filler at 1.0 wt% and dispersed into the epoxy matrix through mechanical stirring at 500 rpm for 30 minutes, followed by hardener addition and mixing at 200 rpm for 15 minutes. The mixture was cast into a plastic mould and cured at room temperature for 24 hours in a fume cupboard, resulting in a crosslinked network with optimum graphene dispersion. Mechanical characterization was performed via uniaxial tensile testing using an Instron machine equipped with an extensometer to determine the Young's modulus.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a covalently crosslinked thermoset network between the DGEBA epoxy and the hardener significantly restricts chain mobility, establishing a rigid matrix baseline. Furthermore, the incorporation of graphene nanoplatelets, which possess an intrinsically high elastic modulus, acts as a reinforcing phase that enhances stiffness through stress transfer mechanisms, particularly given the reported optimum dispersion which maximizes interfacial interaction. Decreasing Factors: The curing process conducted at room temperature for 24 hours may result in a lower final crosslink density compared to elevated temperature curing cycles, potentially limiting the maximum stiffness of the epoxy matrix. Additionally, the relatively low filler loading of 1.0 wt% limits the volume fraction of the high-modulus phase compared to higher concentration composites. Dominant Factor: The establishment of the crosslinked thermoset network provides the fundamental structural integrity, but the addition of rigid graphene nanoplatelets with optimum dispersion is the dominant factor qualitatively elevating the Young's modulus above that of the neat cured epoxy, despite the potential limitations imposed by the ambient curing conditions.

analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol-A epoxy matrix crosslinked with Hardener CP 812P at a 2:1 weight ratio and reinforced with 1.0 wt% Graphene Nanoplatelets. The composite was fabricated by dispersing the graphene nanoplatelets into the epoxy resin via stirring at 500 rpm for 30 minutes, followed by the addition of the hardener and further mixing at 200 rpm for 15 minutes. The mixture was cast into a plastic mould with a 1 cm diameter and cured in a fume cupboard at room temperature for 24 hours. The Young's modulus was subsequently characterized using a uniaxial tensile test performed on an Instron Tensile Test Machine equipped with an extensometer.
analysis_without_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a covalently crosslinked thermoset network between the epoxy resin and the hardener significantly restricts chain mobility, establishing a rigid matrix baseline. Additionally, the incorporation of Graphene Nanoplatelets introduces a high-modulus filler phase with a large aspect ratio, which enhances stiffness through load transfer mechanisms assuming adequate dispersion. Decreasing Factors: The curing process conducted at room temperature for 24 hours may result in incomplete crosslinking conversion compared to elevated temperature curing protocols, potentially lowering the crosslink density and matrix stiffness. Furthermore, insufficient exfoliation or agglomeration of the graphene nanoplatelets during the stirring process could act as stress concentrators, diminishing the reinforcement efficiency. Dominant Factor: The intrinsic rigidity of the crosslinked epoxy network provides the fundamental structural integrity; however, the reinforcement contribution from the high-stiffness graphene nanoplatelets qualitatively dominates the enhancement of the Young's modulus relative to the neat resin, contingent upon the room temperature cure achieving sufficient conversion to enable effective interfacial stress transfer.

title: Synergistic effect of recycled PET and hyperbranched ionic liquids for toughening epoxy resin
processing_history: PET dissolved in NMP at 120 °C then 160 °C, EP added, NMP removed. MHHPA added, degassed. Cured at 100 °C, 120 °C, and 140 °C for 2 h each. Young's modulus measured by tensile property test.

title: A Study About Some Mechanical Properties for Composites Reinforced with Corn Cob Powder
processing_history: Manual casting technique. Bars with free lengths 100, 120, 140, 160, 180 mm. Embedded at one end. Free vibrations test using Bruel&Kjaer accelerometer and Euler-Bernoulli theory. Dynamic modulus of elasticity determined from free vibrations recording.
hierarchical_structure: Composite material with corn cob powder reinforcement in epoxy matrix. Corn cob brought to powder shape by classic mill.

Specimens were fabricated using a manual casting technique to produce bars with free lengths varying between 100 and 180 mm, which were embedded at one end for mechanical testing. Additionally, the incorporation of corn cob powder at a very high loading of 65% significantly reduces the volume fraction of the polymer matrix, theoretically restricting bulk deformation and increasing the composite stiffness relative to the neat resin. Decreasing Factors: The corn cob powder is a lignocellulosic natural filler which may exhibit lower intrinsic stiffness compared to the cured epoxy matrix or synthetic reinforcements, potentially lowering the overall modulus. Furthermore, the manual casting technique used to process such a high filler concentration often leads to incomplete wetting, particle agglomeration, and entrapped voids, which act as stress concentrators and reduce the effective load-bearing cross-section. Dominant Factor: The high volume fraction of the reinforcement is the primary structural determinant; however, the effectiveness of this loading is qualitatively moderated by the manual processing history, where potential voids and interfacial defects likely limit the full stiffening potential of the composite system.

title: Mechanical properties of SWNT/epoxy composites using two different curing cycles
processing_history: SWNTs dispersed in ethanol with ultrasonic bath, resin added, sonicated and hand-stirred. Hardener added, dispersed. Curing Cycle A: Room temperature for 24 h, post-cured at 60 °C for 4 h. Type 1A specimens produced. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test at 1 mm/s crosshead speed, according to ISO 527-2:1993.
hierarchical_structure: Epoxy matrix reinforced with 0.1 wt% SWNT. SWNTs purified by H2O2 and acid reflux. Fracture surface rough, indicating ductile deformation.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises an epoxy matrix synthesized from Bisphenol A and Epichlorhydrin monomers, crosslinked with IB-72 hardener at a loading of 10 volume parts per 100 parts resin. This thermoset system is reinforced with 0.1 wt% single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWNTs) which were purified via H2O2 and acid reflux prior to incorporation. Fabrication involved dispersing the SWNTs in ethanol using an ultrasonic bath, followed by resin addition, further sonication, and hand-stirring before hardener integration. The material was cured at room temperature for 24 hours and post-cured at 60 °C for 4 hours to form Type 1A specimens. The resulting hierarchical structure consists of an epoxy matrix reinforced with purified SWNTs, exhibiting a rough fracture surface indicative of ductile deformation, with mechanical characterization performed via uniaxial tensile testing at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/s according to ISO 527-2:1993.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The presence of aromatic rings within the Bisphenol A monomer units provides intrinsic backbone rigidity, while the formation of a three-dimensional network via the IB-72 hardener restricts segmental chain mobility, both of which fundamentally increase the Young's modulus. Additionally, the incorporation of single-walled carbon nanotubes introduces a filler with an exceptionally high intrinsic modulus, and the use of ultrasonic dispersion aims to maximize interfacial contact and stress transfer efficiency. Decreasing Factors: The relatively low SWNT loading of 0.1 wt% is likely below the percolation threshold, limiting the reinforcement efficiency relative to the matrix volume. The use of ethanol as a processing solvent introduces the risk of void formation upon evaporation or residual plasticization if not fully removed, which would reduce stiffness. Furthermore, the mild curing cycle (max 60 °C) may result in incomplete crosslink conversion compared to higher temperature cures, leading to a lower crosslink density, and the observed ductile deformation suggests energy dissipation mechanisms that often correlate with reduced stiffness. Dominant Factor: The mechanical response is qualitatively dominated by the properties of the crosslinked epoxy matrix rather than the nanotube reinforcement, due to the low filler loading. However, the final modulus is critically modulated by the processing history, where the mild curing temperature likely limits the maximum achievable crosslink density, and the solvent-based processing introduces potential microstructural defects that prevent the composite from reaching the theoretical stiffness of a fully cured, void-free network.

title: The Synergistic Toughening and Strengthening Effects of Cork Particles and Nanocellulose on Rosin-Based Epoxy Resin
processing_history: Rosin-based epoxy resin synthesized from rosin, acrylic acid (220 C, 4 h), and epichlorohydrin (100 C, 90 min). Cured with methyl hexahydrophthalic anhydride (1:1 mass ratio) and 1 wt% cork particles at 160 C for 2 h then 180 C for 1 h. Young's modulus (MOE) measured by flexural test using Shimadzu AG-10TA universal testing machine at 1 mm/min crosshead speed, 40 mm support span, ASTM D 638.
hierarchical_structure: Crosslinked rosin-based epoxy network with dispersed cork particles.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample comprises a crosslinked rosin-based epoxy network containing dispersed cork particles, synthesized from rosin, acrylic acid, and epichlorohydrin. The formulation incorporates methyl hexahydrophthalic anhydride as a crosslinker at a 1:1 mass ratio relative to the resin and 1 wt% cork particles as a filler. Processing involved resin synthesis at 220 °C for 4 hours and 100 °C for 90 minutes, followed by curing at 160 °C for 2 hours and 180 °C for 1 hour. title: Three dimensional orientation angle distribution counting and calculation for the mechanical properties of aligned carbon nanotube/epoxy composites
processing_history: Aligned CNT sheets drawn from vertically aligned MWNT forests. Epoxy resin film impregnated into CNT sheet at 90 °C for 3 min. Cured at 130 °C, 2.0 MPa for 1.5 h using hot press. Note: Resin was not impregnated adequately. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test on Instron 5966 at 0.2 mm/min crosshead speed, room temperature, using video extensometer.
hierarchical_structure: Aligned CNT/epoxy composite. CNT volume fraction 42.3%. CNT-rich region and inadequate molding region observed.

Multi-walled carbon nanotubes were incorporated at a volume fraction of 42.3% via impregnation of an epoxy resin film into aligned CNT sheets drawn from vertically aligned MWNT forests at 90 °C, followed by hot press curing at 130 °C and 2.0 MPa for 1.5 hours. Structural analysis indicates an aligned morphology featuring CNT-rich regions and areas of inadequate molding attributed to insufficient resin impregnation. The Young's modulus was characterized via uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature using a video extensometer at a crosshead speed of 0.2 mm/min.

Decreasing Factors: The processing history notes inadequate resin impregnation, resulting in voids and CNT-rich regions where the matrix is insufficient to effectively transfer stress between nanotubes. title: Bio-based epoxy resins with low molecular weight kraft lignin and pyrogallol
processing_history: Resin C (1+2+L). nOH/nEpoxy ratio 130%. Components dissolved in acetone, solvent distilled off. Cured for 2 h at 80°C and 3 h at 160°C. Young's modulus measured by uniaxial tensile test according to DIN EN ISO 527 using Zwick 020 universal testing machine.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: This material system comprises a thermosetting epoxy network synthesized from 1,3-glycerol diglycidyl ether (58.76 wt%) and pyrogallol (15.98 wt%), reinforced with a low molecular weight fraction of Kraft lignin (25.26 wt%) and catalyzed by imidazole. The precursor components were dissolved in acetone followed by solvent distillation, then subjected to a step-curing protocol involving 2 hours at 80°C and 3 hours at 160°C to establish a highly cross-linked structure where the lignin actively participates in the polymer network formation. Mechanical characterization was performed via uniaxial tensile testing according to DIN EN ISO 527 standards, revealing a heterogeneous network architecture where the modulus fluctuates around an average value.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a highly cross-linked thermoset network between the epoxy groups of 1,3-glycerol diglycidyl ether and the hydroxyl groups of pyrogallol creates a rigid backbone that significantly enhances stiffness. The incorporation of Kraft lignin, which contains rigid aromatic rings and participates chemically in the network formation rather than acting as a passive filler, further restricts chain segment mobility and increases the effective cross-link density. Additionally, the high-temperature curing stage at 160°C promotes high conversion rates, minimizing uncured regions and maximizing the network rigidity. Decreasing Factors: The off-stoichiometric formulation with an nOH/nEpoxy ratio of 130% implies an excess of hydroxyl groups, which may result in unreacted chain ends or dangling chains that reduce the overall cross-link density compared to a stoichiometric balance. The inherent heterogeneity of the low molecular weight lignin fraction introduces structural irregularities, evidenced by the fluctuating modulus, which can act as stress concentrators or regions of lower local stiffness. Furthermore, despite solvent distillation, any residual acetone could act as a plasticizer, though this is less likely given the thermal history. Dominant Factor: The dominant factor governing the Young's modulus is the high cross-link density achieved through the epoxy-pyrogallol reaction reinforced by the chemically bonded rigid lignin domains. While the off-stoichiometry and lignin heterogeneity introduce defects that prevent the modulus from reaching the theoretical maximum of a pristine epoxy network, the intrinsic rigidity of the aromatic-rich, highly cross-linked thermoset structure qualitatively dictates a high stiffness relative to uncured or linear polymer systems.

title: Investigation of mechanical, thermal and electrical properties of hybrid composites reinforced with multi‑walled carbon nanotubes and fused silica particles
processing_history: Air entrapped in epoxy resin released using vacuum desiccator with BYK-A 500 for 2 h. Processing involved vacuum desiccation to release entrapped air, followed by dispersion of the fillers via shear mixing and ultrasonic bath treatment. Furthermore, the post-cure at 80 °C enhances the crosslinking density of the epoxy network, restricting segmental motion and increasing stiffness. title: Unraveling Nanoscale Elastic and Adhesive Properties at the Nanoparticle/Epoxy Interface Using Bimodal Atomic Force Microscopy
processing_history: Monomers mixed at 1:2 molar ratio (HDGEBA:CBMA). Cured at 373 K for ~24 h. Surface smoothed by microtome sectioning at 193 K. Elastic modulus measured by bimodal AM-FM AFM (Cypher S AFM) at room temperature (~296 K) using AC200TS probes in repulsive regime.
hierarchical_structure: Amorphous and highly cross-linked network. Heterogeneous nanostructures with correlation length of 12 ± 1 nm.

title: Characterization of tensile property of high-performance fiber bundles combined with epoxy resin using advanced video extensometer

Decreasing Factors: The epoxy matrix itself possesses a significantly lower modulus than the reinforcement, and its compliance contributes to the overall deformation, particularly if the fiber volume fraction is not maximized. The specific mass ratio of the curing agent may influence the crosslink density, where deviations from optimal stoichiometry could result in a less rigid network or residual unreacted agents that plasticize the matrix. Any voids formed during the impregnation process would also diminish the effective load-bearing cross-section and reduce the measured modulus. Dominant Factor: The high stiffness of the T800HB carbon fiber reinforcement is the dominant factor governing the Young's modulus. In unidirectional fiber-reinforced composites, the longitudinal modulus is primarily dictated by the fiber properties and volume fraction according to the rule of mixtures, overshadowing the contributions of the matrix modulus or specific curing nuances provided that a functional interface is established.

title: Ultrasonic Velocity and Attenuation in Epoxy Resin/Granite (Marble) Powder Composite

title: High mechanical properties of epoxy networks with dangling chains and tunable microphase separation structure

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of a crosslinked epoxy network synthesized from Bisphenol F diglycidyl ether resin cured with a binary mixture of aromatic 4,4'-diaminodiphenylmethane and cycloaliphatic 4,4'-diaminodicyclohexylmethane curing agents at a 55/45 molar ratio relative to the amine component. The preparation involved stirring the components for 10 minutes followed by a multi-step thermal curing schedule comprising stages at 60 °C for 2 hours, 100 °C for 2 hours, 130 °C for 2 hours, and finally 150 °C for 4 hours to ensure complete crosslinking. Furthermore, the rigorous multi-step thermal curing history culminating at 150 °C promotes high conversion of epoxy groups, leading to a high crosslink density that severely limits chain mobility and enhances stiffness. The homogeneous amorphous structure ensures efficient stress transfer throughout the network without weak interphase boundaries. Decreasing Factors: The incorporation of 4,4'-diaminodicyclohexylmethane introduces cycloaliphatic rings into the network nodes; unlike aromatic rings, these saturated rings possess greater conformational freedom, which introduces a degree of flexibility that qualitatively lowers the modulus compared to a fully aromatic amine system. Additionally, the Bisphenol F backbone lacks the methyl pendant group found in Bisphenol A analogs, potentially allowing for slightly easier segmental rotation. Dominant Factor: The high crosslink density achieved through the extended high-temperature curing schedule, combined with the predominant aromatic character of the resin and the majority curing agent, qualitatively dominates the mechanical response. While the cycloaliphatic component introduces some flexibility, the overall network rigidity driven by the dense crosslinking and aromatic backbone structure dictates a high Young's Modulus for this specific sample.

title: Multiscale molecular modeling of SWCNTs/epoxy resin composites mechanical behaviour
processing_history: Computational modeling using Materials Studio 5.0 with COMPASS forcefield. Atomistic periodic systems built with periodic boundary conditions. Multistage equilibration: energy minimization (Steepest descent, Conjugate gradient), NVT-MD (300,000 steps, 1 fs), NPT-MD (1 GPa, 300 K, 5000 steps), annealing (750 K to 300 K). Young's modulus calculated using Discover Analysis tool via virtual uniaxial traction tests along x, y, z directions, averaged.
hierarchical_structure: Amorphous epoxy matrix with dispersed SWCNTs (10,10). Computational bulk models.

analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.descriptive_text: The sample consists of an amorphous epoxy matrix formed by the crosslinking of Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A and Ethylene tetra-amine, reinforced with 9.0 wt% (10,10) single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs). This system was modeled computationally using Materials Studio 5.0 with the COMPASS forcefield, constructing atomistic periodic systems under periodic boundary conditions. The processing history involves a multistage equilibration protocol comprising energy minimization via steepest descent and conjugate gradient methods, followed by NVT and NPT molecular dynamics simulations, and a thermal annealing cycle from 750 K down to 300 K. The Young's modulus was subsequently determined using the Discover Analysis tool through virtual uniaxial traction tests averaged along the x, y, and z directions within the computational bulk models.
analysis_with_hierarchical_structure.reasoning_analysis: Increasing Factors: The formation of a covalently crosslinked network between the epoxy resin and the amine curing agent restricts segmental chain mobility, enhancing stiffness relative to linear polymer precursors. Furthermore, the computational processing history employs a rigorous multistage equilibration and annealing protocol from 750 K to 300 K, ensuring a well-relaxed, dense atomic packing that minimizes free volume artifacts and maximizes the predicted stiffness. Decreasing Factors: The selection of Ethylene tetra-amine as the curing agent introduces flexible aliphatic segments into the crosslink nodes, which reduces the network rigidity compared to systems utilizing aromatic curing agents. Additionally, non-bonded interactions at the SWCNT-matrix interface within the computational model may allow for slight interfacial compliance compared to perfect covalent bonding, potentially limiting the full theoretical reinforcement efficiency. Dominant Factor: The reinforcement effect of the SWCNTs is the dominant factor governing the mechanical behavior. While the flexible curing agent and amorphous matrix establish a moderate baseline stiffness for the epoxy network, the exceptional mechanical properties of the carbon nanotubes at 9.0 wt% loading overwhelmingly dictate the composite's response, leading to a substantial qualitative increase in Young's modulus relative to the neat epoxy system.

title: Effects of fibre loading and moisture absorption on the tensile properties of hybrid Napier/glass/epoxy composites
processing_history: Vacuum infusion method at ~10 mbar. Cured 12h at 25 °C, post-cured 2h at 80 °C. Tensile test (ASTM D638-10) using Instron universal testing machine, 100 kN load cell, 1 mm/min crosshead speed, 50 mm gauge length. Dry condition.

Fabrication was achieved via vacuum infusion at approximately 10 mbar, followed by a curing cycle of 12 hours at 25 °C and a post-cure treatment of 2 hours at 80 °C. Mechanical properties were evaluated under dry conditions using tensile testing according to ASTM D638-10 standards on an Instron universal testing machine with a 100 kN load cell, 1 mm/min crosshead speed, and 50 mm gauge length.

Testing under dry conditions further prevents moisture-induced plasticization of the natural fibres and matrix, maintaining higher stiffness. title: Properties of Epoxy Networks Derived from the Reaction of Diglycidyl Ether of Bisphenol A with Polyhedral Oligomeric Silsesquioxanes Bearing OH-Functionalized Organic Substituents

processing_history: DGEBA mixed with CTBN using mechanical stirrer at room temperature, vacuum 4 h. 5 phr piperidine added, stirred 10 min.
